We propose a minimal model which reproduces the distribution of temporal correlations of the many-body system, suggesting a general description of the time liquid as a time crystal with a finite density of time-solitons. Because these solitons can occur at arbitrary times, ensemble averaging restores continuous time-translation symmetry, raising the intriguing possibility that discrete time liquids can exist in thermal equilibrium.
authors: Zuo Wang; Paul M. Schindler; Marin Bukov; Marios H. Michael

title: Symmetry-Preserving and Scalable Variational Circuits for the Lattice Gross-Neveu Model
abstract: We study variational preparation of ground states and sector-resolved excited states in the $(1+1)$-dimensional lattice Gross-Neveu model. We construct fixed circuits preserving either total fermion number or every flavor number, and a problem-specific scalable-circuit adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (SC-ADAPT-VQE). Classical circuit benchmarks cover massless and massive systems through 30 qubits, using exact-diagonalization and tensor-network reference results. Imposing flavor-number conservation improves the achieved energies in the completed two-flavor comparisons. Selected massive fixed-ansatz benchmarks with one to four flavors have relative energy errors of approximately $1 \times 10^{-5}$ - $2 \times 10^{-4}$, smaller than the quoted literature errors where available, although discretizations and computational resources differ. The adaptive pool combines translated bulk and boundary-sensitive generators with an interaction-sensitive cross-flavor family. Selected massive SC-ADAPT benchmarks with one to three flavors have relative energy errors below $2.1 \times 10^{-3}$. For one flavor, matrix-product-state evaluations extend the transferred circuits to 60-400 qubits without target-side operator selection or parameter optimization, giving energy deviations of approximately $0.35\%$ - $1.76\%$ from density-matrix renormalization-group reference values at maximum bond dimension 256. At fixed flavor number, range caps, and append count, the adaptive construction has a precompilation local-factor count linear in volume and a volume-independent shared-parameter count; fixed-accuracy performance at arbitrary volumes remains unestablished. Sequential deflation also prepares low-lying states within a fixed flavor-number sector, with projector fidelities providing a basis-independent assessment of degenerate target eigenspaces.
authors: Vivan Bhatt; Zhongtian Dong; Kyoungchul Kong; Kwangmin Yu

title: Transversal syndrome extraction: A unifying construction for measuring the error syndromes of any stabilizer code
abstract: Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction is fundamental to stabilizer-code-based quantum error correction, yet existing general protocols incur substantial costs in either circuit depth or width. In this work, we design ancilla stabilizer states for a general transversal circuit to construct a family of fault-tolerant syndrome-extraction gadgets that interpolate between Shor and Steane syndrome extraction for any stabilizer code. The result is a configurable trade-off between circuit depth and width.
authors: Miles D. Gorman

title: Pure states are optimal for total energy-constrained quantum channel discrimination
abstract: We consider the discrimination of two quantum channels acting on bosonic modes, with a probe state of fixed mean photon number and no ancilla. We prove that pure probes are optimal: for every mixed probe there is a pure probe with exactly the same mean photon number that performs at least as well. The result holds for arbitrary channels and for every figure of merit built from the Chernoff quantities $\Tr[ρ_1^sρ_2^{1-s}]$, including the quantum Chernoff exponent, as well as for the single-shot error probability. The proof relies on a decomposition of any state of mean photon number $\nb$ into pure states of mean photon number exactly $\nb$, which extends a matrix rank-one decomposition of Huang and Zhang to density operators of infinite rank.
authors: Christos N. Gagatsos

title: Non-adiabatic Optimisation via Localisation-Delocalisation Transitions
abstract: The promise of efficiently solving classical optimisation problems on quantum computers is tantalizing. As many such problems can be mapped to approximating the ground state of spin-glasses, paradigmatic models for studying many-body localisation, it is natural to ask if some of the intuition coming from quantum statistical mechanics can help guide the construction of novel quantum optimisation algorithms. In this work, we discuss how continuous reverse quantum annealing crossing a many-body localisation transition can be accelerated by considering the density of Landau-Zener crossings as the system is quenched. We provide an interpretation of this behaviour in terms of an effective Fokker-Planck equation for the success probability of the algorithm. This interpretation suggests an improvement in the required annealing time as a function of the system size $N$, which goes from $\mathcal{O}({\rm poly}(N))$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for reference states with non-vanishing energy density. We show that the continuous dynamics can be Trotterised with a number of steps that remains modest as system size increases, making it appealing for near-term devices. For the resulting circuit implementation, we provide a quantitative strategy for determining the parameters of the time-dependent Hamiltonian. We compare the performance of our digitised algorithm, which we call FRIO, against that of the QAOA for finding the ground state of spin-glass problems, in particular the SK model. The numerical results suggest that with suitably selected circuit parameters which can be efficiently found using thermalizing dynamics, FRIO almost always outperforms the conventional QAOA ansatz with pre-optimized angles.
authors: Ryan Smith; Sabrina Yue Wang; Filippo Maria Gambetta; Raul A. Santos

title: Dealing with low-weight errors that lead BP OSD to fail
abstract: Belief Propagation combined with Ordered Statistics Decoding (BP OSD) is an open-source decoding tool used widely within the community due to its versatility and ease of application to Quantum Low Density Parity Check (QLDPC) codes. However, the degeneracy of quantum codes has been observed to degrade the performance of BP OSD, particularly leading to error floors for low physical error rates. Here, we investigate the low-weight error configurations responsible for such failures in Bivariate Bicycle codes. We show that, at code capacity, BP OSD fails on errors whose weight is significantly smaller than d/2, arising from global symmetries of the decoding graph that prevent the convergence of parallel BP. Furthermore, our analysis reveals new pitfalls that can arise when analysing the performance of BP OSD in the rare events regime, such as loss of ergodicity in splitting methods and numerical instabilities in the decoder. We show how to mitigate these failure mechanisms by modifying the BP update rules and the decoder implementation, leading to substantial improvement in logical error rate.
authors: Giacomo Fregona; Matthias C. Löbl; Benjamin J. Brown; Michael J. Kastoryano; Stefano Paesani

title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation
abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.
authors: Filipa C. R. Peres; Selman Ipek; Daniel Lovsted; Joshua Nevin; Anne Broadbent

title: Extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity in the hole-doped Hubbard model
abstract: The two-dimensional Hubbard model was originally proposed as the minimal model of uniform $d$-wave superconductivity in the cuprate high-temperature superconductors, but recent calculations with relevant parameters in a realistic doping regime have often found other ground states. Further, uncertainty remains over such results due to the intrinsic bias of different computational methods. Here we address this uncertainty through state-of-the-art neural tensor network and neural backflow state simulations, enabled by large-scale GPU computation, that together reach an unprecedented variational accuracy on lattices with up to 1024 sites. At $1/8$ doping in the pure Hubbard model, as well as with next-nearest-neighbor hopping relevant to the hole-doped cuprates, we reveal a near degeneracy among a low-energy uniform $d$-wave state, superconducting stripes, and non-superconducting stripe states on the milli-$t$ energy scale. Our work rebalances the narrative that the Hubbard model supports a single dominant order in relevant parameter regimes towards a picture of extreme competition between stripes and superconductivity.
authors: Ao Chen; Johnnie Gray; Si-Jing Du; Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

title: Delta-Doped GeV$^-$ in diamond with isotope resolvable optical spectra
abstract: Group IV color centers in diamond -- silicon, germanium, tin, and lead-vacancy centers -- are a promising platform for quantum networking. Typical Group-IV creation utilizes ion implantation during diamond growth that leaves the color centers with a broad depth distribution and damage-induced strain inhomogeneity. Deterministic placement and damage reduction in Group IV generation are essential for improving this platform. In this letter, we report on the localization of germanium-vacancy (GeV$^-$) to a $<$ 10 nm layer via the timed injection of GeH$_4$ during microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition. In this layer we have realized 17 ppm of Ge and a strain-free environment for the GeV$^-$. Subsequent electron irradiation and annealing have generated a sheet density of 0.12 GeV$^-$/$μ$m$^2$. The minimal damage from color center generation mitigates spectral inhomogeneity and allows spectral resolution of isotopic clusters, with the best cluster having an inhomogeneous distribution of 2.14 GHz and an average linewidth of $47 \pm 11$ MHz. Our study gives insight into formation dynamics of GeV$^-$ in delta-doped systems and estimates our vacancy to GeV$^-$ yield to be $\geq$ 90%, establishing an athermal nearest-neighbor formation model. We further characterized the spin $T_2^*$ and set a lower bound of 730 ns, limited by a paramagnetic defect.
authors: Ian N. Hammock; Kinfung Ngan; Antoni W. Wellisz; Keira Linder; Midrel Wilfried Ngandeu Ngambou; Jiefei Zhang; Xinghan Guo; Benjamin Pingault; Shuo Sun; David D. Awschalom; F. Joseph Heremans; Alexander A. High; Nazar Delegan

title: Memory--Transport Competition in Physical Two-Bath Quantum Reset Dynamics
abstract: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenuators, for which complete positivity and fermionic admissibility hold by construction. Physical attenuation necessarily modifies bath populations as well as cross correlations; the coherence control is not an independent hard-reset knob. Quadratic dynamics reduces the stroboscopic problem to an exact matrix fixed-point equation without a weak-coupling or Markov approximation. Analytically, coherence retention enhances the leading short-cycle transfer rate, including the complete-erasure limit; no general endpoint-vanishing theorem exists. An exact stationary continuity theorem forces the through-current to vanish whenever either reservoir is left entirely unrefreshed, although no analogous theorem suppresses it at complete erasure. For biased structured reservoirs, exact finite-chain calculations display distinct coherence-, current-, and signed energy-transfer operating points; a resolved high-retention boundary layer exposes strong finite-size sensitivity of the coherence peak. The model provides a microscopic, fermion-admissible benchmark for the interplay of reservoir coherence, particle transport, and energetic exchange.
authors: Jishad Kumar; Achilleas Lazarides; Tapio Ala-Nissila

title: Distributed dual-comb spectroscopy
abstract: We propose distributed dual-comb spectroscopy, a quantum-enhanced sensing architecture that simultaneously exploits spatial- and spectral-domain entanglement to improve the extraction of global spectroscopic information across broadband frequency ranges. Our scheme consists of a network of Mach-Zehnder interferometers interrogating spatially separated samples, each driven by a classical frequency comb at the bright port. A single two-mode squeezed frequency comb is distributed through a passive beam-splitter array into $K$ entangled combs, establishing multipartite correlations across sensors while preserving intrinsic spectral entanglement. The protocol is compatible with both heterodyne detection and division detection, and enables parallel estimation of weighted-average absorption features over multiple frequency components. Compared with spatially separable quantum strategies requiring $K$ independently engineered nonclassical comb sources, our approach achieves enhanced signal-to-noise performance using only a single quantum resource distributed across the network. These results establish a scalable route toward broadband distributed quantum spectroscopy with simultaneous spatial and spectral advantage.
authors: Haowei Shi; Kartikeya Arora; Zheshen Zhang; Quntao Zhuang

title: Photon localization: Local measurements, localized states, and causality
abstract: We review what it means for a relativistic particle to be localized and argue that the most useful approach is through local measurement. This perspective ties localization directly to relativistic causality and measurable outcomes in spacetime. Strict localization in quantum field theory is formalized by states that give the same expectation value as vacuum for all local observables outside some spacetime region. With this formalism, single photons cannot be strictly localized, but coherent states can. The structure and interpretation of local observables and local operator algebras are discussed in connection with the Reeh-Schlieder theorem. Since probabilities of local measurement outcomes cannot vanish in vacuum, particle detection events must be phrased carefully. Key characteristics of strictly localized states are surveyed alongside concrete strategies for constructing them. The relationship between localization, causality, and on-demand sources is analyzed, finding that strictly localized states can represent localized, propagating information in quantum field theory. Explicit examples of localized photonic states are presented with an emphasis on quantum optics, including states that approximate single photons and (entangled) Bell states.
authors: Jan Gulla; Johannes Skaar

title: The Pre-Optimization Structure of QAOA: Polynomial Equivalence of Average and Optimal Probabilities
abstract: We develop a theoretical framework connecting problem structure and variational parameter optimization in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). We derive a general bound on how much variational optimization can improve the probability of measuring configurations in arbitrary subsets of computational basis states, relating the maximum probability to its average over variational parameters. For NPO-PB problems at constant depth and with polynomially many distinct mixer eigenvalues, optimization improves the average probability by at most a polynomial factor. This raises the question: to what extent is variational optimization necessary for sampling desirable solutions? Under suitable efficiency assumptions, randomly parameterized QAOA can achieve cumulative success probabilities comparable to variationally trained QAOA, with only polynomial overhead in circuit executions. In particular, under these conditions, efficient sampling of desirable solutions can be achieved without variational training whenever variationally optimized QAOA achieves inverse-polynomial success probability. Beyond its algorithmic implications, the mean--max bound reveals that, under polynomial mean--max proximity, a pre-optimization structural layer determines the asymptotic scaling of optimal measurement probabilities up to polynomial factors. For single-layer QAOA initialized in a uniform superposition, we explicitly characterize this layer for the measurement probability of a reference state using an exact expression for the average probability that captures the interplay between problem structure and mixer dynamics through the overlap of a problem structure matrix and a mixer-dependent matrix. We derive a mixer-dependent capacity bound and identify cancellations between constructive and destructive contributions as a mechanism for additional superpolynomial suppression relative to this capacity.
authors: Guilherme Adamatti Bridi; Franklin de Lima Marquezino; Andris Ambainis

title: Finite-width altermagnetic quantum rings: angular-channel hybridization and Aharonov--Bohm physics
abstract: We study a finite-width two-dimensional quantum ring with a quadratic $d$-wave altermagnetic term, Tan--Inkson confinement, a perpendicular magnetic field, and independently tunable Aharonov--Bohm (AB) flux. The altermagnetic interaction mixes $m$ and $m\pm2$ angular channels while preserving their parity. Circular symmetry renders the crystal orientation spectrally irrelevant and makes the two spin blocks exactly isospectral. The resulting same-parity anticrossings are resolved at low filling, and multichannel mixing is found near the Fermi level of highly occupied rings. Independent converged calculations for $N_e=1400$ and $1800$ establish the reconstructed Fermi edge and magnetic response in a finite field window and the persistent current over a full AB flux period. The analytic conventional reference separates radial-subband depopulation (dHvA-type cycles) from finer finite-ring shell oscillations; we do not assign a global Fourier spectrum to unverified altermagnetic field scans. The few-electron thermal response is obtained from an exact fixed-particle-number canonical partition function, avoiding finite-system errors of a fixed-mean-number approximation. The circular model supports an equilibrium charge current but no persistent spin current.
authors: Edilberto O. Silva

title: Probing quasiperiodic spectral accessibility with a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle
abstract: Quasiperiodic systems combine sharply different spectral and localisation regimes with a dense hierarchy of dynamical time scales. We show that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can use this structure as a thermodynamic probe, revealing which parts of the spectrum become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant during a driven transformation. For a generalised Aubry-André-Harper chain, the resulting response is not determined by the static quasiperiodic regime alone: extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols do not exhibit universal ordering of work fluctuations. Instead, the statistics reflect transition pathways that are simultaneously dynamically coupled, thermally occupied, and energetically significant. The same spectral accessibility separates thermodynamic recovery from microscopic adiabatic recovery. Positive mean work can reappear while the population transfer dynamics remain strongly nonadiabatic because finite-rate population transfer is redistributed toward energetically less costly channels rather than suppressed. The full work distribution reveals a further separation, with a finite rate window in which positive-work cycles form a majority although the mean work remains negative. This behaviour persists in finite-size analysis. A thermally weighted spectral susceptibility connects these effects to a distributed hierarchy of dynamically active spectral regions rather than to a single minimum-gap bottleneck. Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture while introducing a second time scale and intercycle memory. Quantum Otto cycles can therefore provide a fluctuation-resolved thermodynamic probe of quasiperiodic spectral accessibility, complementary to direct spectroscopic and eigenstate-resolved diagnostics.
authors: Shujie Cheng; Lucas C. Céleri; Norton G. de Almeida; Gao Xianlong; G. D. de Moraes Neto

title: Cluster property and entanglement in the superconducting state
abstract: We present the conditions for satisfying the cluster property in the superconducting state. Using these conditions, we show that the cluster property employed when deriving the order parameter of the superconducting state (OPSS) holds true, and that the OPSS is given by ${}_S\langle Ψ| \hatψ(x)\hatψ(x') | Ψ\rangle_S$, where $|Ψ\rangle_S$ is the superconducting state, and where $\hatψ(x)$ is the field operator of superconducting electrons. This provides a resolution to the long-standing concern raised by Leggett et al.\ regarding particle-number fluctuation in the superconducting state. In addition, by considering the entanglement between two particles composed of the maximum geminal of the BCS ground state [J.\ Phys. Commun. 5, 095003 (2021)], it is confirmed that the larger the deviation from the conditions for satisfying the cluster property becomes, the greater the magnitude of the entanglement becomes. This shows not only the effectiveness of the conditions for satisfying the cluster property but also the justification of the OPSS that has been commonly used.
authors: Katsuhiko Higuchi; Masahiko Higuchi

title: Hierarchical Reduction of Invariant Subspaces: From Fragmentation to Many-Body Scars
abstract: We investigate a hierarchy of invariant Hilbert-space structures connecting Hilbert-space fragmentation, partial solvability, and quantum many-body scars. For spin chains with fragmented spin-$1/2$ subspaces and their local deformations, we show, using the spin-$1$ $XXC$ chain as a representative example, how successive local deformations reduce extensive irreducible-string fragmentation through an implicitly embedded spin-$1/2$ invariant space and ultimately to a single scar tower, connecting the $XXC$, perturbed $XXC$, and spin-$1$ $XY$ scar models. Through the intermediate embedded space, local dynamics couples states from distinct frozen irreducible-string sectors and selects a new decomposition into representations, from which smaller invariant spaces can be retained. We also establish a rigidity constraint on isolating nonsymmetric towers and a constructive correspondence that transfers a reduction between locally realizable representations of the embedded dynamics. The latter demonstrates that the reduction hierarchy can be transferred through a unitary transformation within the embedded subspace, yielding an exact scar tower built on a Néel reference state without requiring unitary equivalence of the full Hamiltonians.
authors: Chihiro Matsui

title: Mode-Selective Micromotion Compensation via Coherent Excitation of a Ground-State-Cooled Motional Mode
abstract: Excess micromotion induced by stray DC electric fields limits the control fidelity of trapped-ion experiments. Various techniques have been developed to detect and compensate ion displacements from the RF null by monitoring modulated fluorescence, ion positions, or micromotion sidebands. Although these approaches are effective, they do not probe the displacement through a ground-state-cooled motional mode and therefore offer limited compatibility with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols. Here, we demonstrate a micromotion compensation method based on the driven coherent amplitude of a ground-state-cooled motional mode. In this approach, the ion displacement is converted into a coherent motional excitation by an auxiliary RF drive and detected through the qubit. We determine the optimal compensation field with a $1σ$ statistical uncertainty of 8 mV/m. The method is naturally compatible with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols employing nonclassical motional states, including Fock, squeezed, and Schrödinger-cat states, providing a pathway toward quantum-enhanced micromotion compensation.
authors: Tetsu Kinase; Ippei Nakamura; Atsushi Noguchi

title: On the Structure of Quantum Finite-Level Systems: Decoherence-Free Subsystems, Quantum Nondemolition Variables, and Back-Action-Evading Measurements
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive structural analysis of quantum finite-level systems in the Heisenberg picture, where the evolution of system observables is modeled by bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). Firstly, real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation and anticommutation relations are characterized, and relative admissibility between different orthonormal Hermitian bases is formulated. Secondly, strongly aligned subspaces are introduced, based on which decoherence-free subsystems (DFSs) are constructed in general orthonormal Hermitian basis as well as the generalized Gell-Mann basis. Thirdly, conditions for the existence of quantum nondemolition (QND) variables are given in terms of both linear systems theory and spectral separation by output-signal observables. Finally, a sufficient condition for quantum back-action-evading (BAE) measurements is established. A four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain with collective dephasing illustrates these structural properties of quantum finite-level systems.
authors: Jia Gu; Guofeng Zhang; Ian R. Petersen

title: Coherence and imaginarity of qubit states under vanishing Bargmann invariants
abstract: Set coherence and set imaginarity are two important quantum resources defined by sets of states. We investigate tuples of qubit states under vanishing higher-order Bargmann invariants and show that their set coherence and set imaginarity are each related to whether they contain a pair of orthogonal states. Specifically, when the relevant higher-order Bargmann invariants vanish, the tuple contains a pair of orthogonal states if and only if removing some state makes the remaining tuple incoherent. Moreover, when maximally mixed states are excluded, the same vanishing conditions imply that the tuple is imaginarity-free if and only if it contains a pair of orthogonal states. As a consequence, under these conditions, a tuple of single-qubit states has imaginarity precisely when every tuple obtained by deleting one of its states is coherent.
authors: Hao-Fan Wang; Lin Chen

title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
authors: Ruixuan Deng; Zhengfeng Ji; Jiayu Zhang; Li Zhou

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
abstract: In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
authors: Chia-Hsien Huang; Hsi-Sheng Goan

title: Time-reversal-based quantum metrology in a central-spin architecture: from SATIN to butterfly echo
abstract: We investigate quantum-enhanced time-reversal-based metrology using the central spin model, in which a single ancilla spin of magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ mediates interactions between $N$ bath spins through a star-graph topology. We demonstrate that the SATIN (Signal Amplification Through Time-reversal Interaction) echo protocol can be implemented in this setup to achieve a Fisher information of $N^2/e$ with the collective $\langle J_y\rangle$ readout, corresponding to a $4.34\,\mathrm{dB}$ offset from the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we establish that this platform provides a pathway to perform the butterfly echo protocol by conjugating each evolution step with a random collective bath rotation, thereby achieving axis-agnostic Heisenberg-scaled sensing. Crucially, with a small $N-$independent number of random steps, the butterfly echo reaches a Fisher information of $N^2/4$ ($6\,\mathrm{dB}$ below the Heisenberg limit) for any unknown encoding axis, with the plateau gain tracking the Haar limit. Finally, we demonstrate that the central-spin magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ provides a powerful knob to reduce the optimal protocol timescale without altering the metrological ceiling or the circuit depth required to reach isotropy. The proposed scheme is relevant to cavity QED and NMR quantum processors, where the central spin architecture arises naturally.
authors: Aditya Kumar; Sayan Choudhury

title: Demand-Driven Routing Space for Lattice-Surgery Compilation
abstract: Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.
authors: Hanyu Wang; Wan-Hsuan Lin; Zihan Chen; Eddy Z. Zhang; Jason Cong

title: A simple proof of unitary parallelization via port-based teleportation
abstract: Port-based teleportation (PBT) is a variant of quantum teleportation that does not require corrections on the teleported state: starting with $N$ shared EPR states, Alice can teleport a qudit to Bob by performing a measurement on her system and informing Bob which of his $N$ `ports' to retrieve the state, up to infidelity decaying with $N$. Existing efficient quantum circuits of PBT rely on representation theory tools such as the Schur transform. In this note, we report an elementary efficient circuit for PBT, which has depth $\operatorname{polylog}(N,d)$. As a corollary, this gives a simple proof that all $n$-qubit unitaries can be parallelized to $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ depth, recovering a recent result due to Nehoran--Slote--Yuen and OpenAI.
authors: Anurag Anshu; Quynh T. Nguyen

title: Exceptional point structure and chiral state transfer in a rate-operator-engineered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Bose-Hubbard dimer
abstract: The rate operator quantum jumps (ROQJ) is a general method to unravel a master equation describing the dynamics of an open quantum system into stochastic pure state trajectories. By post-selecting on no jumps occurring, one obtains a trajectory generated by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The ROQJ allows for versatile modification of this non-Hermitian evolution, with each non-Hermitian Hamiltonian corresponding to a different continuous measurement scheme. We apply the ROQJ to modify the non-Hermitian dynamics of the open three-particle Bose-Hubbard dimer model under environmental non-local dephasing to construct a $PT$-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with a general two parameter $PT$-symmetric imaginary diagonal part, which generalizes the well-known gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. We characterize the symmetry structure of the spectrum for different on-site interaction strengths. For vanishing on-site interaction, we find the unbroken $PT$-symmetry region enclosed by order two exceptional lines of different character and four order four exceptional points, two of which are not found in the usual gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. Additionally, we find regions with degenerate imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, also not found in the gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. In this parameter space, we use time-dependent rate operator transformations to investigate state transfer under slowly varying parameter loops. Loops encircling an order four exceptional point exhibit chiral state transfer. Because the loops cross exceptional lines, the final states are superpositions of eigenstates. Chiral state transfer is also found with non-zero homogeneous on-site interaction when the loop crosses over broken $PT$-symmetry regions of different character. Using inhomogeneous on-site interactions, we find direction dependent state transfer between eigenstates without crossing or encircling exceptional points.
authors: Jaakko Luomala; Federico Settimo; Kimmo Luoma; Iiro Vilja; Jyrki Piilo

title: In situ enhanced detectability of axions' responses in a microwave cavity
abstract: Microwave cavities in strong magnetic fields are among the most sensitive detectors for axion dark matter detection. Its sensitivity, however, is fundamentally limited by the second order nature of axion photon energy conversion, which yields an extremely weak signal. Here we propose a feasible approach to break this limitation, by pre-exciting the target cavity mode to generate a first order power response signal in situ. The resulting signal amplitude scales linearly with the axion-photon coupling parameter, which is in sharp contrast to the quadratic scaling of conventional schemes, and is detectable via standard quadrature balanced homodyne detection system, even though its phase remains stochastic. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this pre-excited seed field can effectively suppress thermal noise, and thus the detection sensitivity of the system can approach the lower quantum noise limit. Consequently, the sensitivities predicted by the KSVZ and DFSZ models could be surpassed. This proposal might offer a pathway to a major leap in axion dark matter searches, as it is within reach of current technology.
authors: Li Gao; Suirong He; Hao Zheng; Ni Chen; Xianing Feng; Qingquan Jiang; Jin Li; L. F. Wei

title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures
abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2π=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.
authors: Jiawen Liu; Chengli Wang; Aleksei Gaier; Tianyi Zhang; Gabriel Jülg; Yazan Lampert; André Garcia Primo; Alessandro Tomasino; Hua Li; Xin Ou; Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus

title: A sharp gradient-corrected Lieb--Thirring inequality in one dimension with applications to density functional theory
abstract: We first prove a sharp Lieb-Thirring inequality with semi-classical constant and gradient correction in one dimension. In the periodic setting, the corresponding inequality also includes a parity dependent shell-correction term, which appears to be new. Moreover, we also characterize the optimizers of these inequalities. In particular, the optimizing density profiles form a two-dimensional manifold, which we call here the Poincaré density manifold. We then apply these results to study the Thomas--Fermi--von Weizsäcker (TFW) approximation of the kinetic energy in Density Functional Theory. More precisely, we first obtain an explicit and non-asymptotic bound on the global and local error made by the TFW approximation. These bounds are controlled by the distance of the normalized density profile from the Poincaré density manifold times the number of particles. In particular, these bounds show that the TFW approximation is exact on the Poincaré manifold. We then show that, in the periodic setting, the distance between the Kohn-Sham potential and the inverse TFW potential in the natural dual Sobolev space can also be controlled by explicit density dependent constants times the distance to the Poincaré manifold. As a corollary, we prove that for a fixed density profile, the Kohn-Sham potential converges towards the inverse Thomas--Fermi potential in the high-density limit $N \rightarrow \infty$ with asymptotic rate of order $N^{-2}$. This rate is shown to be optimal.
authors: Thiago Carvalho Corso; Louis Garrigue

title: A Personal History in Quantum Foundations: an Oral History Interview
abstract: This oral history interview provides Yakir Aharonov's personal and conceptual recollections from the 1950s to the 2000s, focusing on his academic trajectory, some of his major contributions to quantum foundations, and his perspective on the development of the field. The interview traces Aharonov's academic career through the Technion, University of Bristol, Brandeis University, Yeshiva University, University of South Carolina, Tel Aviv University, George Mason University, and Chapman University. The interview also traces the development of Aharonov's work and collaborations on the EPR paradox, time-energy uncertainty relations, quantum measurement theory, quantum frames of reference, the two-state vector formalism, weak values, protective measurements, and several other contributions. It includes recollections of meetings and discussions with David Bohm, Niels Bohr, John Clauser, Paul Dirac, Rudolf Peierls, Aage Petersen, and Abner Shimony. Also mentioned: David Albert, Jeeva Anandan, Peter Bergmann, Gideon Carmi, Avshalom Elitzur, Dave Finkelstein, Vladimir Fock, Itzhak Kalugai, Ed Lerner, Joel Lebowitz, Stanley Mandelstam, Yuval Ne'eman, Sandu Popescu, Maurice Pryce, Daniel Rohrlich, Nathan Rosen, Joseph Safko, Paul Singer, Daniele Struppa, Leonard Susskind, Lev Vaidman, Chien-Shiung Wu.
authors: Yakir Aharonov; Guy Hetzroni

title: Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
abstract: We formulate stabilizer-code error correction as a code- and recovery-dependent transformation of the noise channel. For a fixed recovery map, syndrome projection produces a logical channel that is block diagonal with respect to the syndrome partition, whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code-induced error classes, with no physical Pauli twirl required. Concatenation is then iterated redistribution, with the dominant logical error guiding the next code. The bit-flip and phase-flip three-qubit codes with standard recoveries supply a closed-form benchmark, and logically inequivalent recoveries appear as a design degree of freedom for shaping the channel presented to the next decoder. For amplitude damping, the rules select $C_2(\hatσ_y)C_1(\hatσ_x)$ within this family: one level converts the damping into a nearly pure logical-$X$ channel at the price $f_1=1-3γ/4$, the second level suppresses that channel to $f_2=1-\frac94γ^2$, and the concatenated protocol overtakes the unencoded channel below $γ_c=0.2905$ ($f_c=0.8485$) under ideal encoding and recovery; with a per-gate error rate $\varepsilon$ the crossover survives only for $\varepsilon$ below about $5\times10^{-4}$, and then only inside a window of $γ$ that contracts as $\varepsilon$ grows. Across the $n$-qubit repetition family with odd $n$, the suppression order rises as $γ^{w+1}$ with $w=(n-1)/2$, while the gate budget grows as $n^L$. Correlated noise requires joint class statistics, whereas coherent noise retains intra-class coherences that make the same transformation usable in reverse as a tomographic fingerprint, whose local identifiability is established in a companion paper. The construction remains an analytic benchmark, not a universal prescription for an inner code beneath a surface code.
authors: Long Huang

title: Scale-free localization in pseudo-Hermitian quantum walk
abstract: Scale-free localization is a distinctive phenomenon in non-Hermitian systems, where specific eigenstates, known as scale-free localized states (LSs), possess localization lengths that scale linearly with the system size. Here, we show that a single non-Hermitian defect in one-dimensional quantum walks (QWs) induces scale-free localization. Driven by non-Hermiticity, the QW system undergoes a pseudo-Hermitian (PH) phase transition and the PH symmetry breaking is accompanied by the emergence of scale-free localization. As non-Hermiticity is further increased, the system undergoes a second phase transition, marked by the emergence of two pairs of bound states. Crucially, we identify the critical points of both transitions using localization properties. Furthermore, we extend our investigation to two-dimensional QWs, where a single non-Hermitian defect also induces scale-free localization, thereby demonstrating the universality of this phenomenon. Our work provides a valuable perspective for further exploring defect physics and a type of novel LS in non-Hermitian quantum systems.
authors: Haiting Zhang; Lei Xiao; Cui-Xian Guo; Quan Lin; Peng Xue

title: Norm-Aware Product Formulas for Hamiltonian Simulations
abstract: With the target of efficiently solving the quantum-mechanical Schrödinger equation on future quantum computers, first- and second-order product formulas for the time-evolution operator are proposed, designed to exploit hierarchies in the operator norms of the individual Hamiltonian components. Inspired by the THRIFT product formula, these decomposition schemes achieve a suppression of the leading error term by a factor of alpha<1 with respect to the standard Lie--Trotter--Suzuki splitting of the same order, where alpha quantifies the norm ratio between the dominant and subdominant parts of the Hamiltonian. Unlike THRIFT, the proposed formulas retain the general product-formula structure, making them applicable to Hamiltonians whose terms act on an arbitrary number of qubits. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated through numerical experiments on engineered two-dimensional spin-1/2 XY model systems and isolated molecules within the double-factorization framework.
authors: Carlos A. Piñeiro Moreno; Pascal Krause; Annika Bande

title: The limits of magic-state distillation
abstract: Magic-state factories are a major cost of fault-tolerant quantum computing, yet how few noisy inputs they need is known only for restricted protocols. We show that, for tolerating input faults, any stabilizer protocol, however adaptive, postselected or multistage, is no better than a projection onto one stabilizer code, and that for rational targets a fault pattern is harmful exactly when its complement is. Searches over all codes show that quadratic distillation of one T state needs exactly nine inputs and that the eight-input CCZ factory is optimal. At order $d$, one T state needs $n\geq2d$.
authors: Llorenç Balada Gaggioli; Jakub Mareček

title: The often overlooked role of sound in liquid thermal transport
abstract: Formulated a hundred years ago, the Bridgman formula for thermal conductivity of liquids postulates a proportionality between sound velocity and thermal conductivity. This designates phonons as heat carriers in a liquid. Its empirical success has been under-appreciated and its conceptual implications overlooked. Here, we review its origin, its links to hydrodynamic Euler equations and to the fundamental paradox surrounding the parabolic heat equation and its fate across the quantum-classical crossover.
authors: Kamran Behnia

title: Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent
abstract: We propose Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent (QCHD), a continuous-time quantum framework for optimization under smooth equality constraints. The unconstrained counterpart, Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), minimizes a cost function by simulating the Schrödinger dynamics of a particle in the potential given by the cost function. Applying Dirac's formalism to the classical dynamics with constraints, we construct an intrinsic quantum Hamiltonian with a Laplace--Beltrami operator on the constraint manifold in a kinetic term. Its evolution preserves the constraints exactly without penalty terms and is expected to solve quantum-dynamically the constrained optimization problem. We analyze its relation to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent supplemented by a strong penalty term. For a squared-distance penalty, the effective tangential dynamics acquires an extrinsic-curvature potential and, in nontrivial normal-rotation sectors, a coupling to the normal-bundle connection. These embedding-dependent terms remain in the strong-penalty limit, generally yielding quantum dynamics different from QCHD. Numerical comparisons for circular, elliptical, and two simultaneous constraints show faster optimization and improved concentration near global minima for the initial states and finite penalty strengths considered.
authors: Yoshihiko Abe; Ryo Nagai

title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.
authors: Wan-Ling Yang; Shao-Bo Liu; Xiang Luo; Chao Yang; Hai-Lin Li; Yu-Zhou Yang; Yong-Kui Wang; Bing Yang

title: Entanglement certification of attosecond light fields with photoelectron interferometry
abstract: The emergence of entangled quantum optical states in high-harmonic generation raises a fundamental problem about its characterization, namely, \textit{how can entanglement of extreme-ultraviolet radiation be certified for attosecond light fields?} Here, we provide experimentally accessible separability tests, particularly showing that attosecond photoelectron interferometry provides a direct solution to this problem. This is achieved by a quantum optical treatment of mapping photoelectron interferometry to the measurement of optical correlation functions. This yields a negative-partial-transpose witness for infrared-XUV entanglement and a sufficient witness of genuine multipartite entanglement without auxiliary optical measurements. We evaluate both witnesses on explicit optical states and identify how the protocol can be extended to XUV-XUV entanglement certification. Hence, we establish attosecond photoelectron interferometry as a general framework for entanglement certification across a wide range of optical frequencies.
authors: Philipp Stammer

title: Local Dephasing Sustains Continuous Time Crystals in a Spin-1/2 Ensemble
abstract: Local pure dephasing suppresses single-spin coherence, yet we show that it sustains continuous time-crystalline order in a fully connected ferromagnetic spin-$1/2$ ensemble with local decay. An exact operator identity reveals the mechanism: dephasing raises the interaction energy, while energy relaxation on a finite timescale converts this charging into delayed feedback. Within homogeneous mean-field theory, we prove that dephasing is necessary for periodic motion in this model and that feedback exactly balances transverse damping over each cycle. Beyond mean field, the identity fixes the relative amplitude and phase of energy and longitudinal magnetization in oscillatory Liouvillian modes. Liouvillian spectra and stationary two-time correlations characterize temporal order through decay rates that decrease algebraically with system size, frequencies approaching nonzero mean-field values, and comparable per-spin oscillatory weights. Semiclassical trajectories further reveal recurrent switching between a limit-cycle region and two symmetry-related stationary regions: fluctuations interrupt and reactivate collective oscillations, and oscillatory episodes provide an intermediate channel between stationary regions. These results establish local dephasing as a resource for autonomous collective motion and show how the resulting temporal order can participate in metastable dynamics.
authors: Zhen-huan Yang; Dan-Bo Zhang

title: Fluctuation-free Quantum Battery Charging Enabled by Bell-like Entangled and Separable Charger States
abstract: The implication of entanglement in quantum battery charging remains poorly understood. In addition, intrinsic quantum randomness poses a fundamental challenge to charging uniformity across distinct trials. To address these issues, we study a three-qubit system within a cascaded collision frame, with two qubits acting as the charger and the third serving as the battery. After each collision, an adaptive measurement is performed on the charger, yielding four conditional post-measurement battery states with identical expected stored energy. For arbitrary fixed charger states, we derive analytical expressions for the recurrence relation of stored energy. We find that stored-energy fluctuations depend on whether the dynamics relies on the battery phase \(γ_n\). For two Bell-like families of entangled states, together with their computational basis states termed Bell-like separable states, the dynamics is \(γ_n\)-independent and fluctuations vanish, whereas for other entangled and separable states, fluctuations emerge. These insights establish a paradigm for engineering charger states to design uniform-charging quantum-battery architectures despite inherent quantum randomness.
authors: Longyan Gong; Jing Zhang; Yongtao Li

title: Conditional Reset-Enhanced Dissipative Quantum Metrology
abstract: Open quantum sensors work either in a transient regime with finely timed readout or in a steady-state regime with robust but weaker sensitivity. To overcome this trade-off, we ask whether repeatedly resetting a probe to a fixed state, even a suboptimal one, can outperform the optimal single-shot transient protocol. We prove that blind resets, triggered by an external clock, cannot do so even with memory. Conditional resets, triggered by the probe's own state, break this no-go result by capturing parameter-dependent quantum jumps or by recycling heralded losses, for parameters encoded in dissipative rates and Hamiltonians alike. A three-level thermometer capturing thermal excitations outperforms the optimal no-reset protocol in both transient and steady-state regimes, even with a $40\%$ preparation error. Conditional resets can even saturate the ultimate bound of nonequilibrium thermometry with a single readout. Heralded recycling enables steady-state frequency estimation to outperform optimal transient Ramsey interferometry. The advantages extend to interacting probes and to elapsed-time estimation, and both mechanisms can be realized using established experimental techniques.
authors: Silan Li; Qingjun Tong; Ruicheng Bao

title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
abstract: Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Ravi Kumar Jha; Hsuan-Yin Lin; Eirik Rosnes

title: Rank-One Loss Maximizes the Spectral Response Strength of Passive Full-Order Exceptional Points
abstract: We consider finite-dimensional non-Hermitian systems in which all modes coalesce at a single exceptional point. For a rank-one anti-Hermitian contribution, the spectral response strength is computed exactly. For passive systems, we then derive a sharp upper bound at fixed exceptional-point decay rate and show that it is reached only when the decay operator has rank one, corresponding to a single independent dissipative direction. This establishes rank-one loss as the optimal configuration for enhancing the response of a full-order exceptional point. The bound holds for arbitrary order and improves on earlier passive estimates beyond second order. Two third-order trimers illustrate the result: a rank-one-loss system saturates the bound, whereas a passive rank-two-loss realization remains below it. The result turns dissipation into a design resource: concentrating the loss into a single effective dissipative direction maximizes the highest-order spectral response of a passive full-order exceptional-point device.
authors: Jan Wiersig

title: High-fidelity entanglement of two spectrally-distinct solid state emitters
abstract: Solid state quantum emitters with electronic spin properties can be entangled using optical interferometric which-path erasure techniques that rely on identical frequencies and linewidths of the emitters. This promises a powerful, fast and scalable platform for quantum technologies. Using current protocols, a pair of emitters embedded in a waveguide interferometer can be deterministically prepared in a maximally entangled state. However, the amount of entanglement diminishes rapidly with increasing separation of the emission lines and variations in the linewidths of the emitters. Solid state emitters such as quantum dots are subject to intrinsic variations in the fabrication process. Therefore, manufacturing the required number of identical emitters on a chip is not scalable. In this Letter, we present a method that uses readily available pairs of entangled photons to entangle solid state emitters with large transition frequency separations and linewidth variations, circumventing the need to fabricate optically identical emitters. We demonstrate a concurrence of C = 0.95 for typical quantum dots using narrowband photon inputs.
authors: Daniel R. E. Hodgson; Pieter Kok

title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models
abstract: We develop and analyze generative models based on quantum solvers of stochastic differential equations. Unlike the common approach based on layered variational quantum circuits with parameterized rotations, we parameterize the potential of a Langevin process. The associated Fokker-Planck (FP) equations are Hermitianized and solved using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation. By encoding the square root of the stationary density, the model enables sampling through computational-basis measurements and is efficiently controlled by coefficients of the block-encoded diagonal potential. We train the proposed model to match empirical distributions within the family described by FP equations, demonstrating parameter recovery for multivariate probability distributions. Crucially, the model remains trainable at scale. Sample-efficient and convex optimization for in-distribution targets arises from a physics-informed inductive bias and holds regardless of the dimensionality of the problem. We provide circuit constructions and efficient block encodings of the main components of the algorithm and analyze resource requirements. Our approach frames quantum generative learning as quantum model discovery and provides a foundation for extending this framework to high-dimensional, strongly correlated scientific data.
authors: Tariq Mahassen; Marcin Jastrzebski; Oleksandr Kyriienko

title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.
authors: Marcos Crichigno; Steve Flammia

title: Finite Systems in the Space of Projective Measurements
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two-level systems using the quasidistribution $Q$ function projected onto the space of collective measurements. Particular attention is given to evolution under Hamiltonians that are invariant under particle permutations, for pure states that are either invariant or noninvariant under such permutations. This requires constructing an approximate analog of the star product between quasidistribution functions: the projected $Q$ function of a product of two operators is expressed approximately in terms of the individual operators' $Q$ and $P$ functions. We rewrite the Liouville equation to determine approximate state dynamics and compare the result with exact evolution using the Hellinger distance. Overall, the method performs well for permutation-invariant pure states and Hamiltonians, whereas deviations arise for arbitrary pure states and noninvariant Hamiltonians.
authors: Miguel Flores R.; Carlos A. Muñoz

title: Orbital-coherence memory in electrical transport and its self-consistent Maxwell response
abstract: An internal electronic coherence changes electrical transport only when it feeds back on the physical current. We develop a reduced description of this feedback and distinguish its exact consequences from the assumptions required for a microscopic realization. An opposite-parity two-orbital Hamiltonian identifies a current-coupled orbital force. Under an explicitly stated moment closure and collision ansatz, it yields a passive three-state response with an exponentially damped oscillatory memory. The resulting conductivity redistributes a fixed optical weight and predicts a nonmonotonic dependence of dc conduction on coherence damping at fixed remaining parameters. The orbital reduction constrains the coupling and internal frequency through a shared bare splitting, providing a test beyond unconstrained spectral fitting. A charge-conserving spatial extension couples to Maxwell equations through a positive energy balance and separates the constitutive response from longitudinal collective and transverse electromagnetic modes. We formulate complex-conductivity and transmission tests, including the limits of parameter identification over a finite bandwidth. The model supplies a conditional connection between orbital dynamics, transport memory, and electromagnetic observables; conductivity alone does not establish a uniquely quantum mechanism, and a material-specific collision calculation and closure-error assessment remain necessary.
authors: Pengfei Zhu

title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
abstract: Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.
authors: Bikalpa Gautam; Akil Raj Subedi

title: Krylov Complexity and Entropy of Composite Quantum Systems
abstract: We investigate the behaviour of Krylov complexity as the number of degrees of freedom of a quantum system increases. Specifically, we show that for tensor products of commuting subsystems, the leading excess complexity is controlled by a weighted variance of the subsystem Lanczos coefficients. This provides a quantitative measure of dynamical heterogeneity and a precise characterization of synchronous evolution. We also show that Krylov entropy is able to disambiguate the information associated with subsystems composition from that generated by dynamical mismatch, and that the same Lanczos variance controls the leading mismatch contribution to both complexity and the entropy. Our results establish excess complexity and Krylov entropy as complementary probes of the emergence of collective dynamics in large quantum systems.
authors: Jeff Murugan; Victor Van Aswegen; Hendrik J R Van Zyl

title: Predictive electronic feedback control for narrow-linewidth lasers
abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers are essential for various key atom-laser interaction processes and optical setups in quantum coherent control, quantum precision measurement, and quantum information science. The Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique is the standard method for the frequency-stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers, but the inherent time delay in its feedback loop inevitably induces excessive phase noise, commonly known as servo bumps. Previous solutions primarily rely on additional optical components outside the electronic feedback control loop. Here, we propose and implement a generic method based on the Smith predictor to address the time-delay issue entirely within the electronic part of the PDH feedback control loop. We systematically demonstrate its capability to suppress phase noise and reduce servo bumps by adding only a single Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) controller to the loop. This class of methods is demonstrated to be conceptually concise with minimal hardware overhead, effective in practice, and holds potential for a wide variety of future applications.
authors: Jiatian Liu; Xuan Qi; Xiayang Fan; Shenchao Jin; Yuan Sun

title: Nonlinear quantum noise polarization in macroscopic nonlinear QED
abstract: We construct a quantum theory of light in nonlinearly responding materials with dispersion and absorption and, in particular, show the emergence of non-Gaussian noise associated with nonlinear absorption processes. Our theory is based on a path-integral formulation of the microscopic Huttner-Barnett model including cubic matter self-interaction required for $χ^{(2)}$ nonlinear processes. We show that the noise polarization emerges naturally from a decoupling of the stochastic weights of the bath response which, in case of cubic self-interactions, leads to a decoupling via Airy functions. As the theory is, by construction, consistent with the nonlinear fluctuation-dissipation theorem, it constitutes a viable quantum theory of light in nonlinear media.
authors: Arman Kashef; Stefan Scheel; Marco Ornigotti

title: Mutual Information Across Quantum Reference Frame Perspectives
abstract: In quantum information theory, standard notions typically presuppose a fixed partition of the world into subsystems, encoded in a tensor product structure of the Hilbert space. Yet, in some scenarios, the subsystem structure is not uniquely fixed. A case in point is the description of subsystems relative to different quantum reference frames (QRFs), where the tensor product structure, although fixed in a specific QRF, changes across different QRFs. Such a relativity of subsystems underlies many interesting features of QRFs, such as the relativity of entanglement, entropy, and coherence. It also raises a broader question: how do we compare the information across different subsystem perspectives, especially when the corresponding subsystem algebras overlap? Here, we propose a notion of quantum mutual information across different QRF perspectives, which captures the correlations between subsystems relative to different frames of reference. To do so, we focus on an algebraic definition of subsystems. Studying in detail the union and overlap between subsystem algebras relative to different QRFs, we find that the usual definition of mutual information in terms of the chain law overcounts the information associated to the overlap. Based on this insight, we propose a modified chain law and show that the resulting notion of mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures found in the literature [1]. Our investigations not only provide a way to quantify the relation between different QRF perspectives from an information-theoretic point of view but also sheds light on some important features of quantum information in absence of a fixed tensor product structure.
authors: Leonardo Valente; Carla Ferradini; Flaminia Giacomini; Viktoria Kabel

title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
abstract: Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.
authors: Zihao Li; Ji Guan; Mingsheng Ying

title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
abstract: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.
authors: Alexander Jung; Anastasiia Ciers; Hannes Pfeifer; Albert Hansson; Johanna Örgård; Daniel Stachanow; Viktor A. Lilja; Philippe Tassin; Witlef Wieczorek

title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) returns a single decay parameter or gate error rate, but when the noise is gate-dependent that parameter is notoriously difficult to interpret. We study RB and related random-circuit benchmarks under small gate-local Markovian noise by factorizing each noisy gate into its ideal action followed by the exponential of a small error generator and then perturbing the RB $\mathscr{L}$ matrix, which models the RB decay. For any low-error gate set that satisfies the requirements of RB (it is a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design), we show that Pauli-stochastic error rates contribute linearly to the RB decay parameter, while Hamiltonian error rates contribute through a gauge-invariant quadratic form. Pauli-correlation and active generators are absent from the linear term and enter only at higher order. For the single-qubit native gate set $\{X_{π/2},Y_{π/2}\}$ we derive this quadratic form explicitly in terms of three first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) coordinates: the two intrinsic over-rotations and one relational axis-tilt error. The resulting formula explains the dependence of DRB on the sampling distribution and the compilation dependence of CRB. These results turn RB decay rates into interpretable functions of experimentally meaningful elementary error rates.
authors: Anthony M. Polloreno; Timothy Proctor; Robin Blume-Kohout

title: One-shot entanglement generation and distillation via Petz recovery and binary hypothesis testing
abstract: How much entanglement can two distant laboratories share when their connection is noisy? We relate this question to deciding which of two quantum hypotheses is present. Our one-shot bounds apply to entanglement generation over a quantum channel and to one-way entanglement distillation from a shared state. We use Cheng's trace inequality to bound the infidelity of a Petz decoder in terms of a binary hypothesis testing cost. Applying the inequality before averaging over codes reduces the error analysis to computing a second moment of random subspaces. The proof covers every integer target dimension and treats rank-deficient states explicitly. A corollary expresses the achievable entanglement through hypothesis-testing coherent information, with a single logarithmic error slack and exact integer rounding. We also prove an error-preserving conversion from entanglement generation codes to entanglement transmission codes: the target dimension decreases by only a constant factor at fixed error, and the decoder is the original decoder followed by local processing. Consequently, for both entanglement generation and entanglement transmission, arbitrary pure reference-input states yield the same coherent-information rate, second-order Gaussian correction at the original error tolerance, and explicit achievable logarithmic remainder. For commuting testing hypotheses, the logarithmic remainder improves to a constant. These results give a direct route from binary distinguishability to explicit recovery guarantees and finite-resource quantum communication rates.
authors: Matthew Can; Mark M. Wilde

title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
abstract: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.
authors: Brian Coyle; Jonathan H. Fetherolf; Antonio Márquez Romero; Stefano Scali; Giuseppe Buonaiuto; Josh Kirsopp
