We analyze the spatial dependence of the local band edges and its consequences for the global spectral structure, and clarify the role played by the phase-space topology in determining the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization conditions. Finally, we illustrate our results with two representative examples: a homogeneous Rice-Mele chain subject to a harmonic trap and a fully inhomogeneous chain containing a domain wall.
authors: Federico Finkel; Artemio González-López; Martín Zapata

title: Optimal probes for estimating the dephasing of a quantum spin system
abstract: We investigate the optimal estimation of dephasing in finite-dimensional quantum spin systems. We first discuss some properties of the optimal probe states and present an efficient numerical algorithm to compute the optimal precision in dephasing estimation and identify the optimal probe states. For the dephasing channel arising from Gaussian phase diffusion, a spin cat state is known to be optimal for small dephasing. We analytically determine the range of dephasing strengths over which the cat state remains globally optimal for spins $J=1$ and $J=3/2$, and derive upper bounds on its optimality region for larger spins. We then compare numerically several probe states proposed in the literature, showing in particular that the simple class of probes obtained from uniform superpositions of all levels performs near-optimally for stronger dephasing. Finally, we apply our framework to a central-spin model coupled to a nuclear-spin bath, whose dynamics we simulate using the cluster-correlation expansion. Our results show that, while the cat state is optimal for weak Gaussian dephasing, pulse-controlled non-Markovian dynamics can favor states with amplitudes distributed over multiple spin levels, and in some cases the uniform state outperforms the other fixed probes considered. This shows how the choice of probe state depends both on the dephasing strength and on the dynamics.
authors: Leonardo Ratini; Stefano Carretta; Francesco Albarelli

title: Entanglement Asymmetry and Asymmetry Contour under Boundary Symmetry Breaking
abstract: We investigate how symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields affect magnetization and Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry (EA) in the transverse-field Ising model. For the ground state, magnetization exhibits qualitatively distinct behaviors in the ordered and disordered phases. EA also exhibits phase-dependent behavior, which is well captured by the lower and upper bounds derived in this work. In the critical regime, both magnetization and EA exhibit behavior qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical predictions for a related setup. We also study boundary-quench dynamics and find that magnetization propagates from the boundary into the bulk with a velocity consistent with the maximum quasiparticle velocity. In contrast, because EA is a subsystem-integrated quantity, its spatial structure is not directly resolved. We therefore introduce the asymmetry contour, a contour-like finite-difference quantity that provides a spatially resolved characterization of the symmetry-breaking information encoded in the reduced density matrix. The resulting contour is complementary to the local magnetization, retaining sensitivity to nonlocal many-body correlations while its dynamics also reflects the underlying quasiparticle propagation. These results show how EA and its contour can provide complementary information-theoretic characterizations of symmetry breaking and its spatial structure.
authors: Takahiro Orito; Daisuke Yamamoto

title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
abstract: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.
authors: Ruben Ortiz Cordero; Gaven K. Smart; Harshada Gothankar; Emilio Supsupin; Priya Bhosale; Mayur Virarkar

title: Bounding single-copy information causality violations
abstract: Information causality is a physical principle that constrains bipartite post-quantum nonlocal correlations from information-theoretic assumptions. A direct characterization of the correlations satisfying it, however, remains difficult because the defining entropic condition must hold for all admissible protocols in the corresponding task. Here, we formulate the single-copy information causality problem as an optimization over all protocol parameters and simplify it by proving a deterministic reduction. We then show that generic adaptive multi-copy protocols can be represented as single-copy protocols applied to an effective behavior obtained by local wirings. As a consequence, for families of correlations closed under wirings, excluding single-copy violations suffices to exclude all finite-copy adaptive-protocol violations. We formulate the resulting membership and set-inclusion problems as optimization problems and discuss possible semidefinite programming relaxations. As an application, we study expansions of the information causality functional around zero-capacity channels, generalizing a method recently employed by Gachechiladze and Miklin to derive the Tsirelson--Landau--Masanes boundary from information causality. For expansions centered on channels whose output distribution has full support, imposing the second-order constraints for all single-copy protocols characterizes exactly the set of macroscopic locality in the CHSH scenario. Expanding instead around appropriate constant-output channels with perturbations that change the channel support, we show that every single-copy IC violation can be witnessed already at first order with a channel of arbitrarily small capacity.
authors: Marco Pompili; Costantino Budroni

title: Exploiting the Weyl-Chamber Structure for Hardware-Aware Quantum Circuit Compression
abstract: Quantum circuit compression based on tensor networks enables long-time simulation of quantum many-body dynamics on near-term hardware. While Riemannian optimization has been successfully employed for this purpose, it typically optimizes over the manifold of generic two-qubit unitaries. Consequently, the resulting gates must still be synthesized into the hardware's native gate set via KAK decomposition, an overhead that partially negates the original compression gain. We show that Riemannian-optimized gates already exhibit a predictable Weyl structure: near-$R_{ZZ}$ for the Ising model and near-fSim for the Heisenberg XXZ model. Building on this insight, we investigate whether parameterized optimization directly over the native gate set can offer a beneficial trade-off between expressivity and circuit efficiency by reducing the circuit's dimensionality. When comparing the two approaches, we find that the small residual Weyl parameters neglected by the latter are essential for high compression of the Ising propagator, whereas for the Heisenberg propagator, the native XXZ structure can be exploited directly to build a more efficient compressed circuit.
authors: Neel Misciasci; Isabel Nha Minh Le; Christian B. Mendl

title: Minimal unitary representations of time-invariant causal quantum channels
abstract: In this work, we study quantum channels that respect causality in single-input-single-output linear time-invariant systems. We show that positive semidefinite kernels satisfying certain analyticity constraints, which we call Schur-class kernels, provide a suitable description of such channels through multiplicative maps (Schur multipliers). Using the Moore-Aronszajn Theorem, we establish that these multipliers admit a minimal analytic Stinespring representation, which, in the unital case, is given by multiplication by a left inner function. We then relate the output rank of pure-state inputs to the dimension of the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Using de Branges-Rovnyak realizations, we derive a stability criterion for the existence of two-sided inner completions of these vector-valued functions. We further show that the adjoint of the Julia embedding associated with the realization is minimal, and that its characteristic function essentially coincides with the canonical two-sided inner completion suggested by the Beurling-Lax-Halmos Theorem. Finally, we provide algorithms for explicitly computing minimal two-sided inner completions in the case of finite McMillan degree.
authors: Antonius Jacobus Hasenack; Boris Škorić

title: The Cost of a Real Grover Oracle: Minecraft Seed Search from Software to Quantum Hardware
abstract: We present the resource estimation of how known-constant arithmetic changes the cost of a Grover oracle for Minecraft 1.13.1 seed recovery, an application of quantum search to procedural content generation. The oracle developed here combines a structure-placement predicate with a reversible inverse transform of the linear congruential generator for the 32-bit residual search. Reduced-width arithmetic, phase marking, uncomputation, and complete Grover loops are verified against an independent Java reference, while production-width circuits are structurally audited. Direct Fourier-basis constant arithmetic reduces the placement-predicate width from 6n+3 to 4n+3 qubits and the structural scaling of the two-qubit gate counts from Theta(n^3) to O(n^2). Under backend-agnostic common-basis Qiskit level-0 {u, CX} accounting, the representative nonzero-r folded residual-search construction uses 275 circuit qubits, 48,896 CX gates, and depth 4,482, versus 467 qubits, 2,038,804 CX gates, and depth 186,328 for the original register-to-register baseline. Multi-placement conjunctions expose a width-recomputation tradeoff, and exact enumeration identifies a plateau in candidate reduction for the benchmark. We executed reduced-width placement circuits within complete Grover loops on IBM processors and Quantinuum H2-1 and show larger one-iteration increases in marked-state probability for the specialized construction than for the baseline. These results quantify the resource benefits of arithmetic specialization and show substantial routing sensitivity in the reduced-width IBM hardware experiments. Together, the results quantify the effect of specializing known-constant arithmetic within a PCG-derived oracle and show that its compiled hardware behavior strongly depends on routing and execution context.
authors: Evan M. Reeves; Elias Sopkin; Thomas A. Searles

title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations
abstract: We introduce a factory--processor interface architecture for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that separates code-dependent encoded-resource preparation from reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical processor. Beyond encoded resources, the interface specifies logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. As a concrete realization, we combine an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated $C_4$ code with physical Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits with an online time-domain measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) processor. Under the specified additive-displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy, simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering $P_5<P_4<P_3<P_2$ at 12.25 dB of effective GKP displacement-noise quality, both with and without the prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise. At 15.6 dB and $L=2$, a separate fixed-sample evaluation gives one-sided 95$\%$ Clopper--Pearson upper bounds below $10^{-5}$ for both conditions under the binomial model. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard constructions with tracked code permutations. Given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length of these constructions. These results identify a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.
authors: Kosuke Fukui; Takaya Matsuura; Yohji Chin; Shohei Kiryu; Takaya Hoshi; Kan Takase; Warit Asavanant

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
abstract: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.
authors: Hari Hara Suthan Chittoor; Thirumalai Manimaran

title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
abstract: Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.
authors: Steven Abel; Michael Spannowsky; Simon Williams

title: Fully quantum training of parametric circuits with Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
abstract: Parametric quantum circuits are usually trained by classical, local optimizers, which use the quantum computer only to evaluate the cost function, or its gradient, one point at a time. Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) takes a different route: in this quantum algorithm for continuous optimization, the parameters become the position of a quantum particle, with the cost function as its potential, and two time schedules control kinetic and potential energy so that the wavefunction explores the whole landscape and tunnels towards the global minimum. QHD, however, assumes a classically computable cost function, and its digital implementation is poorly understood: standard error bounds grow exponentially with the number of qubits per parameter, and the schedules are borrowed from classical optimization. Here we propose to train parametric circuits with QHD entirely on the quantum computer, through an online step in which the qubits encoding the parameters coherently control the circuit on a second register. We prove that, for cost functions with a smooth periodic extension, including those of parametric circuits, the simulation error admits a bound independent of the grid resolution, and that for circuits the bound grows at most linearly with the number of parameters. We also show that the ideal dynamics depends on the two schedules only through a single curve, which controls the adiabaticity of the search, and that the remaining freedom can be used to minimize the gate count. Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show that, at equal cost, schedules designed in this way markedly increase the probability of finding the global minimum.
authors: Marco Burato; Leonardo Banchi

title: Nonclassicality from Incomplete Fock-State Statistics
abstract: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. The method contains known analytical criteria as special cases while generally detecting substantially larger nonclassical regions. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms. As a case study, we apply it to the resonant Jaynes--Cummings model with thermal states and reveal nonclassicality at short interaction times and close to thermal balance, where detection of nonclassicality is otherwise challenging.
authors: Martin Žonda; Pavel Baláž; Lukáš Lachman; Darren W. Moore; Tomáš Novotný; Radim Filip

title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.
authors: Bohnishikha Ghosh; Chithra Raj; Shubhayan Sarkar

title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
abstract: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.
authors: Chunjing Jia; Valentin Walther; Laimei Nie

title: Certain Quantum States Already Require Quantum Time Evolution
abstract: Model-independent tests of quantum theory, such as Bell inequality violations, focus on static properties of the theory and do not rely on its dynamical aspects. Hence, this core part of quantum theory remains largely untested in a model-independent way. We show that the structure of quantum time evolution can be examined by testing the consistency between the state space and the dynamical laws. Considering a class of generalized phase-space theories, we find that certain quantum states can only be part of a theory if the time evolution is quantum: their evolution in anharmonic potentials would otherwise result in unphysical, negative marginal distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of the first excited state of a quantum harmonic oscillator is already sufficient to single out the Moyal bracket (quantum dynamics) to leading order in $\hbar^2$. We outline how theory-independent Wigner tomography of this state can be used to empirically exclude nonquantum dynamical theories.
authors: Joel D. Huber; Matthias Kleinmann

title: Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing
abstract: Block-encoding has emerged as a core primitive in many quantum algorithms, including quantum simulation. In this work, we design efficient and extensible methods for generating low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians built from repeated local interaction patches through a technique we call "patch routing". We construct block encodings for a full Hamiltonian by first block-encoding a small local patch and then using a SWAP-style routing network to coherently apply the local patch encoding across the lattice. The expensive, local block-encoding cost is paid only once per query and is independent of lattice size, whereas the comparatively inexpensive routing network grows linearly with the lattice size, dominating at large sizes. Our method allows for a hierarchical structure in which larger patches can be block-encoded with small normalization factors, albeit at a higher (local, non-extensive) block-encoding cost, thereby reducing overall query complexity in an algorithm. We exploit symmetries and algebraic structures in local interactions to construct efficient block encodings, and we apply these techniques to the Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models. For a $120\times 120$ square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model near maximal frustration ($J_2/J_1=0.4-0.6$), our methods result in a $15-17\times$ reduction in the leading $T$ cost per qubitized-QPE run (ignoring initial state preparation and overlap) relative to prior state-of-the-art Pauli LCU constructions. Corresponding reductions are approximately $3\times$ for the $120\times120$ Fermi-Hubbard model at half-filling. For time evolution of the honeycomb spin-liquid model on $120\times120$ unit cells, the leading cost is reduced by $5\times$. Our framework provides a systematic way forward for larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.
authors: Minzhao Liu; Abeynaya Gnanasekaran; Ananth Kaushik; Siddharth Hariprakash; Alireza Marefat Khah; Martin Roetteler; Grant Salton

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
abstract: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.
authors: Chayan Patra; Prayas Ghosh; Adwait Patkhedkar; Rahul Maitra

title: Ideal interaction dynamics of defects and background fields in condensed matter
abstract: While defect dynamics in condensed matter systems is widely studied and several methods are available to track the defect position over time, the formulation of dynamical models for the coupled evolution of both defects and background field quantities seems to be more challenging. Yet, the overall behavior of a system containing moving defects is strongly influenced by this defect-field interaction. Here, we propose a modeling framework for the conservative coupled evolution of the defect density and the background fields upon focusing on two relevant cases of study: the Gross-Pitaevskii theory of quantum fluids and the Ericksen-Leslie model of nematic liquid crystals. To achieve the coupled evolution, we combine the Euler-Poincaré variational setting of continuum dynamics with the gauge theory of topological defects. While the latter allows us to overcome certain ambiguities in definition of the defect density, the Euler-Poincaré method provides a unified modeling approach in the absence of defect reconnection. Suitable variational regularizations are also proposed to deal with the motion of singular defect lines.
authors: François Gay-Balmaz; Tudor S. Ratiu; Cesare Tronci

title: Maximal Orbital Entanglement from Non-Interacting Fermions
abstract: Orbital rotations are used in quantum many-body physics and chemistry to reduce the complexity of quantum states by compressing their correlation into a small set of relevant orbitals. In striking contrast, quantum information processing strives for the opposite: orbitals that maximize entanglement as a resource. Motivated by this, we prove that Slater determinants of $N$ fermions on a lattice of $d_A + d_B = d$ sites, although free of particle correlation, can carry up to $\min\{d_A, d_B, N, d-N\}$ ebits of orbital entanglement. Given enough particles and holes, this equals the maximum over all fermionic states. For arbitrary free states, we derive the maximal orbital total correlation in closed form for all bipartitions, the finest partition, and all partitions of up to five sites, using new majorization relations for Hermitian matrices. Taken together, these results turn mean-field states, the starting point of most many-body methods in physics and chemistry, into a viable resource for quantum information processing.
authors: Damiano Aliverti-Piuri; Julia Liebert; Christian Schilling

title: Direct tests of conformal symmetry with Rydberg atoms: assessment and proposals
abstract: We propose a direct test of conformal symmetry using Rydberg-atom arrays. By arranging the atoms on a circle and measuring equal-time two-point correlation functions, the characteristic functional form predicted by conformal field theory can be tested directly. We estimate the number of experimental snapshots required to resolve this behavior with sufficient statistical precision. We further optimize the time-dependent ramp profile of the Rabi frequency~$Ω$ and detuning~$Δ$ used to prepare the target critical state adiabatically. The optimized profile achieves higher fidelity over much shorter evolution times than those employed in previous experiments. Taken together, these results suggest that a direct experimental test of conformal symmetry is feasible with current Rydberg-atom technology.
authors: Junchen Rong; Slava Rychkov

title: Genuinely multipartite entangled qudits: one rule to link them all
abstract: Links of rings offer an intuitive picture of multipartite entanglement. Cutting one ring can free some of the others, just as losing a particle, i.e. tracing it out, can disentangle some of the remaining ones. This analogy classifies multipartite entanglement according to which groups of particles stay entangled when others are lost, a question at the heart of robust quantum networks. However, pure states realizing a given link class were known only in special cases. Here, we close this gap. Recasting link polynomials as hypergraphs, we give an explicit formula for pure qudit states and prove that, for every link class, their entanglement under any pattern of particle loss matches the link exactly. The same construction also controls genuine multipartite entanglement, determining exactly which of the groups that stay entangled are genuinely multipartite entangled, and all of them can be made so. As a consequence, we prove the conjecture that $m$-resistant pure qudit states, which stay entangled after the loss of any $m$ particles but become fully separable after the loss of $m+1$, exist for any number of particles and any $m$.
authors: Gonçalo M. Quinta; Rui André

title: Post-Quantum Perfect Zero-Knowledge Arguments for NP From Any One-Way Permutation
abstract: In this paper, we show for the first time that post-quantum one-way permutations are sufficient for perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for all of NP with security guaranteed against quantum adversaries. We first establish that Naor, Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung's bit commitment scheme built from any permutation using interactive hashing, called the NOVY scheme, is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum polynomial-time committers provided the permutation is post-quantum one-way. We then show that the collapse-binding property of the NOVY scheme allows for Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE to remain so exactly as it stands against quantum adversaries.
authors: Frédéric Dupuis; Rémi Ligez; Khaireddine Medhioub; Louis Salvail; Louis-Charles Thibodeau

title: Quantum Heuristic Separation of Comb Inequalities for the Travelling Salesman Problem
abstract: Comb inequalities are essential cutting planes for the travelling salesman problem, yet their separation remains computationally challenging. We propose a quantum heuristic separation algorithm for this family of inequalities. The algorithm uses a procedure that prepares a uniform superposition of all combs with a fixed number of teeth using polynomially many gates and qubits. As part of this procedure, we present a circuit that coherently encodes the Hamming weight of a data register in one-hot form in an auxiliary register. The separation algorithm then searches for violated inequalities using the Grover-Mixer Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz. Its running time is polynomial under prescribed polynomial budgets for the number of QAOA rounds, parameter optimization steps and samples gathered, although we provide no evidence that such budgets suffice to find a violated comb with constant probability when one exists. We provide an explicit circuit construction for the mixer unitary, the full problem Hamiltonian and a resource analysis.
authors: Yohan Finet; Victor Drouin-Touchette

title: Study of localization properties under subsystem periodic driving
abstract: Periodic driving provides a powerful route for controlling localization and engineering effective Hamiltonians in quantum systems. A localized one-dimensional Aubry-André chain can be driven into a fully delocalized phase when the entire system is driven below a critical frequency. Here, we ask whether such delocalization can be achieved by driving only a part of the system. We address this question using a two-leg ladder comprising an Aubry-André chain coupled to a periodically driven clean tight-binding chain. Exact numerical calculations show that, starting from a localized static ladder, subsystem driving below a critical frequency cannot achieve complete delocalization. Instead, a mixed phase emerges, with localized and delocalized states coexisting and the fraction of delocalized states varying nonmonotonically with the driving frequency. This behavior can be understood using local effective Hamiltonians. Although these effective Hamiltonians are derived analytically in the high-frequency regime, they can nevertheless predict the localization transition occurring in the moderate-frequency regime. In fact, by quantifying the emergent nonlocality of the Floquet Hamiltonian, we show that these effective Hamiltonians provide a valid description up to a crossover frequency that is lower than the critical frequency associated with the localization transition. Our results demonstrate an alternative route to Floquet engineering, in which the transport properties of a quantum lattice system can be modified by driving only a subsystem.
authors: Arpita Goswami; Ranjan Modak; Shaon Sahoo

title: Classification of the Karlsson-Szollosi Intersection
abstract: We show that $K_6^{(2)} \cap X_6^{(2)} = D_6^{(1)} \cup C_6^{(1)}$ up to standard Hadamard equivalence, where $C_6^{(1)}$ is a non-affine one-parameter family of complex Hadamard matrices. This demonstrates that the intersection of the two-parameter Hadamard families of Karlsson and Szöllősi is strictly larger than the affine Diţă curve $D_6^{(1)}$. Our new parametrisation of the Szöllősi family $X_6^{(2)}$ in Karlsson coordinates and our constructive classification of the Karlsson-Szöllősi intersection shed light on the intersection of block-reducible forms and hypocycloid constraints. This may support the search for mutually unbiased bases in composite dimensions.
authors: André Ranchin

title: Quantum-Relativistic Anomalous Proper Time
abstract: We investigate surprising consequences of the hypothesis that gravity and proper time obey the quantum superposition principle. We show that, for a massive body prepared in a superposition of two positions and post-selected in a suitable final state, the elapsed proper time in another region of space can assume an anomalous effective value lying outside the range allowed by classical general relativity. Remarkably, the effective elapsed proper time can even become negative, corresponding to an effective evolution backward in time. We also propose an experiment to observe an anomalous effective proper time associated with the internal degrees of freedom of a quantum particle in an interferometer under Earth's gravitational field. The proposed experiment is, in principle, feasible with current technology, and its realization could provide the first experimental evidence of an interplay between quantum mechanics and general relativity beyond the effects of the Newtonian potential in flat spacetime.
authors: Pablo L. Saldanha; Nelson Yokomizo

title: Trial-space co-design for quantum simulation on noisy hardware
abstract: Quantum simulations on noisy hardware are often designed as if the machine were ideal, with device limitations considered only after the basis and measurement plan have been chosen. We instead use information about the physical problem and the device at an earlier stage, to decide which states and evolution times should form a compact simulation basis. Because the target problem remains unchanged, the method adapts only the representation used to solve it. Tests on many-body and molecular models show that this approach can reveal useful directions that ordinary time evolution misses, while also exposing an important limitation: some of these directions can become too similar to estimate reliably. Realistic device data further show that hardware response can change the preferred states and evolution times before execution. Across seven acquisition days, a four-qubit experiment shows a median 54\% reduction in projected-energy error from problem-informed time choices relative to uniform sampling under matched hardware conditions. These results provide a proof of principle for simulation-basis design as a practical interface between quantum algorithms and the hardware that executes them.
authors: Bo Peng; Vibin Abraham; Himadri Pathak

title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.
authors: Timur Javid; Brian Doolittle; Colin P. Lualdi; Brittany Conner; Michael Vayninger; Eric Chitambar; Paul G. Kwiat

title: Twirled and swirled worlds: a compositional approach
abstract: Twirled and swirled worlds describe generalised probabilistic theories (GPTs) restricted by symmetry-imposed superselection rules. We extend these constructions to a fully compositional setting for finite-dimensional GPTs and compact groups, treating states, effects, and multipartite transformations uniformly as processes. We distinguish system actions from process-space actions. We define actions on a theory as a whole by requiring the corresponding process-space actions to respect sequential and parallel composition. Averaging physical theory actions defines twirling, while averaging nonphysical theory actions defines swirling. We show that invariant subtheories might not satisfy process tomography, and establish conditions under which they do, involving invariant dynamically faithful states or internal classical reference frames. For locally tomographic parent theories, we prove that every theory symmetry admits a representation by linear system actions and that the invariant subtheory satisfies process tomography. An invariant multipartite process space fails local tomography if and only if some bipartition has sides sharing a non-trivial irreducible representation. We characterise when ancillary systems are necessary, which representations they must carry, and when entanglement is required for ancilla-free process tomography. We develop a framework for unifying twirled subtheories and extend incoherent simulations to compact groups. Finally, we recover bilocal classical theory as a twirled subtheory of classical theory and real quantum theory as a swirled subtheory of complex quantum theory, deriving their tomographic properties from their representation structure.
authors: Sina Soltani; Thomas D. Galley; Marco Erba; John H. Selby

title: Impact of nonlinear electrodynamics on quasinormal modes of rotating black strings
abstract: We study massless scalar perturbations of rotating anti-de Sitter black strings sourced by a power-Maxwell field with negative exponent $s$. The charge enters the metric function as $-Qr^{p}$ with $p=2/(1-2s)$, and the case $s=-1/2$ gives a linear term with an algebraic horizon. Since rotation is a local boost of the static string, the rotating spectrum follows exactly from the static one evaluated at a frequency-dependent momentum. We compute the spectrum with the Horowitz-Hubeny series, Chebyshev collocation and time-domain evolution, each implemented in two independent codes and checked against the planar Schwarzschild-AdS limit. The charge acts in two ways. At the reduced charge $\hat q_c=0.72626$ the least damped pair of modes meets on the imaginary axis, so more strongly charged strings ring down without oscillation, and at the endpoint of the branch the spectrum is exactly hypergeometric. At large transverse momentum the distance of the modes from the light cone grows as $k^{1/(1-4s)}$, replacing the $k^{-1/5}$ law of the neutral brane. Rotation continues the exceptional point into a line in the plane of charge and rotation, adds a purely damped axisymmetric tower, and never produces superradiant growth. A near-horizon estimate used earlier for this geometry misses all of these effects.
authors: F. S. Mirekhtiary; I. Sakalli

title: A new analytical finding for the Born-Infeld integral potential
abstract: A new finding regarding the Born-Infeld potential for short range distances from the charge revealed that its integral form can be almost exact written as the difference between a Coulomb-type potential and a Yukawa-type potential. This allowed for an immediate physical interpretation in terms of classical vacuum polarization and an effective mass. Subsequently, a new U(r) is proposed to cover the entire space. This formulation is then applied to calculate, in a closed manner, the first-order energy shifts in hydrogen-like atoms; a comparison of these shifts with high-precision spectroscopic data provides a model-dependent lower bound for the maximum field intensity parameter b.
authors: Leonardo Paulo Guimarães De Assis; Priscila Valdênia dos Santos; Sergio de Oliveira Vellozo; José Abdala Helayël Neto

title: Junction Hook Errors in the Color Code
abstract: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules have been proposed to mitigate hook errors in the triangular color code. Recent work by Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852) identifies distance-reducing hook errors by the type of anyon for which they provide a shortcut and chooses the CNOT ordering for stabilizers of each color to avoid these errors. We identify an additional class of distance-reducing hooks, which we call junction hook errors, that is not captured by this classification. The two data qubits of a junction hook error terminate anyon strings of two different colors at the point where the three colored strings of a logical operator meet, which we call the junction. As such, the hook error does not correspond to a single type of anyon, yet it still reduces the distance. For distances $d=7,9,11$, we verify that every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled hook error that, together with $d-2$ single data qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using $d-1$ faults. Each of these is a junction hook error. Because of this, every stabilizer, including those in the bulk, still requires additional protection from hook errors (such as flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance with this schedule. A minimum weight logical operator has at most one junction, however, so junction hook errors cannot accumulate on one minimum weight logical operator in the way that single-color malign hook errors can. This helps explain why the schedule still improves the circuit-level distance to $d-\lfloor (d+3)/6\rfloor$, rather than the $d/2$ distance associated with spatially uniform color code scheduling.
authors: Salahedeen Issa; Margaret Martonosi

title: Semiclassical dynamics of higher-order squeezing: self-adjoint extensions and coherent returns
abstract: Higher-order squeezing Hamiltonians have several self-adjoint realizations, while their classical trajectories reach infinity in finite time. We relate these extension problems through boundary amplitudes and the semiclassical propagation of coherent states. A discrete Fourier transformation gives the sink-to-source ray matrix of each quantum realization. After the first passage through infinity, the full Husimi probability measure converges to point masses on outgoing classical branches, with weights equal to the squared moduli of the matrix entries. The proof combines finite-order approximate tail solutions satisfying the exact extension boundary condition with full-norm Gaussian matching and a square-summable residual estimate. For positive energy, we determine the limit after any fixed number of passages: amplitudes evolve by powers of the unitary ray matrix, not by iterations of its squared-modulus matrix. We also realize these limits by concentrated complex amplitudes for an energy-preserving Liouville extension, distinguishing deterministic classical gluings from coherent boundary mixing.
authors: A. E. Teretenkov

title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes
abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is usually validated by the accuracy of mitigated observables, yet variational quantum optimization uses those observables to select parameters. We ask whether, and by how much, an accuracy gain from ZNE coincides with a worse decision. In depth-one simulations of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut on four to six qubits, each sampled $120\times120$ landscape yields both its mean-squared error (MSE) and the ideal regret of its selected grid minimum, comparing Richardson orders one to three with unmitigated estimation at the same total shot budget per grid point. In an exploratory screen of 675 conditions, whose per-point random seeds collide, a familywise (Holm) analysis retains only four of 540 replication conditions as showing both directional MSE improvement and regret increase. A frozen confirmation with 100 fresh paired repetitions per condition reproduces all four: median MSE improvements of 7.65-73.09% accompany median normalized regret increases of only 0.0031-0.0073. We distinguish a bias route, in which residual bias reorders the mean landscape, from a variance route, in which Richardson weights amplify finite-shot noise. Exact first and second moments on a bounded control grid find no bias-route reversal: mitigated mean landscapes preserve the ideal minima, and ZNE can more than halve expected MSE, yet finite-shot selections incur higher mean regret. Decision losses that survive strict testing are few and small in this benchmark, but reproducible and not revealed by aggregate MSE. We present a paired benchmark and recommend reporting decision regret alongside estimation error when mitigation is assessed for optimization. Results concern simulated exhaustive grids, not hardware or optimizer loops.
authors: Vicenzo Scavino Alfaro

title: Controlling transport with structured long-range hopping
abstract: The combined effects of disorder and long-range hopping play an important role in determining localization and transport in low-dimensional quantum systems. We study transport in a one-dimensional disordered chain with nearest-neighbor hopping supplemented by a long-range hopping term. The long-range coupling is characterized by site-dependent amplitudes that may be either uniform or random. We investigate the interplay between diagonal disorder and long-range hopping, characterizing the resulting transport efficiency. We find that nearest-neighbor hopping in the presence of uniform long-range hopping amplitudes strongly suppresses delocalization over a range of weak disorder. The disorder-enhanced transport regime, established in previous studies, can be understood here as the recovery of delocalization from this strongly suppressed regime. An analytical solution in the Anderson eigenstate basis reveals the microscopic origin of this behavior. In particular, we show that the low-disorder regime of strongly suppressed delocalization can be eliminated by introducing randomness into the long-range hopping amplitudes, providing an additional mechanism for enhancing transport and qualitatively changing the response of the system to disorder.
authors: Boris Gurevich; Michael H. Kolodrubetz

title: Dephasing-powered open quantum-dot battery
abstract: We propose a simple realization of an open quantum battery powered by local dephasing. The setup consists of a triple-quantum-dot chain coupled at one end to a thermal reservoir, with the dot at the opposite end strongly detuned to form a high-energy storage element. Local dephasing populates this highly excited state and autonomously drives the system into a nonequilibrium steady state with high ergotropic efficiency. We find a limit where the ergotropic efficiency approaches unity, while the ergotropy itself approaches one-third of the energy detuning. We characterize the battery through its energy-storage performance, charging time, and stability, showing that the charged state remains long-lived after the dephasing source is switched off. We then demonstrate two complementary protocols for extracting the stored energy. First, nearly all the available ergotropy can be recovered through a simple cyclic unitary protocol involving only modulation of the detuned-dot gate. Second, coupling the detuned dot to an electronic load allows the extraction of electrochemical work exceeding the initial ergotropy, thereby accessing part of the battery's passive energy. Our results establish local dephasing as an autonomous resource for charging open quantum batteries and demonstrate simple routes for extracting the resulting stored energy in experimentally accessible mesoscopic platforms.
authors: Alok Nath Singh; Rafael Sánchez; Andrew N. Jordan

title: Zeptojoule Microwave Calorimetry with Nanosecond Recovery in Graphene
abstract: Graphene calorimeters are predicted to combine extreme energy sensitivity with rapid thermal recovery, yet experiments remain far from ideal estimates. Here, we directly calibrate a graphene Josephson-junction microwave calorimeter using nanosecond pulses and independently determine the thermal parameters of the same operating device. At 110 mK, calibrated pulse measurements yield a characteristic switching-energy scale of 18.1 meV (2.90 zJ), while time-resolved two-pulse thermometry gives an intrinsic relaxation time of 19.5 ns. Pulse-width-dependent calorimetry and bolometric thermometry show that the electronic heat capacity is 12.4 times and the electron-phonon coupling is approximately 50 times larger than ideal estimates. A thermal model using these measured parameters predicts 21.2 meV, quantitatively reproducing the observed switching response. These results identify the microscopic origin of the sensitivity gap in graphene calorimeters and establish a self-consistent calibration framework for ultrafast nanoscale thermal detectors.
authors: Seunghan Lee; Woochan Jung; Jayeon Kim; Dongsung T. Park; Seong Jang; Seongeun Jeon; Kenji Watanabe; Takashi Taniguchi; Jong-Chul Park; Philip Kim; Kin Chung Fong; Gil-Ho Lee

title: Exact operator bounds on Leggett-Garg violations
abstract: Leggett-Garg (LG) inequalities test whether correlations measured at different times admit a positive joint probability distribution over histories. A violation requires negative values in any joint quasiprobability distribution reproducing those correlations, but such distributions can have negative values even without a violation. Spacetime density kernels extend the density-matrix description to multiple times and are used to study timelike entanglement. We establish a universal bound that relates LG violations to their negative eigenvalue weight. For LG tests involving any number of measurements, we determine the least compatible kernel negativity through an exact relation valid for any system dimension, initial state, dynamics, or measurement rule. This minimum is nonzero if and only if at least one LG inequality is violated. Three-time Lüders LG tests certify at most one eighth of negativity, whereas measurements resolving individual spin levels can approach one half. Including additional incompatible qubit observables gives a further exact minimum that can exceed the LG-only ceiling without increasing the LG violation.
authors: Rathindra Nath Das; Arnab Kundu; Nemai Chandra Sarkar

title: Communication Complexity of Integer Matrix Singularity
abstract: Alice and Bob hold complementary halves of the columns of an $n\times n$ matrix of $k$-bit integers and decide whether it is singular over $\mathbb Q$. Up to constant-factor dimension growth, this partitioned problem is equivalent to additive singularity, where Alice and Bob hold $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ of $k$-bit integers and test the singularity of $A+B$ over $\mathbb Q$. We prove a bounded-error quantum lower bound $Ω(\min\{n^{3/2}\sqrt{k\log n},n^2\log(nk)\})$ and a randomized upper bound $O(n^2\min\{k,\log(k+\log n)\})$. The bounds match at $Θ(n^2\log(nk))$ for $k\ge n\log n$. The lower bound holds even under the promise of rank $n-1$ versus $n$. Its proof combines an integer witness with a local digit encoding, while the upper-bound protocol lifts modular kernel relations using short messages. Bitwise sharing changes how the communication complexity depends on the entry bit length $k$. If Alice and Bob instead hold $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ of $k$-bit integers and test whether their entrywise bitwise XOR $A\oplus B$ is singular over $\mathbb Q$, we prove a quantum lower bound $Ω(n^2k)$, matching the trivial upper bound. This lower bound holds even under the promise of rank $n-1$ versus $n$. Our proof uses a dense weighted equation and a signed Fourier witness whose exceptional dyadic frequencies can be removed at small variation cost.
authors: Chengu Wang

title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.
authors: Benjamin Rossdeutscher; Jingbo Wang

title: When is a bosonic operator a Hamiltonian?
abstract: Hermitian polynomials in the quadrature operators $x$ and $p$ are the basic ingredients of continuous-variable quantum information, and increasingly exotic ones are now routinely engineered in superconducting circuits and trapped ions. However, such a polynomial need not define unique quantum dynamics: it may define exactly one, none, or an infinite family of physically distinct ones. Such obstructions are invisible to algebraic arguments and can compromise finite-dimensional truncations, which may fail to converge or silently converge to the wrong dynamics. We develop a method, implemented as an algorithm, which decides which case occurs, and how large the family is, from the coefficients alone, with no functional-analytic input from the user. For Gaussian operators the answer is always one; for non-Gaussian ones, a regime continuous-variable quantum computing cannot do without, the other outcomes occur already for simple and physically natural Hamiltonians. We apply the algorithm to operators drawn from the recent literature.
authors: Felix Fischer; Hermann Schulz-Baldes; Daniel Burgarth; Davide Lonigro

title: Admissible Subspaces for the Collective Haar Twirl: Schur-Weyl Classification and Heredity under Tensor-Factor Reduction
abstract: Quantum private broadcasting (\textsf{QPB}) asks whether a quantum message can be encrypted once, broadcast to several recipients, and decrypted locally while the joint ciphertext reveals no plaintext information. Broadbent, González-Guillén, and Schuknecht showed that the full tensor-power space \(\mathcal H_d^{\otimes t}\) is generally unsuitable for \textsf{QPB}, identified \(\mathrm{Sym}^t(\mathcal H_d)\) as a natural plaintext space, introduced symmetric unitary \(t\)-designs, and asked which other subspaces support private broadcast. Using Schur-Weyl duality, we classify all subspaces \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal H_d^{\otimes t}\) on which the collective Haar twirl \(\mathcal T^{(t)}\) is a replacement channel. Precisely, every Schur-Weyl block weight must be independent of the encoded state, and in each active block \(V_λ\otimes W_λ\), the reduced state on the multiplicity space \(W_λ\) must be fixed. This yields explicit two-block and general multiblock constructions and realizes the classification as the Schur-Weyl form of the Knill-Laflamme conditions for a complementary channel of \(\mathcal T^{(t)}\). We also introduce a canonical reduction under deletion of a recipient and characterize privacy heredity, design heredity, and \textsf{QPB}-heredity for exact restricted designs. The symmetric tower is fully \textsf{QPB}-hereditary, whereas the antisymmetric tower is fully privacy-hereditary and is design-hereditary from level \(s\) to \(s-1\) exactly when \(s\leq(d+1)/2\). For canonical carriers in arbitrary Schur-Weyl blocks, hereditary reduction is governed by multiplicity-free branching along the Young graph and inclusion of the associated Peter-Weyl coefficient spaces.
authors: Sayantan Ganguly

title: Competing Fault Histories in Lattice-Surgery Decoding
abstract: Different physical faults can produce the same detector record while carrying opposite logical labels. We investigate the consequence of this ambiguity for a lattice surgery parity measurement. In a distance-three merge--split circuit, single-gate faults compete with reset/readout pairs on three complete syndromes. Full-syndrome probabilities give a simultaneous 95\% lower confidence bound of $16.64$ parts per million on the cost of retaining the selected single-fault decisions at one noise point. Changing those decisions is harmful at low noise and beneficial at higher noise. To test the physical explanation, we attenuate eight implicated channels and compare the change in override effect with a matched non-target suppression. The two interventions change the decoder effect differently, resolving a contribution associated with those locations. Likelihood predictions fixed before sampling then select useful decisions under mixed Pauli noise and after extending preparation and recovery. The latter test gives a reduction of $13.20$ parts per million, with simultaneous 95\% bounds $[5.55,20.84]$. The mechanism is limited in scope: the revised decisions give up certain single-fault corrections, and under the same witness-selection rule no candidate is identified in the fully expanded distance-five circuit. These results connect a finite-noise decoding trade-off to specific physical channels and test how far that explanation can be used to predict logical-parity performance.
authors: Niharika Verma

title: Krylov geometry and optimal recovery under uncertain coherent noise
abstract: Recovery from a coherent rotation with an unobserved angle depends on both the encoding and what calibration reveals about the noise. We determine their combined limit for a known finite-dimensional generator and one final recovery. Two polynomial projections organize the answer. A physical Krylov chain separates correctable error amplitudes from their first state-dependent distortion; projection onto lower-angle powers identifies the part that a coherent decoder can cancel. Under explicit rank and moment conditions, their combination gives the exact leading optimal entanglement infidelity at weak noise and a recovery attaining it for any finite logical dimension. The optimal worst-input error lies between one and $d$ times that infidelity at leading order, for logical dimension $d$. When the angle distribution is unknown, we optimize one decoder for every distribution compatible with the calibration. When spectral and calibration frequencies are integer multiples of a common frequency, moment positivity turns this into an exact finite optimization. Small measured means can still allow rare finite rotations. If the sole calibration datum is $β_r=\mathbb E[\sin^{2r}(θ/2)]$, with $θ$ the wrapped rotation phase at that common frequency, the optimal worst-prior infidelity is $O(β_r)$ exactly when generator powers through degree $r-1$ are correctable. When the first uncorrectable power has degree $m<r$, the optimal loss scales as $β_r^{m/r}$, with a sharp coefficient fixed by a universal moment problem. In a loss-free four-photon memory, population measurements at two calibration durations retain the fully informed quartic error coefficient for a fixed symmetric narrow-noise family with positive variance and finite fourth moment; a single duration permits loss quadratic in the noise width.
authors: Abhishek Chowdhury

title: The Coherent State Projection Eigenvalue Theorem
abstract: Recent papers have developed a cyclic symmetry projected extension for coherent state representations of bosonic Hilbert space. This extension can greatly reduce sampling errors in phase-space simulations of bosonic quantum systems that have symmetries. Here we prove an eigenvalue theorem for the continuum limit of the projected coherent states. Our intuitively appealing result is that in the continuum limit the projected coherent states are eigenstates of the symmetry generating operator. This result gives a differential identity in phase-space that includes the conserved eigenvalues. Detailed applications of these differential identities to obtaining improved Fokker-Planck and stochastic equations in many-body physics will be given elsewhere.
authors: Peter D. Drummond; Margaret D. Reid

title: Path-Distinguishability Gaps at Fixed Visibility in Noisy Qubit Interferometers
abstract: The wave--particle duality relation bounds visibility and path distinguishability but does not determine their attainable values in a fixed noisy interferometer. We characterize the complete attainable region for a two-path interferometer with a qubit marker, varying the marker input while fixing the source, preparation channel, path-dependent interaction, and subsequent marker channel. At each feasible fringe visibility, the Helstrom-optimal distinguishabilities form at most two closed intervals, which can be separated by a gap. The intervals arise from opposite axial marker polarizations with the same fringe-amplitude modulus. Fixing the complex fringe amplitude instead gives a connected interval; for balanced original-path discrimination, a gap requires nonunital marker preparation. For a balanced pure source, relative $π$ rotations, and no subsequent marker noise, we obtain a necessary and sufficient geometric criterion for a gap under some rotation axis perpendicular to the preparation displacement. Explicit channels and a time-independent Lindblad realization show how the gap depends on preparation geometry and evolution, with exact onset and optimization formulas at fixed fractional visibility. We also give sufficient bounds for excluding distinguishability intervals under calibrated finite-resolution errors.
authors: Mohd Asad Siddiqui

title: Deep-Microscopic Photonic Bandstructure of a Two-Dimensional Honeycomb Lattice
abstract: Conventional descriptions of light in materials rely on macroscopic models that average the optical response over the microscopic lattice structures. These models are deployed in the semi-classical limit, where the collective local response over many lattice sites is adequate. However, they fail to capture the full spatial dispersion, which requires a lattice-resolved description of light. We address this limitation by formulating a deep-microscopic nonlocal theory of the photon based on the Maxwell Hamiltonian and its characteristic equation. The solution reveals the full spatial dispersion in the form of deep-microscopic photonic bandstructure, and corresponding real-space Bloch field textures. We demonstrate our theory for a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a gapped honeycomb lattice. Our framework thus extends photons to the same microscopic footing as electrons or phonons, providing a unified route to studying topology, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations of light in dispersive materials.
authors: Pronoy Das; Sathwik Bharadwaj; Wenbo Sun; Zubin Jacob

title: Task-Directed Spectral Design for Local Quantum Tomography
abstract: Many tomography tasks require only a low-dimensional function of the state. We study local pure-state tomography under projective-fidelity access when a parametric model, a credible center, and a differentiable downstream task are known before acquisition. The pullback Fubini--Study metric and the task metric define coordinate-invariant generalized eigendirections, which we realize as a fixed library of geodesic fidelity probes. We prove two optimality results: the probe aligned with a task coordinate is its unique variance-minimizing location up to orientation, and, when prior and measurement information are diagonal in this basis, a diminishing-return greedy rule exactly minimizes the integer-budget local task-variance surrogate over the spectral library. Under common per-shot information and the stated large-budget condition, the absolute and relative gaps to arbitrary probe directions are respectively \(O(B^{-3})\) and \(O(B^{-2})\). A closed-form local estimator is followed by a task-metric localization projection that cannot increase quadratic task loss when localization holds. In six-qubit numerical experiments, the Schmidt-spectrum design activates only one or two settings and has lower mean task error than the post hoc best adaptive results across all tested dimensions and copy budgets. For full-state tomography, it likewise has lower mean infidelity throughout the tested local regime. The fixed batch uses no feedback loops and far fewer settings; under the illustrative latency model, its acquisition cost is roughly three to four orders of magnitude lower than that of the adaptive methods.
authors: Guy Hay; Nir Sharon

title: Induced Bell-CHSH observables in the Fewster-Verch measurement scheme
abstract: The Summers-Werner theorem shows that the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory violates the Bell-CHSH inequality maximally on complementary wedges, but it is an existence statement: it exhibits neither the observables nor an apparatus that measures them. We give an explicit operator-level realization within the Fewster-Verch measurement framework, obtaining dichotomic Bell observables of a free Majorana field in $1+1$ dimensions as observables induced by local couplings to Majorana probes. The induced system smearing factorizes exactly as $f_h=k\,b_{λ,h}$, so its support is controlled by the compactly supported coupling profile $k$; dichotomy is imposed by calibrating and normalizing the induced smearings rather than required of the probe observable; and a probe-only normal ordering yields the product of Alice's and Bob's induced bilinears, which the non-multiplicative induced map alone does not provide. Under explicit attainability hypotheses the induced observables saturate the Tsirelson bound in a state prepared from the vacuum. The construction extends to coupled scalar fields.
authors: M. S. Guimaraes; I. Roditi; S. P. Sorella

title: Efficient Block Encodings of Vibrational Hamiltonians
abstract: Simulation of molecular vibrations is emerging as a promising application of quantum computing in quantum chemistry. In this work, we develop new strategies for block-encoding the second-quantized $n$-mode representation of the vibrational Hamiltonian, whose algebraic structure closely parallels that of the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. We derive linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) representations of this Hamiltonian based on Pauli decomposition and tensor hypercontraction (THC) and construct efficient circuits for the corresponding block encodings. We also extend the Block-Invariant Symmetry Shift (BLISS) technique to vibrational Hamiltonians, yielding a lower LCU 1-norm and, consequently, a lower overall circuit cost. For the molecules considered here, BLISS-THC reduces the Toffoli cost of quantum phase estimation by more than two orders of magnitude relative to existing block-encoding approaches. In comparison with recent Trotter-based methods, it shows up to a ninefold reduction in the T-gate count, with the relative savings tending to increase with system size. Asymptotically, and up to polylogarithmic factors, both the Pauli and THC LCUs trade additional ancillas for a quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modes, while THC provides an additional quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modals. These results highlight the importance of Hamiltonian factorizations and Toffoli-qubit tradeoffs for reducing the computational cost of quantum simulations of molecular vibrations.
authors: Shashank G. Mehendale; Ignacio Loaiza; Shreyas Malpathak; Stepan Fomichev; Danial Motlagh; Artur F. Izmaylov

title: Banach-Cesaro positive operator-valued measure
abstract: We construct a family of bounded, finitely additive, covariant positive operator-valued measures (POVMs) on the real line by applying generalised Banach-Cesaro asymptotic averaging to locally finite covariant POVMs. In contrast to the strictly shift-invariant case, where countably additive operator measures are restricted to scalar multiples of a single fixed operator, the introduced covariant setting allows for non-commuting averaged operator values while successfully normalising the total mass. We develop an integration theory for complex-valued functions by taking the completion of simple integrable functions with respect to the continuous operator norm induced by the positive integral of their absolute values. The integration spaces for the original and the averaged measures are shown to possess distinct null classes. Finally, we introduce the operator-valued Fourier transform on these integration spaces and analyze the core algebraic constraints imposed by the covariance property on the exponential multipliers.
authors: Sviatoslav V. Dzhenzher

title: Initial-State Preparation for Strongly Correlated Molecules from Matrix Product States: Benchmarking and Environment-Aware Divide-and-Conquer Compilation
abstract: Compiling classically optimized matrix product states (MPSs) into quantum circuits is a promising route to initial-state preparation for strongly correlated molecules, but the accuracy, gate cost, and classical scalability of existing MPS compilation methods have not been systematically assessed. Here, we benchmark representative analytical, variational, and hybrid MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated systems including hydrogen chains and iron-sulfur clusters. We compare state infidelity, CNOT gate count, classical runtime, and parallel scalability across different system sizes and bond dimensions. We also introduce a divide-and-conquer environment-aware compilation algorithm (DCE), which optimizes each local isometry approximation according to its contribution to the prepared-state fidelity. The results reveal complementary operating regimes: direct variational compilation methods are gate-efficient for some smaller molecular systems with $O(10)$ qubits and $O(10)$ bond dimensions or moderate accuracy targets with infidelity of order $10^{-1}$, whereas divide-and-conquer methods scale more favorably for larger systems and relatively higher bond dimensions of $O(10\text{-}10^2)$, particularly when target infidelities below $10^{-1}$ are required. Within the latter family, environment-aware optimization improves accuracy over unitary-distance-based compilation while retaining task-level parallelism. For the FeMo-cofactor (FeMoco), we find the DCE algorithm together with the MPS obtained in the entanglement-minimized orbitals (EMOs) provides a resource-efficient route to initial-state preparation. Our results provide practical guidance for selecting and developing MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated molecular simulations.
authors: Haiqi Liu; Longfei Chang; Zhendong Li; Wei-Hai Fang

title: V-Representability Beyond Singular Times in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory: The Hubbard Dimer Case
abstract: We study the global $V$-representability problem in time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) for the two-particle Hubbard dimer model in the spin-singlet sector. In particular, we investigate whether the time-dependent density of the interacting system obtained for a given one-body external potential $u$ (the tunable control variable) can be reproduced by a non-interacting Kohn--Sham system beyond the singular times at which the usual inversion formulas break down. We deal with both the conventional formulation of TDDFT based on some time-dependent variational principle and the recently introduced geometric formulation of TDDFT (Phys. Rev. Lett. 136 (2026) 256401, Phys. Rev. A 113 (2026) 062222). For both principles, we prove global-in-time $V$-representability, show that singular times induce non-uniqueness of the time-dependent effective potential, and classify the set of solutions.
authors: Éric Cancès; Théo Duez

title: Helstrom geometry with time-dependent spectral calibration
abstract: In a recent work we introduced a finite scalar-qubit-scalar spectral triple whose Connes distance reproduces the Bloch-ball trace metric up to a factor $2/Λ$, where $Λ^2=μ_L^2+μ_R^2$ for isotropic link strengths $μ_L,μ_R$ appearing in the proposed Dirac operator. Here we analyse time-dependent variation of these links, independent of the qubit dynamics. In doing so, we separate the distinguishability and calibration contributions to the spectral rate. A depolarizing example demonstrates spectral growth despite a monotonic contraction of the trace-distance. More generally, we characterize the admissible trace-distance histories compatible with a given positive spectral record and exhibit contracting and reviving realizations. At fixed $Λ$, we also study a sinusoidal link imbalance that preserves the Dirac spectrum and qubit metric, while the scalar-scalar distance oscillates with half the period of the imbalance.
authors: Kaushlendra Kumar

title: Hidden Fisher Information in Many-Body Quantum Sensors
abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) determines the ultimate precision of a quantum sensor after optimization over all allowed measurements, but it does not quantify how difficult the optimal readout is to implement. We introduce a moment Fisher hierarchy $F_M^{(k)}$, which measures the fraction of QFI accessible to collective spin moments up to degree $k$, together with a readout-complexity scale $k_{90}$ defined by the minimum degree required to recover $90\%$ of the QFI. Applying this framework to a nonlinear collective-spin sensor, we show that many-body dynamics can preserve large QFI while transferring the optimal readout into high-rank $SU(2)$ tensor sectors inaccessible to low-order collective observables. For system sizes up to $N=100$, first moments access only $\sim 10^{-2}$ of the available QFI, while the degree required to recover $90\%$ of it grows to $k_{90}\simeq 28$.
