title: Multipartite entanglement swapping with homodyne and single photon detection
abstract: Establishing multipartite entanglement across lossy optical networks remains a central challenge for distributed quantum information processing. Here, we consider a non-Gaussian continuous-variable entanglement-swapping protocol combining a symmetric discrete Fourier transform (DFT) interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. In the ideal limit, single-photon heralding generates a $W_N$-class state across remote modes, with Fourier symmetry rendering all single-click outcomes equivalent up to local phase corrections. We find that conditional pairwise entanglement can exceed that of conventional Gaussian homodyne swapping in weak-to-moderate squeezing and lossy regimes, remaining nonzero beyond the channel-loss thresholds at which Gaussian pairwise entanglement vanishes. These results demonstrate that combining non-Gaussian measurements with symmetric interferometric mixing can improve both the resilience and operational efficiency of multipartite entanglement distribution in lossy quantum networks.
authors: Tarek Assaf; Josephine Dias

title: Quantum resource trade-offs of mixed sparse single and double factorization for qubitization-based phase estimation
abstract: We study a mixed block encoding of quantum-chemistry Hamiltonians for quantum phase estimation (QPE) on fault-tolerant quantum computers. Following a Cholesky decomposition of the electron repulsion integral tensor, we assign each Cholesky tensor to either a double-factorization (DF) branch or a sparse-single-factorization (SPSF) branch. This freedom permits a trade-off between reducing the block-encoding normalization factor $λ$ with DF and reducing the coefficient data loaded through quantum read-only memory (QROM) with SPSF. Resource estimates across molecular benchmarks show, however, that the mixed circuit does not generally reduce the Toffoli count relative to the less expensive pure circuit. The main obstacles are the overhead of loading substantial data through separate branch-specific QROMs and the limited benefit of mixing when the pure DF and SPSF circuits have dissimilar costs. Modest savings occur only in restricted parameter regimes, most clearly when logical-qubit requirements are included in the cost metric. These results identify the circuit-level conditions that a useful mixed block encoding must satisfy.
authors: Troy Losey; Jacob Z. Williams; Avanish Mishra; Jian-Xin Zhu; Yu Zhang

title: A Study of Fluctuation Growths of Observables in Open Quantum Systems
abstract: The rate at which quantum fluctuations of observables can change provides a useful characterization of the dynamical behavior of quantum systems. For closed quantum systems undergoing unitary evolution, previous work has established a general upper bound on the growth rate of the uncertainty of an observable in terms of the standard deviation of its dynamical velocity. This result is closely related to quantum acceleration limits and provides a compact constraint on fluctuation growth. In this work, we will briefly review the closed system results and extend this perspective to open quantum systems, where the state evolves nonunitarily as a consequence of interactions with an environment. The central result is an upper bound on the rate of growth of the uncertainty of an observable that remains valid for general density-matrix dynamics. We develop two complementary derivations. The first introduces a Hermitian pseudo-Hamiltonian describing the local unitary evolution of the eigenvectors of the density matrix. The second, and more general, derivation proceeds directly from the density-matrix derivative and therefore does not require knowledge of the generator of the dynamics. Both approaches lead to the same fluctuation-growth bound. An important practical advantage is that the bound can be evaluated from the observable, the state, and its time derivative without requiring reconstruction of the complete dynamical generator.
authors: Newshaw Bahreyni; Paul M. Alsing; Carlo Cafaro; Walid Redjem; Christian Corda

title: Tensor-network simulation of strongly coupled multi-fluxonium circuits
abstract: Designing a superconducting quantum processor rests on predicting the low-lying spectrum of its coupled circuit. The Hilbert-space dimension of the circuit's lumped-element model grows exponentially with the number of circuit nodes. The usual methods split the circuit into subsystems, but that split is hard to choose when the elements are strongly coupled. We present a tensor-network method that chooses no subsystems and whose memory and run time per solve are set by the number of modes and two truncations, the Fock cutoff of each normal mode and the bond dimension of a matrix product state (MPS), not by the Hilbert-space dimension. From the capacitance matrix, the inverse-inductance matrix and the junction list alone, the linear circuit is diagonalized into normal modes. Each junction cosine is then a sum of two products of single-mode operators, so the complete lumped-element Hamiltonian is a matrix product operator (MPO) of small bond dimension with one site per mode, solved by the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The normal modes make the method generic, and the tensor network makes it affordable. For two fluxonia joined by a tunable coupler, the method agrees with exact diagonalization of the same truncated space to within 1 MHz. Our circuit of three fluxonia joined by two couplers has 11 normal modes and a truncated space of $10^9$ states, out of reach of exact diagonalization in dense or sparse storage. At a bond dimension of 32, its lowest eight levels are converged to within 1 MHz in both truncations, and each state is stored in a small fraction of the numbers a dense vector needs. One solve at that bond dimension takes 81 min and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node.
authors: Christian Hensel; Andrés N. Cáliz; Pau Torrente; María Hita-Pérez; Arnau Riera

title: Efficient training of a 128-modes 3D continuously coupled photonic chip via limited quantum resources
abstract: Integrated photonics provides a promising route towards the development of large-scale, stable and low-loss quantum hardware. Existing implementations of universal quantum photonic chips generally rely on architectures consisting of localised interactions between the modes that can be programmed with known algorithms to implement specific operations. Recent advances have shown that interferometers based on 3D continuously coupled waveguide arrays may allow to significantly scale up the number of modes with reduced overhead. However, for this class of devices, optimal strategies to set the controllable parameters and obtain the desired transformation have not been demonstrated generally. In this work, we report the use of a machine learning algorithm driven by quantum data to program the operation of a reconfigurable three-dimensional continuously coupled photonic device comprising 128 modes. We show experimentally the capability of reaching a target unitary matrix, among those achievable by the device, through a limited number of one- and two-photon measurements. Our results demonstrate that this approach results to be effective in the presence of noise and with a limited amount of resources, also allowing to partially compensate imperfections in the experimental setup. This method can thus represent a viable route towards programming large scale integrated photonic devices, unlocking the possibility of controlling photonic systems for which an analytical decomposition is not trivial.
authors: Denis Stanev; Simone Di Micco; Francesco Hoch; Taira Giordani; Nicolò Spagnolo; Marco Gardina; Andrea Crespi; Francesco Ceccarelli; Roberto Osellame; Fabio Sciarrino

title: Dynamical Signatures of Selective Gap Closing in Multi-Dimensional Monotone Quasiperiodic Operators
abstract: We translate the spectral gap-closing criterion for multi-dimensional monotone quasiperiodic Schrödinger operators into a concrete dynamical protocol and verify it by large-scale numerics. For a non-principal label we construct a sampling function whose leading eigenfunction weight at the origin vanishes; a local bump then drives the residual weight through zero. The height of a weighted oscillatory time average of the origin-to-localization-center correlator exhibits a deep minimum precisely at the closing, while the site-control label remains featureless and orders of magnitude larger. The signature is robust and maps directly onto superconducting-circuit and photonic platforms.
authors: Leonid Parnovski; Roman Shterenberg

title: Exact Mirror-Parity Selection Rule for Electron-Phonon Coupling in Two-Dimensional Crystals
abstract: The electron--phonon (e-ph) interaction underlies conventional superconductivity and plays a central role in transport and other many-body phenomena in solids. Here, we derive a symmetry selection rule for e-ph scattering in two-dimensional crystals possessing a horizontal mirror plane, $σ_h$. For electronic states of mirror parity $s_n(\mathbf{k})$ and $s_m(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})$, and a phonon mode of parity $χ_ν(\mathbf{q})$, we show that the e-ph matrix element $g_{mn,ν}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})$ vanishes identically unless $s_n(\mathbf{k})\,χ_ν(\mathbf{q})\, s_m(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q})=+1$. The rule follows from the covariance of the phonon-induced deformation potential under $σ_h$, constitutes the $C_s$ case of the general group-theoretical selection rule for matrix elements, and partitions the e-ph interaction throughout the Brillouin zone into symmetry-allowed and symmetry-forbidden scattering channels. Consequently, mirror-even phonons couple electronic states of the same mirror parity, either even--even or odd--odd, whereas mirror-odd phonons couple only states of opposite mirror parity, for both intra- and interband processes. We illustrate the selection rule through first-principles calculations for the two-dimensional superconductor $\mathrm{Sc_2BCH_4}$, where mirror parity is well defined throughout the entire Brillouin zone and symmetry-forbidden matrix elements vanish up to numerical precision. We then extend the analysis to bulk $\mathrm{MgB_2}$, where the rule applies exactly only on mirror-invariant planes of the three-dimensional Brillouin zone. Moving away from these planes removes the exact mirror constraint and activates scattering channels that are symmetry forbidden when the mirror eigenvalues are well defined. Our results establish horizontal mirror symmetry as an exact and practical filter of e-ph scattering processes.
authors: Nicolás F. Barrera; Javiera Cabezas-Escares; Francisco Munoz; Carlos Cardenas; Julia Contreras-García

title: Trinetra.Q: Statistical and Behavioral Detection of Attacks on the Quantum-Error-Correction Layer and Classical Control Stack of Quantum Computing Systems
abstract: Most quantum-computer security work targets physical-layer attacks on qubits, while two surfaces remain inadequately defended: the quantum-error-correction (QEC) syndrome-and-decoder pipeline, and the classical control and software stack that runs it. Tampering on these surfaces can corrupt a computation while the physical error rate appears normal, and can stay within a single-circuit integrity tolerance. We present Trinetra.Q, a detection layer of cooperating detectors, each monitoring a statistical or behavioral property of quantum-domain data against an envelope calibrated from honest operation, and raising an indication only on a statistically significant deviation. The detectors cover (A) QEC integrity over per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect-count, and repeated-syndrome rate; (B) decoder confidence over the margin between minimum-weight error explanations in distinct logical classes; (C) behavioral output divergence, flagging crosstalk-class and novel attacks by their effect on a victim's output relative to a matched control; (D) control-stack tampering via known-answer canary circuits, built to be indistinguishable to a resident implant, with a cross-job consistency statistic; and (E) compilation/execution integrity. Each gates on significance, so honest operation raises no alarm. We evaluate in faithful simulation and on three production IBM Heron processors, and bound the physical attack surface with a systematic negative map: most physical-layer attacks return statistically null, the exception an implemented, measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive. Every detector is also evaluated against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of it. To our knowledge this is the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC layer and classical control stack of a quantum computing system, demonstrated on production hardware.
authors: Garrv Sipani

title: The most entangled states of four and seven qubits
abstract: Pure states of four and seven qubits cannot be maximally entangled across every balanced bipartition; we determine how entangled they can be on average. For four qubits we prove the conjecture of Higuchi and Sudbery: the mean von Neumann entropy of the three $2|2$ cuts is at most $1+\tfrac12\log_2 3$ bits, with equality exactly on the local-unitary orbits of their state $M_4$ and its complex conjugate. For seven qubits the mean purity of the 35 balanced $3|4$ cuts is at least $121/917$ and their mean entropy is at most $2.965356029\ldots$ bits, each with a unique optimiser up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. The two optimisers are distinct members of one icosahedral family, so minimum purity and maximum entropy select different states. The proofs bound moments of the marginal spectra by positive identities on several copies of the state, some of them spin flipped, and bound the entropy by a polynomial in those moments. The four-qubit maximum has an analytic proof; the seven-qubit proofs, and some of the four-qubit refinements below, are computer-assisted, with exact arithmetic and rigorous error bounds. We also prove the Gour--Wallach conjecture for Rényi entropies of all orders, with the maximiser changing from $M_4$ to cluster states at $q_*\approx1.588$, and obtain sharp Tsallis bounds, mixed-state bounds and quantitative stability.
authors: Antony Lewis

title: Static and dynamical Casimir effects in a wedge within the worldline formulation
abstract: We study a real massless scalar field in $d+1$ dimensions confined to a wedge of opening angle $α$, in the presence of a semitransparent circular arc that may oscillate radially. Within the worldline formulation, and for an arbitrary strength $λ$ of the $δ$-potential that models the arc, we expand the effective action in powers of the radial displacement $R$ of the arc. In this formulation, all the information about the media is contained in the propagator of a non-relativistic point particle, so that known results for that propagator can be used directly. At zeroth order we obtain the Casimir energy of the wedge, with Dirichlet, Neumann or mixed walls, and the contribution of the arc in closed form for arbitrary $λ$. We show that the worldline integrand is, point by point, the energy density obtained from the energy-momentum tensor of the scalar field with curvature coupling $ξ=1/4$; with this identification, and using dimensional regularization for the integrated quantities, we recover the known results for the wedge and for the wedge closed by a Dirichlet arc. At second order in $R$, we reduce the form factor that determines the imaginary part of the in-out effective action, and hence the probability of pair creation by the moving arc, to a one-loop expression involving the radial Green's functions of each angular sector. In the narrow-wedge limit, each angular sector behaves as a field with a mass set by the angular quantization, coupled to a moving $δ$-mirror; for a Dirichlet arc, the pair creation spectrum of the exterior region approaches that of a planar massive mirror, while the interior region behaves as a tapered cavity. Finally, by decomposing the electromagnetic field into TE and TM scalars, we obtain the Casimir energy of wedges with perfectly conducting, perfectly permeable and mixed walls.
authors: César Daniel Fosco; Bruno Cardin Guntsche

title: Exact teleportation bounds for fermionic Hawking thermality beyond the single-mode approximation
abstract: Fermionic teleportation near a Schwarzschild horizon involves two physically distinct ingredients that are often varied together: Hawking thermal mixing and the relative composition of the right and left Unruh modes. We separate them by factorizing the reduced map of the detected exterior fermionic mode into a mode-preparation channel and a Hawking thermal channel. At fixed right-left Unruh-mode composition, we then solve a global constrained quantum-channel optimization over all two-qubit resource states whose fully entangled fraction remains at or below the standard teleportation threshold immediately before thermal mixing. A parity twirl and positivity reduce the arbitrary-state problem exactly to a two-variable quadratic optimization. The solution yields a necessary-and-sufficient activation boundary, a second exact boundary for attaining the universal optimum, and explicit optimizing states. The resulting phase diagram contains a strict no-go region, a composition-limited activation region, and a universal-bound region. The analysis converts state-specific observations of Hawking-assisted teleportation into exact channel-level bounds over the full two-qubit state space.
authors: Zhiming Huang

title: Coherence Spreading Law in Quenched Homogeneous Bose Gases
abstract: We investigate nonequilibrium coherence spreading in quenched homogeneous bosonic gases both analytically and numerically. Our ensemble-averaged Gross-Pitaevskii trajectory approach and kinetic analysis confirm the linear-in-time growth of the squared coherence length, and explicitly give the spreading-law dependence on the ratio of initial energy to healing energy. When the ratio is relatively small, the squared coherence length grows at a universal rate determined by the ratio of Planck's constant to the particle mass, insensitive to interaction strength and initial momentum distributions. However, our further calculations uncover fundamental limitations to such universality and establish its phase boundaries governed by low system energies, weak interparticle interactions and many-body integrability. Our theory fully reproduces the key experimental signatures and resolves the puzzle of the dynamical origin of the recently observed universal coherence-spreading speed limit [Nature 647, 608-612 (2025)]. Going beyond existing experimental observations, we provide some testable predictions for ultracold-atom experiments and clarify the conditions for the emergence of universal coherent dynamics in nonequilibrium bosonic many-body systems.
authors: Yi Cao; Li-Chen Zhao; Jie Liu

title: Emergent Incompressibility in Polariton Condensates for Scalable XY Spin Simulation
abstract: Driven-dissipative polariton networks offer a powerful analog platform for simulating continuous-spin Hamiltonians. However, their practical scalability is fundamentally limited by amplitude-phase coupling and metastable trapping in highly frustrated energy landscapes. Here, we present an \textit{in situ} dual-enhancement mechanism to address these bottlenecks without requiring external site-specific fine-tuning. First, a renormalization-group analysis based on density rescaling shows that higher-order nonlinear loss drives the condensates toward an incompressible regime, intrinsically suppressing amplitude fluctuations and enforcing phase-only dynamics. For macroscopic XY networks (up to 10,000 spins), this phase-amplitude decoupling yields a more than 50-fold reduction in energy, while simultaneously shrinking the standard deviation by a factor of six. More generally, it restores the extensive scaling of the optimized XY energy with system size. Second, to navigate the rugged, nonconvex energy landscape, we introduce weak Hermitian pulses. When implemented through a multistage protocol, these pulses enable repeated escapes from local minima and drive the system to deeper energy minima. Benchmarking shows an increasing advantage with system size, with the polariton simulator outperforming the classical Monte Carlo-SQP baseline in every sampled macroscopic realization. Our work provides a physical framework for scalable polariton analog computing.
authors: Chengyong Yu; Youya Xu; Xuan Ye; Yan Zhou; Sanjib Ghosh

title: Structural Lower Bounds for Quantum Property Estimation with Persistent Memory
abstract: In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees. We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling. Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.
authors: Ye Tao; Hong Shen

title: Analytic two-body density-matrix spectrum of the Fermionic Tonks-Girardeau gas
abstract: The two-body density matrix (TBDM) of a quantum many-body system provides information about particle correlations, e.g., pairing. In this work, we derive the complete spectrum of the TBDM of the fermionic Tonks-Girardeau gas using its exact ground-state wavefunction in second quantization. We obtain analytical expressions for all eigenvalues and eigenvectors for an arbitrary number of particles and identify two different types of eigenstates: collective states, formed by superpositions of paired momentum modes, and single-determinant states. We provide a physical interpretation of this structure, explaining the origin of the different eigenstates and their degeneracies. We further derive an asymptotic expansion for the largest eigenvalue, improving on previous estimates and analytically confirming its linear scaling with the particle number, thereby indicating off-diagonal long-range order. For the high-index collective states, we obtain simpler expressions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, showing that the eigenvalues decay as $n^{-4}$ and that the eigenvectors become independent of the number of particles. Finally, we discuss the connection between the collective states and an effective description in terms of composite bosons, whose spectral properties suggest a behavior consistent with Tan's contact for interacting bosonic systems.
authors: Abel Rojo-Francàs; Joan Martorell; Francesc Sabater; Bruno Juliá-Díaz

title: Classical records and Bell correlations in a dynamically formed quantum body
abstract: Competing quantum contacts can create a boundary that was absent from the specification of a subsystem. We construct approximately isolated bodies from bare field vacuum and zero-centred contact packets. A binding contribution with vanishing mean energy density nevertheless changes a bounded formation signal by order one at the same clock. On the formed material spins and their original memories, coarse collective records precede an all-outcome Bell violation. The field evolves dynamically, with the finite bath, residual boundary interaction, failed records and preparation costs retained. The result connects dynamical subsystem formation, classical collective records and microscopic nonlocality, with polynomial resources in the stated preparation and measurement class.
authors: XinXin Qi; Hao Sun

title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization
abstract: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert-Schmidt asymmetry $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$, which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit $S$-wave $p+{}^3\mathrm{He}$ two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from $\textit{ab initio}$ many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.
authors: Eunjin In; Kristina D. Launey; Darin C. Mumma; James A. Sauls

title: Efficiently tracking errors and outcomes in universal quantum circuits
abstract: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.
authors: Thomas R. Scruby; Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente

title: Quantum Advantage in Sensing and Imaging through Coherent Nuisance Suppression
abstract: Many sensing and imaging problems must contend with unknown nuisance parameters such as aberrations, background fields, and drift, and the cost of removing these noise sources can dominate the sample budget. In contrast to classical receivers, a quantum receiver can processes samples jointly to directly access observables in which common nuisance is suppressed. We introduce a relational Fourier sampling algorithm for optimal, source-independent imaging with a programmable quantum camera, which uses quantum pixels and a quantum computer to capture and process photon states. We demonstrate its relevance for general astronomical imaging as well as super-resolution and transient-object tracking through drifting atmospheric turbulence. A quantum camera that resolves an optical wavefront across $2^q$ spatial modes using $q$ receiving qubits, with a full-rank and strongly-correlated nuisance over those modes, can yield an exponential sample-complexity reduction of $\exp[Ω(2^q)]$. For typical seeing conditions at leading ground-based observatories, we predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer photons to resolve point-source positions using only 15 processing qubits and a depth-9 circuit. Our work identifies coherent nuisance suppression as a novel mechanism for provable quantum advantage with direct relevance to many sensing tasks.
authors: Maxim Sirotin; Aleksandr Mokeev; Ishaan Kannan; Julian C. Christou; Jayadev Rajagopal; Babak Saif; Mikhail D. Lukin; Johannes Borregaard

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.
authors: Yuya Kawamata; Keisuke Fujii

title: Algorithmic Wave-Particle Duality: Pathfinding in Welded Trees is Hard
abstract: In the welded trees problem, an algorithm navigates a randomly labeled graph formed from two binary trees joined at their leaves through a "weld" of connecting edges. A quantum walk can navigate from root to root exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, recording its path destroys the constructive interference responsible for the speedup, leaving open whether some quantum algorithm can efficiently find a path between the roots. We prove that, for trees of height $n$, the quantum query complexity of finding a path between the roots with constant probability is $\tildeΘ(2^{n/3})$. This establishes an algorithmic wave-particle duality, adapting the double-slit experiment to the high-complexity regime: interference between many paths lets a quantum algorithm reach the exit efficiently, but finding a single path (the algorithmic analog of the route of a particle) requires exponentially many queries. Furthermore, the bound is tight, matching the cost of a quantum algorithm that finds collisions between paths from each root to the weld. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle to track the information about the graph that an algorithm retains and forgets. We show that the compressed database remains close to a space of states that do not record a path between the roots by bounding the error introduced by each compressed oracle query.
authors: Joseph Carolan; Andrew M. Childs; Matthew Coudron; Amin Shiraz Gilani; David Miloschewsky; Supartha Podder

title: Rotated-Frame Determinant Discovery for Ground- and Excited-State Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction
abstract: Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI) constructs a variational determinant space from measurements of a prepared electronic state, but finite-shot sampling can repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, limiting efficient discovery of configurations important for an accurate selected-CI description. We introduce rotate--sample--unrotate (RSU) determinant discovery, in which the same state is sampled in complementary orbital frames and the observed rotated determinants generate a finite set of candidates in the canonical basis. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in an orthonormal selected-CI space without enumerating the full determinant space. State-targeted orbital frames are constructed from an initial selected-CI wavefunction and its external residual. For excited states, we combine RSU with the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) to prepare target-specific sampling states. Candidate GQE circuits are evaluated by classical selected-CI diagonalization in finite sampled spaces, so the quantum procedure requires only state preparation and determinant sampling. For N$_2$, exact-state controls isolate the determinant-discovery effect: at the stretched geometry, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots, compared with 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI. The improvement persists with approximate GQE-prepared states and is also observed for target excited states. These results demonstrate improved finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states.
authors: Yukihiro Okuno

title: Norm Bounds on Sums of Positive Operators with Applications to Monogamy Games and Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Bounding the acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is a recurring task in quantum information theory. An acceptance probability averaged over a random measurement setting can be bounded uniformly over the input state by the operator norm of an average of positive semidefinite operators. We prove a general inequality for such norms, valid for arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators and averaging distributions. We give two applications of our operator-norm inequality. First, we determine the sharp robustness threshold for the parallel BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game. For error thresholds $β,γ\in[0,1/2]$, when the two players may make at most $βn$ and $γn$ errors, respectively, the optimal winning probability decays exponentially if $(1-2β)^2+(1-2γ)^2>1$, tends to one exponentially fast under the reverse strict inequality, and remains bounded away from zero on the boundary. Second, we establish the achievability of every asymptotic key rate $0<R<1- 2h_2(γ)$ for one-sided device-independent BB84 quantum key distribution with tolerated bit-error rate $γ$ and asymptotically optimal reconciliation, where $h_2(\cdot)$ is the binary entropy function. Alice's measurements are trusted, while Bob may perform an arbitrary joint measurement depending on the entire basis string, subject to the protocol's receipt and isolation requirements. This recovers the usual BB84 rate in this model.
authors: Salman Beigi; Marco Tomamichel

title: Magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems in nonuniform periodic magnetic fields: a Fourier-finite difference approach
abstract: We study magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems for two-dimensional magnetic Schrödinger operators with nonuniform periodic magnetic fields and periodic scalar potentials, and develop a hybrid Fourier-finite difference discretization. A Landau-type gauge is constructed by solving a periodic Poisson equation. Under the integer magnetic flux condition, the magnetic Bloch boundary conditions are incorporated through shifts of Fourier-mode indices. The method combines link-variable-based covariant central differences in the $x$-direction with a Fourier pseudospectral discretization in the $y$-direction, yielding a Hermitian discrete Hamiltonian. The resulting eigenvalue problems are solved using a LOBPCG method. Under appropriate regularity assumptions, we establish a fully discrete consistency residual estimate of order $O(h_1^2+N_2^{-s})$. With suitable spectral separation and eigenspace dimension-preserving conditions, error estimates of the same order are derived for isolated eigenvalues and their associated eigenspaces. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence in the finite difference direction and rapid error reduction with increasing Fourier resolution, and illustrate band degeneracies and eigenstate distributions in nonuniform periodic magnetic fields.
authors: Xueyang Li; Yuanwei Lai

title: The Structure of Shared Classical Facts in Quantum Systems
abstract: Perfectly matching local outcomes need not constitute a nondisturbing shared classical record. For finite-dimensional multipartite states, we prove that nontrivial exact records are equivalent to a spectrum sharing structure with a unique finest decomposition into locally distinguishable sectors, where entanglement may persist. For a fixed complete pointer, exact sharing is equivalent to strong quantum Darwinism together with global nondisturbance, while spectrum broadcast structure additionally requires conditional independence. Arbitrarily weak full-rank admixtures eliminate exact sharing, but two-sided distance bounds quantify robustness through disturbance and disagreement, while information bounds connect accurate local readouts to observer consensus.
authors: Jie Gu

title: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization via Density Matrix Renormalization Group
abstract: We introduce SqDMRG, which combines sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). SqDMRG expands the sampled determinant space into a product of fragment spaces constructed from the samples, and solves the Hamiltonian in this product space using DMRG. We demonstrate the method on benzene pentamer and decamer clusters using classical reference samples, and on the pentamer using quantum samples obtained from the IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor ibm phoenix. It achieves sub-kcal/mol accuracy with far fewer configurations than direct diagonalization.
authors: Yuto Sugimoto; Tomonori Shirakawa; Yukio Kawashima; Toshinari Itoko; Seiji Yunoki

title: Collectively pumped superradiant laser with coherence scaling beyond the standard quantum limit
abstract: For more than half a century, the standard quantum limit (SQL) was thought to limit the laser coherence $\mathfrak{C}$ -- the number of photons emitted from the laser into the beam in one coherence time -- to a scaling $Θ(μ^2)$, where $μ$ is the mean number of optical-frequency excitations stored inside the laser. However, recently it has been shown [Baker et al., Nat. Phys. 17, 179 (2021)] that the Heisenberg limit -- an achievable ultimate limit set by quantum mechanics for the task of producing a beam with the standard properties of a laser beam -- is $\mathfrak{C}=Θ(μ^4)$, a quadratic enhancement. So far, proposals to demonstrate beyond-SQL scaling of $\mathfrak{C}$ have been limited to circuit QED, at microwave frequencies (i.e., a maser). Here, we introduce a class of generalized far-above-threshold (FAT) laser models, obtained by replacing the ordinary bosonic lowering operator $\hat{a}$ by a general lowering operator $\hat{L}$ in the superoperators appearing in the master equation that governs the FAT laser dynamics. We then show that an optical-frequency superradiant laser in the bad-cavity limit, with feedback-controlled collective pumping, realizes one such model, in which $\hat{L}$ is identified with the collective superradiant lowering operator $\hat{J}$. This model can surpass the SQL scaling, with the coherence exhibiting a scaling as large as $\mathfrak{C}= Θ(μ^{8/3})$ in the optimal parameter regime. Here, in the bad-cavity limit, $μ\approx N/2$, where $N$ is the number of superradiant atoms.
authors: Ori Somech; Howard M. Wiseman

title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
abstract: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs). Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys. [Kitagawa, Morimae,Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.
authors: Eli Goldin; Tomoyuki Morimae

title: Quantum Computing for Entanglement Asymmetry and the Quantum Mpemba Effect in Field Theory
abstract: We construct a quantum measurement protocol for estimating the Rényi entanglement asymmetry, which quantifies symmetry breaking at the level of a subsystem and provides a probe of the quantum Mpemba effect. The protocol combines the SWAP test with a charge-resolving procedure based on randomized symmetry rotations. For a fixed additive accuracy $ε$, the required number of measurements scales as $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ without explicit dependence on the total system size, making the protocol particularly attractive for quantum many-body systems and lattice quantum field theories. As a representative application, we study the quantum Mpemba effect in the lattice Schwinger model with a $θ$ term using classical state-vector simulations. We further estimate the resources required to implement the protocol on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs), and a representative early-FTQC architecture. Our results provide a measurement-efficient framework for investigating anomalous symmetry-restoration dynamics in quantum many-body systems and quantum field theories.
authors: Keisuke Fujii; Harunobu Fujimura; Masazumi Honda; Duc Truyen Le

title: Shadow bootstrapping: Nearly minimal-setting pure-state tomography with shallow Clifford measurements
abstract: We present a pure-state tomography algorithm that uses a nearly minimal number of measurement settings while achieving optimal sample complexity with nonadaptive single-copy shallow Clifford measurements. For an arbitrary $n$-qubit pure state $|ψ\rangle \in \mathbb{C}^{d}$, where $d=2^n$, the algorithm uses $O(d/ε)$ copies and $\widetilde{O}(1)$ measurement settings to output a state vector $|\hatψ\rangle$ satisfying $1-|\langleψ|\hatψ\rangle|^2\leε$ with high probability. Each measurement is implemented by a Clifford circuit of depth $O(\log n)$. Reusing each measurement setting allows the data to be stored compactly as per-basis outcome histograms. Given these histograms, classical post-processing runs in $\widetilde{O}(d)$ time. Our key technique, \textit{shadow bootstrapping}, uses the current estimate to reduce the variance of subsequent residual estimation, enabling progressively more accurate reconstruction with only a constant number of new measurement settings per stage.
authors: Gyungmin Cho; Dohun Kim

title: Classical Clifford+T Sampling without Computing Marginals
abstract: We introduce a new exact classical sampling algorithm for Clifford+T circuits, called T-by-T sampling. For a circuit with T-count t, it reduces sampling to evaluating 2t amplitudes of circuits with successively increasing T-counts 1,2,...,t, without the need to compute costly marginal probabilities. Crucially, the number of amplitude evaluations is completely independent of the surrounding Clifford structure. This makes T-by-T sampling well suited for use together with low-rank stabiliser decompositions, which enable efficient amplitude evaluations as long as the T-count is not too high. In that sense, T-by-T sampling is an improvement over the gate-by-gate sampling technique introduced by Bravyi, Gosset, and Liu (Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 2022), where the number of amplitudes instead scales with the number of non-monomial operations such as Hadamard gates, which can remain large even in circuits with low stabiliser rank. Concretely, T-by-T sampling offers significant speedups in regimes where T gates are embedded within large Clifford computations. This makes it well suited for applications such as simulating quantum error correction experiments, which typically have lower T complexity but involve extensive Clifford operations and measurements. In particular, we show how T-by-T sampling allows us to take samples from recent end-to-end magic state cultivation circuits with escape up to distance 19 in a couple of seconds.
authors: Mark Koch

title: A Post-Quantum Interactive Hashing Theorem
abstract: Interactive hashing, introduced by Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung [OVY93], is a building block in many cryptographic protocols, including perfectly hiding commitments from one-way permutations [NOVY92]. Its multi-output generalization is a key ingredient in constructions of statistical zero-knowledge arguments for NP and statistically hiding commitments from arbitrary one-way functions [NOV06,HR07]. In this note, we give a post-quantum security proof for this multi-output interactive hashing protocol with arbitrary relations.
authors: Céline Chevalier; Laurent Holin; Quoc-Huy Vu

title: Robust Geometric Gates for QCCD Architecture
abstract: The trapped-ion quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) is a promising route toward scalable quantum computing. However, the frequency offset during shuttling operations introduce significant decoherence and control errors, severely degrading gate fidelity on transported ions. Here, using a room-temperature planar chip trap, we demonstrate a robust and universal single-qubit gate set in the QCCD architecture. Based on a recently proposed path-optimizable noncyclic geometric scheme, we show that dynamic noise is strongly suppressed even when multiple shuttling operations are interleaved with gate execution, achieving substantially higher fidelities than conventional dynamical gates. This robustness is further validated in a multi-ion system containing up to 33 qubits. With inherent robustness and adaptability to varying shuttle distances and ion numbers, our work offers a plug-and-play solution for building robust quantum primitives for the QCCD platform.
authors: Xin Zhang; Yi Tao; Hong Yang Wang; Gang Fan; Jie Zhang; Wei Wu; Ting Chen; Chun Wang Wu; Yi Xie; Ping Xing Chen

title: Statistical mechanics and hierarchy of learnability in quantum codes: From generalized symmetries to non-Abelian topological orders
abstract: Local weak measurements provide noisy information about observables encoded in a quantum code. We formulate the corresponding Bayesian inference problem for a broad class of topological stabilizer codes by mapping it to classical spin models with generalized symmetries. When the wavefunction deformation and Gaussian measurement strengths coincide, the replicated model acquires an enlarged symmetry. We use this symmetry to derive exact identities among correlators averaged over measurement records that quantify the learnability of nonlocal observables associated with fractionalized excitations. Together with correlation inequalities in the associated clean ferromagnetic models, these identities establish hierarchies of learnability: if two observables remain learnable at long distances, their product must also remain learnable. We demonstrate these relations in the rank-2 toric code and the X-cube model, whose classical descriptions exhibit modulated and subsystem symmetries, respectively. We further extend the analysis to finite group quantum double models, including non-Abelian ones. We derive exact relations between learnability and correlations in the corresponding classical models, and show that the representation structure and fusion rules of anyons impose further constraints under suitable positivity conditions. These results constrain which types of nonlocal information can be learned simultaneously, providing a guide to learning phase diagrams in quantum codes under local weak measurements.
authors: Hiromi Ebisu; Masazumi Honda

title: Geometric limits of quantum recovery across an Ising transition
abstract: How many physical spins must a receiver retain to recover an unknown qubit? Four Ising duality defects encode a qubit over a common pure bulk ground state in a fixed charge sector. We vary that state at fixed defect geometry and optimize over preselected spins and joint decoders, taking the infinite-chain limit before increasing defect separation. At every fixed finite positive reference field, exact recovery costs the central spacing plus the shorter outer spacing to leading order. For an error falling as any fixed inverse power of separation, the leading cost is the central spacing in the ordered phase, the shorter outer spacing in the disordered phase and their sum at criticality. Order and disorder records in discarded spins explain the contrast. In a critical benchmark, single-spin measurements, a one-way classical message and an output correction preserve reference entanglement on two separated blocks at budgets where every connected interval is entanglement breaking.
authors: Yi Liang

title: Resetting a Superconducting Qubit with a Compact Colder Resistive Dissipator below the Qubit Frequency
abstract: Efficient qubit reset has become a key requirement for large-scale superconducting quantum processors, as initialization fidelity increasingly lags behind gate performance and quantum error correction demands rapid, high-fidelity state re-initialization. This work proposes a compact on-chip dissipator consisting of two transmon dissipation modes and a thin-film resistor, and experimentally demonstrates an unconditional reset protocol. With no additional control lines and negligible impact on the qubit $T_1$, the effective temperature of the transmon qubit is reduced from $49$~mK to $35$~mK. Quantum process tomography is employed to benchmark the reset process, achieving a process error of $0.0028$. This reset protocol is robust to pulse parameter deviations, thereby relaxing calibration requirements. The dissipator architecture provides a practical, calibration-friendly reset solution for large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
authors: Jiajia Tian; Meiling Li; Weijie Sun; Yanjun Ma; Zhenyu Mi; Fei Yan; Huikai Xu; Pei Liu; Guangming Xue; Haifeng Yu

title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}λ^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.
authors: Stavros Athanasiou; Olivier J. F. Martin; Francisco J. García-Vidal; Johannes Feist

title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
abstract: Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.
authors: Moeto Mishima; Toshihiko Sasaki; Yasunari Suzuki; Koji Azuma; Masato Koashi

title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
abstract: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.
authors: Junkai Zeng; Hao Liang; Yong-Ju Hai; Xiu-Hao Deng

title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
abstract: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.
authors: Angela Sara Cacciapuoti; Claudio Pellitteri; Marcello Caleffi

title: Semi-Device-Independent Certification of multi-qubit Entangled Basis Measurement
abstract: The entangled basis measurement plays a pivotal role in fundamental information-processing tasks, such as dense coding, quantum teleportation, and entanglement swapping. Consequently, certifying such measurements in a device-independent manner remains an important task. In this work, we present a semi-device-independent (SDI) protocol in a prepare-and-measure (PM) scenario for certifying a class of m-qubit entangled basis measurements. Specifically, we consider a tripartite PM scenario featuring two senders and one receiver, where each sender sends an arbitrary number of 2^m inputs and the receiver performs a measurement with 2^m outcomes. We adopt a classical causal model framework to demonstrate the non-classicality of quantum measurements. We introduce nonlinear witnesses in classical causal models and demonstrate that the optimal quantum value exceeds the classical bounds. Further, we demonstrate that the optimal quantum value of the witness SDI certify the entangled basis measurement and the prepared states of the two senders.
authors: Rajat Pandey; Alok Kumar Pan

title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication
abstract: In the world of quantum computing, quantum Fourier transform (QFT) has been one of the most important subroutines for quantum algorithms, as exemplified by Shor's factoring algorithms and phase estimation (which in itself has been used as a primitive in various quantum algorithms). In fact most of the well known quantum algorithms can be divided into two classes, QFT based algorithms and search based algorithms. The usual circuit for QFT (covered in almost every basic quantum algorithms course) needs $O(q^2)$ gates (and $O(q)$ qubits) to perform the exact Fourier transform over $\mathbb{F}_{2^q}$. Cleve and Watrous (FOCS 2000) improved this gate count to $O(q (\log q)^2 (\log \log q))$ using the integer multiplication algorithm in $O(n (\log n) (\log \log n))$ time for two $n$-bit integers (best known at that time). Our first main result shows that this gate count can be improved to $O(q (\log q))$. In fact, if there is a multiplication circuit, to multiply two $n$-bit integers, with $O(n (\log n)^α)$ gates; we get a QFT circuit with $O(q (\log q)^α)$ gates (improving upon $O(q (\log q)^{α+ 1})$) gates from the construction of Cleve and Watrous). Given the recent claim by OpenAI about integer multiplication, this opens up the possibility of having a QFT circuit with $o \left( q (\log q)\right)$ gates. On approximating the QFT over $\ZZ/(2^q \ZZ)$, the result of Ahokas, Cleve and Hales (ERATO 2003) showed that an approximating circuit can be built with $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^{α+1} \right)$ gates, where $ε$ is the approximating parameter. Our second main result again improves this to $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^α \right)$ gates.
authors: Chandrima Kayal; Rajat Mittal; Manaswi Paraashar; Nitin Saurabh

title: Kardar--Parisi--Zhang density hydrodynamics in a coherent XXZ--ASEP Lindbladian
abstract: Coherent interactions can generate quantum correlations without changing a stationary density current. Whether that current still determines long-wavelength transport is a dynamical question. We study an XXZ chain with asymmetric Lindblad hopping, whose stationary current has the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) form although its populations do not evolve autonomously. The current curvature and static susceptibility fix the leading Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) length and amplitude without a fitted length or amplitude conversion factor. The density-visible Liouvillian spectrum, real-space spreading, and Fourier relaxation support KPZ scaling at the finite coherent couplings studied. Central and intermediate stationary density correlations are consistent with the Prähofer--Spohn profile at this microscopic scale, with resolved finite-time corrections. Reservoir-matched classical references quantify boundary effects, while symmetric hopping recovers diffusion and reduced asymmetry produces the expected crossover. These results connect an exact nonlinear current to the observed long-wavelength KPZ transport of the physical density in an interacting open quantum chain away from the isotropic Heisenberg point.
authors: Yansheng Liu; Daoguang Li; Kaixiang Lu; Mingdi Xu; Lei Pan

title: Constraining Lorentz Invariance Violation via Precision Atomic Spectroscopy
abstract: This paper investigates Lorentz violation arising from quantum gravity effects in electronic and muonic hydrogen atoms. The violation is modeled through a modified dispersion relation parameterized by a dimensionless coefficient $ξ$ and suppressed by the Planck scale. Using high-precision spectroscopic data and a chi-squared fitting procedure that carefully accounts for theoretical uncertainties in the Rydberg constant and the proton radius, the analysis yields a 95% confidence level constraint $ξ\in [-14.3,\; 1.37] \times 10^5$. The mass scaling of the effect reveals two distinct regimes: for the lowest-order deformation, the heavy nucleus amplifies the signal, while for higher-order corrections, the lepton dominates the sensitivity. These bounds approach Planck-scale sensitivity using the simplest atomic systems, thereby circumventing ambiguities inherent in more complex quantum systems.
authors: A. S. Lemos; J. E. J. Matias; F. Dahia; I. P. Lobo

title: Helium States Inspired by Quantum Photonics Circuit
abstract: We present a four-mode Fock-state photonics implementation of the variational quantum deflation (VQD) algorithm to calculate the ground-state and excited-state energies for the neutral helium atom in a CAS(2,2) Subspace. Its CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space is encoded into a bosonic Fock-space representation and subsequently optimized using a continuous-variable quantum circuit. The circuit architecture under study is constructed of single-mode phase shifts, beam splitters, and cross-Kerr interactions. The variational circuit is initialized in the Fock state $\ket{1100}$ and its performance is benchmarked against exact diagonalization of the active-space configuration-interaction (CASCI) Hamiltonian. We also extend the method to optimize from the first to three excited states of the helium atom with the aid of the variational quantum deflation $(VQD)$ method in a CAS(2,2). We then investigate the performance of this circuit architecture as a basis for implementing the VQD method. In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $α$ and $β$ are preserved. We demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the determination of the ground and excited-state energies within the CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space using a continuous-variable quantum circuit and the variational quantum deflation ($VQD$) algorithm, while satisfying the orthogonality conditions with negligible errors.
authors: Forouzan Mirmasoudi; Badie Ghavami

title: Beyond the Gap: What Imaginary-Time Evolution Reveals About the Edge of the Continuum
abstract: The spectral gap, the energy separating the ground state from the first excitation, governs many quantum phenomena, yet it is far harder to compute than the ground state. We propose a mathematically rigorous method for extracting the gap from imaginary-time evolution in infinite-dimensional Hamiltonians, where the first excitation typically marks the edge of a continuous spectrum. We show that a gap is not automatically detected: detection depends on how the initial state and observable couple the ground state to excitations at the bottom of the continuum. When this coupling follows a power law, the gap is recovered together with a logarithmic correction whose coefficient yields the exponent of the spectral density near the edge of the continuum, which reflects the physics of the excitations. We confirm both predictions numerically for an exactly solvable model. Our results offer a new numerical approach to many-body quantum physics, in which both the gap and the threshold exponent are obtained merely at the cost of a ground-state calculation.
authors: Ruben Karapetyan; Denys Bondar; Jakub Mareček; Aleš Wodecki

title: Universally Certifying Partially Self-Correcting Quantum Memories in 3D Translation-Invariant Stabilizer Codes
abstract: Achieving passive protection of quantum information at finite temperature is a central problem at the intersection of quantum information and quantum many-body physics. Yet a general, computable criterion for determining self-correcting behavior directly from the form of local interactions remains elusive. Here we develop a unified algebraic-geometric framework for certifying partial self-correction in three-dimensional translation-invariant local stabilizer codes, encompassing the cubic code as a special case. From the algebraic curves defined by the codes' defining polynomials, we construct valuation matrices on the boundaries of their normalized projective closures and derive a computable rank criterion. Together with a polynomial-time decoder, this criterion guarantees super-Arrhenius memory lifetimes for code families satisfying it under the specified local Davies dynamics. We apply the framework to certify several classes of partially self-correcting quantum memories, including nearest-neighbor models with stabilizer weight as low as six and long memory lifetimes at modest system sizes. These results establish an algebraic-geometric connection between local stabilizer structure and the recoverability of quantum information at finite temperature, providing a systematic approach to certifying and designing passive quantum memories.
authors: Chong-Yuan Xu; Yong Xu

title: Quasi-Normal Modes and thermalization in integrable Quantum Field Theories from the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz
abstract: We propose a Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) approach for describing thermalization in integrable quantum field theories. The exponential damping and oscillations when approaching thermal equilibrium can be understood as the analogs of quasi-normal mode (QNM) frequencies of black hole perturbations within the framework of holography. Holographic intuitions and some general properties of thermal Green's functions motivate the existence of such a TBA formulation, as well as lead to the imposition of a nonstandard analytical structure on the QNM TBA, while comparison with integrable form-factor expansions fixes the remaining ingredients. We conjecture the QNM TBA to be equivalent to performing an all-order resummation of secular terms in a thermal form factor expansion of retarded 2-point correlation functions. We compare the predictions with tensor network simulations of the E8 deformation of Ising CFT at nonzero temperature. We conjecture that the QNM TBA framework should also be applicable for describing out-of-equilibrium approach to Generalized Hydrodynamics (GHD).
authors: Zoltan Bajnok; Romuald A. Janik

title: Physical regimes of quartic quantum advantage in elastic media simulation
abstract: Quantum algorithms for elastic media simulation have been conjectured to offer up to a quartic quantum advantage over classical methods; however, the devil is always in the details. Here, we determine key physical conditions under which this quartic separation could be achieved in the relevant parameters. For continuum elastic dynamics at fixed volume with spatial convergence order $m$, we find that the end-to-end speedup is of order $(m+4)/(m+1)$ in the simulation time, and $4/(m+1)$ in the accuracy, with exponential memory advantage. For elastic lattice systems, we define microscopically resolved bulk observables (MRBOs) as those that can be efficiently extracted from a quantum state, but cannot be resolved by a known continuum model with fewer degrees of freedom than the lattice. We then argue that the estimation of MRBOs is a candidate problem for quartic quantum advantage in problem size. We propose MRBOs for pseudorandom heterogeneous materials as an explicit end-to-end application where this occurs, while admitting efficient `quantum cheese' encodings of the material properties. We thus demonstrate how the interplay between regularity, physical scale, observable sensitivity and quantum encodability constrains the relation between classical and quantum complexity.
authors: David Jennings; Kamil Korzekwa; Matteo Lostaglio; Tamás Vaszary

title: Coupling between molecular exchange qubits
abstract: Spin triangles are promising systems for defining and manipulating scalar degrees of freedom, such as chirality, partial spin sums, or combinations between the two. Here we extend this analysis to dimers formed by pairs of spin triangles, coupled by exchange or dipolar interactions. We show that the weak-coupling limit warrants the introduction of an effective two-qubit picture, and derive the expressions of the related Hamiltonians as a function of the underlying physical interaction between the triangles. We benchmark this two-qubit Hamiltonian against the microscopic one, and discuss the observable effects of the inter-triangle coupling on the spin-electric transitions between states with different chiralities or partial-spin sums.
authors: Filippo Troiani; Jason S. R. McCoombs; Athanassios K. Boudalis

title: Quantum Advantage needs Multiple Perspectives
abstract: The origin of the quantum speedup is a topic of ongoing research. We propose a logical criterion for the possibility of a speedup within the continuous-variable and odd-prime qudit settings. There, Wigner function nonnegativity signals the possibility of efficient classical simulation in the state-injection scenario. We consider representations of quadrature/Weyl measurements in a single von Neumann algebra that reproduce the Born statistics in a particular state. If in that state, the set-theoretic universe of the algebra is ZFC-satisfiable, i.e. every ZFC-theorem holds with unit probability, all measurement contexts can be represented in a single commutative algebra of `beables'. Furthermore, the statistics admit a noncontextual hidden variable model, ensuring Wigner nonnegativity for two or more modes or qudits. For a single mode, a stronger notion of linear representation ensures commutativity, and with it, ZFC-satisfiability independently of the state, as well as Wigner nonnegativity. In consequence, in any setting that cannot be efficiently simulated, it must be impossible to merge the models associated with every context into a single ZFC-satisfiable one: quantum advantage needs multiple perspectives.
authors: Jochen Szangolies

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling
abstract: Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.
authors: Raul Martinez; Miguel Sánchez-Beato; Matilde Osa; Jorge Parra; Mario Calonge

title: Stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter
abstract: In quantum many-body physics and quantum field theory, it is often assumed that gapped systems remain gapped under sufficiently weak local perturbations. However, to what extent this assumption holds is elusive, except for some special systems. In this work, we examine the stability of energy gap of macroscopic quantum matter that is only subject to two physically natural conditions, locality and translation invariance. We first show that in any spatial dimension, there are gapped local Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap, i.e., they become gapless under certain arbitrarily weak local perturbation in the thermodynamic limit. We then prove that for both spin and fermionic systems in one dimension, such Hamiltonians with an unstable gap must not only break translation invariance but also be fine-tuned. We further show that in any dimension greater than one, there are fine-tuned local translation invariant Hamiltonians with a unique ground state and an unstable gap. These results greatly sharpen our understanding of the fundamental problem of the stability of quantum phases of matter. We also discuss implications of our results on, for example, anyon superconductivity and higher-form symmetries.
authors: Kangle Li; Liujun Zou

title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics
abstract: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. Global spectral formulations in this setting have so far relied on Fourier bases, restricted to periodic problems, or on collocation, which does not preserve the variational structure exploited by tensor-network solvers. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev-Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet-Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. A six-parameter cantilever design study covering $1.7\times10^{7}$ designs is solved in a single 92s run, and a stochastic problem with ten random coordinates is represented with $2.4\times10^{6}$ times less memory than its full coefficient array.
authors: Juan José Rodríguez-Aldavero; Ángel de la Rosa Velasco; Juan José García-Ripoll

title: Spectral properties of twisted soft waveguides
abstract: We discuss a model of a soft waveguide described by Schrödinger operator whose potential is a twisted straight channel of non-circular profile. We show that a compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, the property being expressed in terms of a Hardy-type inequality. On the other hand, a periodic twist raises the essential spectrum and its local slowdown may give rise to isolated eigenvalues below the essential spectrum threshold.
authors: Pavel Exner; David Spitzkopf

title: Parrondo's paradox for three discrete-time quantum walks with distinct shift operators
abstract: Parrondo's paradox describes a surprising phenomenon in which certain combinations of biased quantum walks result in an unexpected reversal of their bias direction. To date, research on this effect has predominantly focused on one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walks that employ fixed sequences of two or three quantum coins, paired with a single shift operator. In this work, we first introduce a wide class of unitary shift operators which allow for three movement options (left, right or stay in place) of a walker in one time step, and we then demonstrate that Parrondo's paradox can also arise with a single coin and three distinct shift operators. Furthermore, we investigate how this paradox influences the time evolution of quantum entanglement between the walker and the coin in such quantum walks.
