title: Spin-Exchange-Controlled Nonclassical Light in Cavity Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
abstract: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.
authors: Jing Tang; Junyu Su; Jie Chen; Ziyang Li; Yuangang Deng

title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
abstract: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $Ω_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $Ω_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.
authors: Yusheng Zhao; Han Wang; Mingrui Jing; Zhongyi Ni; Hongshun Yao; Xin Wang; Jie Wang; Jinguo Liu

title: Extensions of the Haldane gap proof: higher dimensions, near degeneracy, fermions and tensor-network states
abstract: A recent remarkable paper by OpenAI showed that the spin-one Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit. The proof elegantly deduces this gap from the Hamiltonian's spectrum on a finite system. This basic idea is an inequality involving the purity of the original Gibbs state and a dual Gibbs state that is defined via space-time rotation. Here we consider a few generalizations of this purity bootstrap argument. We first extend it to arbitrary spatial dimensions. Our main result uses the space-time duality between symmetry generators and symmetry twists to obtain upper bounds on the splitting of nearly degenerate low-energy states, together with a nonzero gap above them, from finite-system information. As applications, we show that finite-system calculations for the 2+1-D toric code in a field and the 2+1-D transverse-field Ising model establish parameter regimes with four and two low-lying states whose splittings are bounded from above by $e^{-cL}$ and $e^{-cL^2}$ respectively for arbitrarily large system size $L$, while the gap above these states remains nonzero in the thermodynamic limit. Next, we extend it to fermionic systems and use a finite calculation to establish a symmetric mass generation phase in a $2+1$-D fermionic model. Finally, we apply the bootstrap to tensor-network states and establish exponential decay of connected correlations of all local operators in the symmetric square-lattice spin-one state introduced by Jian and Zaletel.
authors: Tarun Grover

title: Higher-order topological quantum battery
abstract: A quantum battery is a next-generation energy-storage device that exploits genuinely quantum properties such as superposition and coherence. We propose a second-order topological quantum battery coupled to a photonic crystal described by the breathing-Kagome model, where optical loss is present on all lattice sites while nonlinear gains are introduced selectively at the output sites. Under these realistic non-Hermitian conditions, the system exhibits a clear topological phase transition manifested in both the ergotropy and the charging power. Remarkably, perfect work extraction is realized in the topological phase, where the maximum value of the ergotropy is quantized and acts as a good topological-phase indicator. The triangular geometry coherently distributes energy into two quantum batteries, where mirror-symmetry-protected phase synchronization gives rise to collective energy storage.
authors: Motohiko Ezawa

title: Weak Values in Postselected Quantum Trajectories
abstract: Weak value (WV) describes the amplified response of a meter when the measured system undergoes postselection. While conventional WV theory mainly rests on a single system-meter interaction setting, it remains unexplored whether WV can act as an effective pointer for sequential quantum measurements under postselection. Here we introduce the concept of WVs to the setting of sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories. We find that WV naturally emerges in postselected quantum trajectories of sequential weak measurements, by establishing a connection between the WV of the measured observable and the postselected statistics of quantum trajectories. Using sequential weak measurements on a qubit or an oscillator implemented by Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit, we show that postselection shifts the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned ones, with an effective bias described by the WV. Our predictions are feasible to test in various platforms.
authors: Janarbek Yuanbek; Yuan-De Jin; Wen-Long Ma

title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
abstract: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.
authors: Xiao Liang; Takashi Yamakawa; Chak Fai Yung

title: Information flow control in hybrid quantum networks
abstract: Quantum resources can change the dynamical features and operational behaviors of conventional networks. Long-distance entanglement supports information transfer between nodes lacking a direct connection. This entanglement link not only modifies the stationary effective connectivity of the network but can also be used to suppress undesirable classical dynamics. By examining information flow control mechanism, we demonstrate that classical collective behavior can be well-balanced by altering the initially distributed entanglement. We show the entanglement thresholds for two distinct control approaches: linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability.
authors: Michael Siomau

title: Demystifying Graviton Detection
abstract: Detecting single gravitons is possible through the extraction of discrete energy quanta from passing gravitational waves. For decades, this was considered hopeless, with estimates suggesting a detector the size of Jupiter. Here, I explain how these earlier estimates relied on the highly inefficient electron ionization process, while the absorption through the full mass quadrupole of a macroscopic system can bring graviton detection within experimental reach. Operating in the LIGO frequency band solves the challenges of graviton sources and noise suppression, allowing gravitons to be extracted from known passing gravitational waves and detection events to be heralded by classical gravitational-wave observations. Combined with the ability to resolve single energy quanta in macroscopic systems, such as in quantum acoustics, this opens a realistic path toward graviton detection. I also discuss the general limitations of particle detection in establishing an underlying quantum theory, illustrated by an energy-nonconserving semiclassical alternative. Nevertheless, the semiclassical alternative is not standard classical wave physics, and extracting $E=\hbarω$ from a passing wave constitutes bona fide particle detection. This opens the way not only to the first detection of individual gravitons, but also to experimentally probing linearized quantum gravity and the graviton counting statistics of gravitational waves.
authors: Igor Pikovski

title: Elimination of quantum causal confusion in the presence of dual states
abstract: There is a rich class of bipartite quantum correlations between qubits which are consistent both with measurements performed in parallel and measurements performed in sequence. This phenomenon has recently been termed \emph{quantum causal confusion}, which is made mathematically precise by the notion of a dual state---a bipartite density operator whose associated correlations are causally ambiguous. A natural question is then whether or not the spatial and temporal scenarios associated with a dual state are fundamentally indistinguishable from a causal perspective. Here we show that as long as the reduced density operator of a dual state is oblique---meaning that all coefficients in its Pauli expansion are non-zero---then the underlying joint probabilities giving rise to such causally ambiguous correlations will differ in the spatial and temporal scenarios. Specifically, the temporal joint probabilities will inherently violate the no-signalling condition, thus eliminating quantum causal confusion. Moreover, as oblique states form an open dense subset of the Bloch ball, the elimination of quantum causal confusion is the norm rather than an exception.
authors: James Fullwood; Weixiang Ye

title: Bell Test and Quantum State-Space Geometry
abstract: We explore a minimal phenomenological model of coupling between the geometry of the classical spacetime and the quantum state space. Assuming a simple structure of the combined manifold, bilinear interaction between the corresponding geometric scalars and the simplest case of the two-qubit entanglement dynamics, we derive an illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant from the requirement of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality violation over a finite time interval.
authors: Michael Siomau

title: Probing Non-Abelian Topology through Quench Dynamics
abstract: Quench dynamics offer valuable insights to topological matter, wherein the emergent topological phenomena serve as a dynamic probe to the topology of static Hamiltonians. While such a practice has been widely applied to detect the Abelian band topology or the Euler-class topology of band nodes, little is known regarding the quench dynamics of non-Abelian topological insulators in multiband systems, where the intertwining geometry of all eigenstates necessitates the description of noncommutative topological charges. Here we propose a quench protocol for non-Abelian topological insulators, so that the underlying topology can be systematically probed using dynamic signatures. Specifically, we develop a band-projection scheme to extract the gap-resolved topology from dynamic skyrmions in the emergent quasimomentum--time manifolds of the quench processes. These skyrmions are characterized by a series of gap-resolved dynamic Chern numbers, which enable us to reconstruct the full non-Abelian topology of the post-quench Hamiltonian, including the global non-Abelian topological charge and edge-state patterns under the open-boundary condition. Our proposal offers dynamical access to non-Abelian topology in multiband systems, and can be readily implemented using photons or cold atoms.
authors: Zhenming Zhang; Tianyu Li; Wei Yi

title: Information-Spectrum General Formulas for the Capacity Region of Classical-Quantum Multiple Access Channels
abstract: For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error ($\varepsilon=0$), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every $0\le\varepsilon<1$, the $\varepsilon$-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.
authors: Takuya Kubo; Hiroshi Nagaoka

title: Efficient Pauli Truncation from Operator Stabilizer Rényi Entropy
abstract: Operator stabilizer Rényi entropy (OSE) quantifies the magic of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of their compressibility in the Pauli basis. We establish rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be efficiently approximated by Pauli truncation in terms of the scaling of its OSE. Specifically, we prove that volume-law scaling of OSE for $α\geq1$ prevents efficient Pauli truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error. On the other hand, logarithmic growth of OSE for $0<α<1/2$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation approximability uniformly over all states. A counterexample shows that this sufficient range cannot be extended on the basis of OSE scaling alone. If we restrict to correlations over suitable low-average state ensembles, then the sufficient range extends to $0<α<1$. We further derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and approximation guarantees for fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators. Moreover, under an independent-sign assumption, we show that logarithmic OSE for $0<α<1$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation with the prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding when operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation and for guiding the development of classical simulation methods.
authors: Haihui Wang; Yongming Li

title: Optimal quantum metrology with restricted controls
abstract: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-$1/2$ examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.
authors: Li Sun; Haoze Wang; Chong Chen

title: Observing mixed-state Uhlmann winding numbers in integrated photonic quantum walks
abstract: Integer winding numbers provide a well-established classification of topological phases protected by chiral symmetry at zero temperature, but extending this classification to thermal mixed states remains challenging. The Uhlmann phase, a mixed-state extension of the Berry phase, provides a geometric framework for characterizing finite-temperature topology. However, this geometric phase is restricted to two quantized values and therefore cannot resolve the multiple thermal regimes associated with high winding numbers. Here, we experimentally observe integer mixed-state winding numbers in a photonic quantum-walk chip. We prepare and reconstruct thermal states associated with high-winding chiral Hamiltonians and their spectrum-preserving dimensional extensions. The reconstructed Uhlmann overlaps form closed trajectories in the complex plane, and their integer windings around the zero-overlap point are directly observed. As temperature increases, the Uhlmann winding number undergoes multiple discrete changes, accompanied by switches of the Uhlmann phase and the successive disappearance of momentum-resolved topological kinks. These results highlight an integer-valued topological characterization alongside the mixed-state geometric phase.
authors: Baichu Yu; Qin-Qin Wang; Huilong Huang; Bin-Tong Yin; Xiao-Ye Xu; Feng Gao; Xin Wang; Keren Li; Sen Yang; Yuan-Yuan Zhao

title: Majorana corner modes and tunable braiding in an altermagnet-superconductor heterostructure
abstract: Zeeman fields are usually required for realizing and manipulating Majorana corner modes at the cost of suppressed superconducting pairing. Altermagnetism offers a new route toward realizing Majorana corner modes under zero net external magnetic fields. Here we propose a theoretical scheme to host Majorana corner modes in a honeycomb-lattice altermagnet-superconductor heterostructure. In contrast to previous studies on square lattices, altermagnetism yields distinct effective low-energy edge masses on various inequivalent edges of the honeycomb lattice. Within a low-energy edge-theory framework, we establish the conditions under which Majorana corner modes emerge for both bearded and zigzag edge terminations. We further explicitly construct a complete set of Clifford gates by tuning the altermagnetic anisotropy and chemical potential of the heterostructure. Our results provide a promising platform for the realization and manipulation of Majorana corner modes.
authors: Yingli Gao; Kai Zhang; Ling-Zheng Meng; Junpeng Hou; Ning Li; Ya-Jie Wu

title: Universal Phase Locking from Slowly Varying Inhomogeneity in Tunnel-Coupled One-Dimensional Condensates
abstract: The sine-Gordon model can be experimentally realised by tunnel-coupled one-dimensional Bose condensates. However, the experiments show relaxation to a phase-locked state, which conflicts with the predictions of the homogeneous integrable theory. Here we combine the truncated Wigner approximation with an asymptotic analysis, and show that this locking is produced by a slowly varying density profile through a universal mechanism, whereby the relative phase near the density maximum drifts towards zero. We show that this drift is already present in the linearised theory and its timescale is determined by the density curvature alone, while it is independent of the tunnel coupling. Rescaling time by the relaxation time scale collapses the dynamics for different system sizes and density profiles, while non-linearity suppresses the excitation returning from the edges.
authors: Bence Fitos; Gábor Takács

title: Separability and lower bounds of concurrence via symmetric measurement correlations
abstract: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement is a central issue in quantum information science, particularly for unknown quantum states. Based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices, we present a family of separability criteria that can be experimentally applied without state tomography, and recover some related existing criteria as special cases. Using the constructed correlation matrices, we further derive a class of lower bounds of concurrence. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that our criteria outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and that the obtained lower bounds on concurrence are tighter than known counterparts.
authors: Yuhang Xie; Yanjun Chu; Shao-Ming Fei

title: Efficient preparation of spin-squeezed states with Grover's algorithm
abstract: We propose a scheme for preparing spin-squeezed states in an ensemble of $N$ spin-$1/2$ particles based on Grover's algorithm. With only a few oracles, the scheme can exactly prepare superpositions of a few neighboring Dicke states with the Wineland squeezing parameter scaling as $N^{-1}$. The scheme requires only global rotations and Dicke-selective phase shifts, thus avoiding the need to engineer a dedicated many-body Hamiltonian for the squeezing dynamics. We further discuss the feasibility of realizing the scheme in cavity QED systems, with the phase-matched Grover iterations realized by single-photon reflection from a dispersively coupled cavity. Full-sequence scattering calculations accounting for finite photon bandwidth and loss show that appreciable spin squeezing can be achieved with high fidelity for suitable system parameters.
authors: Zhi-Yuan Zeng; Wen-Long Ma

title: Observation of Inter-Transition Interference
abstract: Many well-known quantum interference phenomena are associated with coherent superpositions of quantum states. Recent theoretical work showed that dissipative coupling between transition coherences can give rise to a distinct form of quantum interference in open quantum systems, termed inter-transition interference (ITI). Here we experimentally observe ITI through coherent microwave reflection spectroscopy of a superconducting artificial atom realized by a Kerr parametric oscillator. Using strong parametric driving, we access a regime in which two transitions become nearly degenerate and simultaneously contribute to the reflected response. The observed spectral lineshapes are not adequately captured by a model of independent transitions. By contrast, theoretical calculations that incorporate dissipative coupling between the corresponding transition coherences reproduce the essential features of the measured spectra. These results provide experimental evidence for ITI and demonstrate that dissipative coupling between transition coherences can qualitatively modify spectroscopic responses. More broadly, our work identifies transition coherences as a new arena for quantum interference in open quantum systems.
authors: Toyofumi Ishikawa; Shumpei Masuda; Akiyoshi Tomonaga; Kosuke Mizuno; Kunihiro Inomata

title: Detecting Nonbilocal Correlations via Parameterized Elegant Joint Measurement
abstract: Quantum networks constitute a defining resource for quantum information processing; however, their nonclassical behavior is jointly governed by the choice of measurement basis and the independence of the distributed sources. We study a bilocal entanglement-swapping network in which the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM). For two independent Bell-state sources, we construct two binary edge observables and then derive a quantum prediction involving three parameters, which surpasses the classical constraints. In particular, the parameter θ controls both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction. These results provide an analytic and directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.
authors: Ye Tian; Ying-Qiu He; Zan-Jia Li; Yu-Yan Zhang; Dong Ding

title: Development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy using heralded emission spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials
abstract: Organic light-emitting materials are widely used in optoelectronics and bioimaging, but sometimes conventional fluorescence spectroscopy techniques can be limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up and photobleaching. We report a quantum-spectroscopic approach using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection, to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities. We demonstrate this approach across three organic light-emitting material classes: the fluorescent dye Rhodamine 6G, an organic semiconducting conjugated polymer poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), and a fluorescent protein mOrange. The intrinsic timing correlation between signal and idler photons enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Across all materials and integration times of 500, 1000 and 3600 seconds, heralded detection yields signal-to-noise ratios 1.6-3.0 times higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range. For MEH-PPV, this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Our measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical pulsed-laser reference values.
authors: Nicola J. Fairbairn; Koya Onoda; Ozora Iso; Masahiro Yabuno; Hirotaka Terai; Shigehito Miki; Yuji Kagotani; Motoyasu Adachi; Gordon J. Hedley; Ryosuke Shimizu

title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
abstract: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.
authors: Itzhak Roditi

title: Constrained Quantum Imaginary Time in Krylov Space
abstract: We introduce constrained quantum imaginary time evolution (CQITE), extending quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to constrained-search dynamics for ground-state preparation with prescribed expectation-value constraints. A central challenge in practical QITE is constructing a compact unitary representation of the imaginary-time evolution while maintaining accuracy and controlling the approximation error. We resolve this challenge by deriving an exact characterization of the imaginary-time evolution from the Krylov space generated by repeated applications of the Hamiltonian to the initial state. This characterization induces a hierarchy of operator directions expressed through nested anti-commutators. Truncating the hierarchy produces a systematic static operator pool, with polynomial size in the system size at any fixed truncation order. The resulting construction provides a principled route to compact unitary approximations of imaginary-time dynamics. Numerical tests on spin models show close agreement with exact constrained imaginary-time evolution and small constraint deviations, while a fermionic example yields energies close to the analytic constrained-search reference.
authors: Daniele Cuomo; Luis Cort Barrada; Michał Studziński; Robert van Leeuwen

title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
abstract: We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.
authors: Meri Harutyunyan; Stéphane Guérin

title: Continuous variable payload transmitter for the SPOQC mission
abstract: The continuous variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme enables two parties to share a secret key separated by a certain distance. Here we propose, design, build, test and show results of a CV payload transmitter, intended to demonstrate downlink based QKD from a CubeSat in low earth orbit. This is part of the SPOQC mission by Quantum Communications Hub, UK which was successfully launched on March 2026.
authors: Vinod N. Rao; Killian Murphy; Timothy Ayers; Fadi Ahwal; Timothy P. Spiller; Rupesh Kumar

title: Negative non-linear differential dissipation in mechanical quartz resonators
abstract: We observe negative non-linear differential dissipation in a low-frequency (32.7 kHz) miniature quartz tuning fork, representing a high-Q piezoelectric resonator, at temperatures below 0.3 K. Similar drive-induced dissipation suppression has previously been reported in superconducting microwave resonators, and high-frequency MEMS devices, associated to coupling with tunneling two-level systems (TTLSs). In the case of low-frequency resonators, the equivalent temperature of the mechanical mode is orders of magnitude lower than the thermodynamic temperature of the device, implying that accessible TTLS states are largely saturated. We demonstrate that the observed temperature and drive dependence of the losses fit well within the framework of an interacting TTLS bath, indicating the presence of a channel for energy transfer between the mechanical mode and thermally activated TTLSs. As a possible coupling mechanism, we suggest microwave phonon modes in the metallic electrodes of the tuning fork.
authors: Elena Sergeicheva; Juuso Manninen; Juha Tuoriniemi; Weijun Zeng; Francesco Massel; Pertti Hakonen

title: Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
abstract: Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.
authors: Oliver O'Brien; Atsushi Ueda; Etienne Granet; Henrik Dreyer; Frank Verstraete

title: Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.
authors: Wan-Peng Gao; Xiao-Liang He; Zheng-Qi Niu; Si-Qi Li; Da-Qiang Bao; Kuang Liu; Jian-Qiang You; Jaw-Shen Tsai; Zhen Wang; Zhi-Rong Lin

title: Crosstalk-Induced Row Hammer Attacks on Quantum Random Access Codes
abstract: Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of $60\%$. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the practical relevance of these attacks, we study their impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs), observing a degradation in their average success probabilities.
authors: Fernando Almaguer-Angeles; Victor F. dos Santos; Jonas Maziero; Marcin Pawłowski; Akshata Shenoy H

title: Quantum Relative Entropy and Information Flux Resolve Wavefunction Collapse in Spacelike-Separated QED Waveguides
abstract: Resolving how first-order quantum coherence and definite measurement outcomes emerge from entangled vacuum fluctuations across spacelike-separated regions is unified here by the principle that quantum relative entropy governs the energy-information flux across causal boundaries [P.~Dorau and A.~Much, Phys.~Rev.~Lett.~\textbf{136}, 091602 (2026)]. We establish the exact quantum-optical realization of this principle using dual, spacelike-separated entangled nonlinear biphoton sources implemented in quantum electrodynamics waveguides pumped by an optical frequency comb and seeded by a continuous-wave laser in a coherent state $|α\rangle$. We demonstrate that single-photon-added coherent states (SPACS) generated via coherent seeding possess a quantum relative entropy that precisely quantifies the entanglement deficit between signal and idler fields. Tracing over the unmeasured idler continuum yields an exact spatial Lindblad master equation along the propagation axis, proving that spatial dephasing is driven by an information divergence flux determined by the SPACS overlap fidelity $F = |α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$. Uniting this relative-entropy flow with quotient measurement theory (detailed in Section~S3 of the Supplemental Material), we rigorously resolve nonlocal wavefunction collapse into local coset projections---explaining macroscopic state reduction without superluminal signaling. This exact open-system framework simultaneously saturates the wave-particle-entanglement triality [T.~H.~Yoon and M.~Cho, Sci.~Adv.~\textbf{7}, eabi9268 (2021)] and anchors hardware-native time--frequency Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill stabilizers to the comb symplectic structure.

title: Quantum transport of vortex electrons in bending magnets and circular accelerators
abstract: Controlling the sizes and phase structure of single-particle wave packets in accelerators remains an experimental challenge and requires understanding how bending magnets transform these states. An important example is transporting relativistic vortex electrons through the magnets to a collision point while keeping a narrow orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) distribution. We derive an effective Hamiltonian that accounts for the packet acceleration, employ it to obtain a generalized BMT-like equation, match the electron state at both magnet boundaries, and calculate the mean OAM and its variance. A half turn can reverse the mean OAM relative to the momentum while broadening its distribution, so recovering the mean does not ensure state recovery. We identify windows in packet sizes and bend angles for a small OAM spread and show that weak bends can produce narrow distributions with the mean OAM tilted relative to the momentum, making these states candidates for spatiotemporal vortices. For a few MeV electrons, we propose to use half-turn magnets that leave the mean OAM nearly antiparallel to the momentum while keeping its distribution narrow. For a circular orbit in a uniform field, the OAM variance after the exit grows as $N^2$ over $N$ turns, favoring linear accelerators, such as LINAC at JINR, for first experiments in MeV range.
authors: D. Karlovets; I. Pavlov; A. Murtazin; D. Grosman; X. Chen

title: From maximum work to maximum power in an optimally controlled quantum Ising Otto engine
abstract: In finite-time quantum Otto engines, maximizing power requires balancing the duration of the unitary strokes against the losses from nonadiabatic excitations. We address this trade-off in an Otto engine with a free-fermion working medium, using quantum optimal control. Having determined the single-particle energy scales that maximize ideal work at fixed reservoir temperatures, we realize them as the two endpoint Hamiltonians of a transverse-field Ising chain, connected by a path that crosses the quantum critical point. Optimal control of the unitary strokes yields near-ideal work on a time scale growing linearly with system size, instead of quadratically as for linear driving. We derive a time-rescaling relation that maps protocols with different energy scales onto a single reference problem and, for complete thermalization strokes of fixed duration, use it to build an analytical model of the cycle power. The model predicts two competing maximum-power regimes: a slow branch that approaches the ideal work, and a fast, size-independent branch that trades work for a shorter cycle and dominates above a crossover size, in quantitative agreement with numerical optimal-control results. It also identifies power-optimal energy scales that differ from the work-optimal ones and further increase the power. Our results provide a predictive approach to jointly optimizing the operating conditions and finite-time dynamics of quantum heat engines.
authors: Vincenzo Roberto Arezzo; Davide Rossini; Giuseppe E. Santoro; Giulia Piccitto

title: Approaching quantum limits in sub-Rayleigh resolution using phase modulation optimization
abstract: Spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) has made significant progress in incoherent optical imaging and has been implemented through various experimental approaches. Holography-based SPADE is widely used in proof-of-principle experiments because of its low cost, stable optical arrangement, and ease of implementation. However, its low photon utilization severely limits its practical applications. Alternating Fourier transforms and phase modulations can implement unitary optical transformations. Building on this idea, we use backpropagation to optimize the phase profiles of spatial light modulators (SLMs) and thereby design quantum measurements that are efficient in both information and energy. We study centroid--separation estimation for two incoherent point sources, using Fisher information or the estimation errors of an auxiliary neural network estimator as optimization objectives. As the number of SLMs increases, the optimized measurements approach the quantum limits characterized by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound and the information-regret tradeoff relation. With a few SLMs, our method can outperform direct imaging, showing its potential for superresolution imaging.
authors: Chao-Ning Hu; Jun Xin; Xiao-Ming Lu

title: Effective Thermodynamics of a Volume-Dependent Qubit
abstract: We develop an effective thermodynamics for a qubit whose energy gap depends inversely on a volume-like control parameter, $Δ(V)=Δ_0/V$, where $V$ is a spectral-control coordinate rather than a literal mechanical volume. Starting from the canonical Gibbs state, we derive a complete thermodynamic structure from the Helmholtz potential and its Legendre and stability properties, including the fundamental relation $S(U,V)$, a generalized pressure conjugate to $V$, the equation of state $U=PV$, the first law, and the associated Maxwell relations. Reversible adiabats preserve the Gibbs populations and satisfy $TV=\mathrm{const.}$ and $PV^2=\mathrm{const.}$, corresponding to an effective exponent $γ=2$. The resulting effective Carnot cycle attains the Carnot efficiency, $η_{\mathrm{Carnot}}=1-T_C/T_H$, whereas the Otto cycle yields $η_{\mathrm{Otto}}=1-V_{\min}/V_{\max}$ and remains strictly sub-Carnot at finite work output. We identify the source of Otto irreversibility exactly: entropy is produced entirely during the isochoric thermalizations, and the cycle entropy production quantifies the informational mismatch between the adiabatically transported states and the reservoir-selected Gibbs states through the sum of the corresponding quantum relative entropies. Finally, we show that unitary-generated nonpassivity can act as a nonequilibrium battery, producing an apparent efficiency above Carnot when its preparation cost is omitted. At the same time, complete work accounting restores the thermodynamic bound.
authors: André T. Cesário; Marcela Herrera

title: Exponential mixing time for the Davies dynamics of the quantum random energy model
abstract: We prove exponentially slow thermalization for the quantum random energy model (QREM) under Davies dynamics. The QREM is the $n$-qubit Hamiltonian $H=ΓT+U$, where $U$ assigns independent Gaussian energies with variance equal to the system size to computational-basis configurations and $T$ is the transverse field generated by single-qubit Pauli $X$ operators. Let $β_c=\sqrt{2\log 2}$ be the freezing inverse temperature of the classical random energy model. For every inverse temperature $β>β_c$ and every transverse-field strength $0\leqΓ<Γ_c(β)$, where $e^{ββ_c}=2\cosh(βΓ_c(β))$, we show that the mixing time of the dissipative Davies dynamics associated with single-qubit Pauli system--bath couplings grows exponentially with the system size, almost surely; the bound is unchanged if the standard zero-Bohr-frequency dephasing terms are included. The result is uniform over all Davies rates satisfying detailed balance and a polynomial upper bound and does not assume primitivity. In the spin-glass phase, the Gibbs weight is carried by a sparse family of deep classical configurations that are separated by an extensive Hamming distance. A localization theorem for the QREM [Manai, Warzel, Comm. Math. Phys. 402, 1259 (2023)] transfers this geometry to the corresponding low-energy quantum eigenstates. Consequently, the Gibbs weight of the intermediate spectral sector is exponentially small, while single-qubit bath operators have exponentially small matrix elements between the two macroscopic sides of the bottleneck. A Davies-specific flux estimate then converts these two facts into an exponential lower bound on the mixing time. This gives a rigorous open-system dynamical manifestation of the frozen, localized low-energy structure of the QREM throughout its equilibrium spin-glass phase below the quantum transition line.
authors: Giacomo De Palma; Emanuele Mingione

title: Nonuniform Time-bins for Making Raw QRNG Outputs Uniform
abstract: Random numbers play a vital role in scientific simulations and cryptography. Both randomness and security are critical requirements for random number generators (RNGs). However, classical RNGs often rely on mathematical assumptions that can compromise security, while quantum RNGs (QRNGs) face challenges, including non-uniform output due to the lack of specialized single-photon sources. In this work, we propose a QRNG model that generates uniformly distributed random numbers using a standard coherent photon source, without requiring heavy attenuation or post-processing. Although the raw data is theoretically free of bias, post-processing, if any, may be required to suppress any classical noise and device imperfections. The proposed method analytically equalizes the output probabilities under the assumed photon-arrival-time model, potentially reducing the need for heavy attenuation and post-processing to correct binning bias. We evaluate the method using real photon-detection timestamps and compare its statistical performance with conventional uniform time binning using the NIST, Dieharder, and ENT test suites. The results demonstrate improved statistical performance for the proposed binning scheme under the tested conditions.
authors: Nirupam Basak; Goutam Paul

title: Quantum trajectory of a spin oscillator, continuous retrodiction beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
abstract: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation in quantum mechanics limits the precision of predicting the outcome of measurements of any non-commuting observables. However, this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of the outcomes of past measurements. Here, we experimentally demonstrate this using a spin oscillator consisting of $ 5.17 \times 10^{10}$ rubidium atoms. Through weak continuous measurements, we monitor canonical spin observables $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ with $[\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}},\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}] = i\hbar$. By combining information obtained before and after time $t$, we retrodict the outcomes of measurements of $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ at time $t$ with variances that remain, concurrently over 1.4 hours, $\sim$ 1.01 dB below the bound set by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We also infer and demonstrate the ability to retrodict, with the same precision, the measurement outcomes for arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator. This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies.
authors: Peiying Li; Junlei Duan; Suotang Jia; Klaus Mølmer; Yanhong Xiao

title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls
abstract: High-fidelity quantum gates are a central requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet their implementation is limited by the sensitivity of qubits to environmental noise and by control non-idealities. To mitigate these effects, quantum gates can be designed as dynamically corrected gates (DCGs), where control sequences are engineered to suppress the impact of errors on the resulting operation. Many methods in the literature are able to synthesize DCGs, but they typically rely on numerical optimization, with synthesis times on the order of minutes per gate. Here, we propose an automated semi-analytical method that reduces this cost by orders of magnitude, synthesizing smooth, robust control pulses in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness. Our approach is based on the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, where quantum evolution is mapped onto a geometric space curve whose geometric properties determine the target gate and its robustness. We parameterize the curve in the Frenet-Serret frame and employ the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) to design controls that are robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. The PMP is formulated as a boundary-value problem and solved using a shooting method. The Frenet-Serret frame is integrated using Rodrigues' formula. Starting from a reference solution, we gradually vary the target rotation angle to construct a library of solutions, whose interpolation provides initial guesses for the shooting parameters of new target gates. We evaluated the method on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, obtaining a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparation of the interpolation base. Quantum propagation yielded nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.
authors: Eduardo Willwock Lussi; Rafael de Santiago; Eduardo Inacio Duzzioni; Hector Bessa Silveira

title: Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
abstract: Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.
authors: Justin Provazza; Oliver Knitter; Joshua Goings; Evgeny Epifanovsky; Chi Chen; Martin Roetteler; Luning Zhao

title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.
authors: Tong Jiang; Andrew Zhao; Shashwat Kumar; Jigyasa Nigam; Eliott Rosenberg; Ryan Babbush; Andrew D. Baczewski; William J. Huggins; Joonho Lee

title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
abstract: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.
authors: Paul Argyle; Djamil Lakhdar-Hamina; Sarah H. Miller; Victor Galitski

title: Primitive Quantum Gates for an $SU(3)$ Discrete Subgroup: $Σ(216\times3)$
abstract: We construct a primitive gate set for the digital quantum simulation of the $648$-element discrete subgroup of $SU(3)$, $\dsb$. The five algorithmic primitives are the inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates, for which we provide qubit and qutrit--qubit decompositions. For a fiducial shear-viscosity calculation on a $10^3$ spatial lattice with $50$ time steps and a total synthesis-error budget of $10^{-8}$, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are $2.3$--$6.8\times10^{10}$ $T$ gates in the qubit architecture and $1.3$--$5.9\times10^{12}$ $R$ gates in the qutrit--qubit architecture.
authors: Erik J. Gustafson; Henry Lamm; Edison Murairi; Sebastian Osorio Perez

title: Coherent phase slips in coupled rings: from weak to strong interactions
abstract: We study the coherent transfer of circulation between two weakly coupled lattice rings of ultracold bosons, in which a persistent current initially prepared in one ring oscillates back and forth between the rings without net transfer of particles. Combining Bose--Hubbard simulations with their Gross--Pitaevskii and quantum phase model limits, we show that similar current oscillations arise from two distinct microscopic mechanisms. At weak interactions, particles in each occupied momentum mode tunnel independently between the rings, leading to a transfer time inversely proportional to the inter-ring tunnelling, extensive particle-number fluctuations and entanglement distributed over many Schmidt components; this mode-exchange dynamics is suppressed by self-trapping as the interactions increase. At stronger interactions and large filling, in the phase-dominated regime, circulation is instead transferred through a second-order collective process between many-body persistent-current states, with a transfer time scaling as the inverse square of the inter-ring tunnelling in the weak-link limit. Number fluctuations then remain of order one instead of growing with the particle number, and within each number sector the system evolves into coherent superpositions of two many-body configurations, distinguished by which ring carries the circulation. The entanglement accessible under number-conserving operations therefore reaches up to approximately one bit. We propose a quench protocol to prepare the initial state and estimate transfer times within reach of current ring-lattice experiments, identifying coupled rings as a platform to study coherent quantum phase slips and to manipulate persistent-current states.
authors: Axel Perez-Obiol; Malcolm G. Boshier; Luigi Amico; Juan Polo

title: Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between $\mathsf{StoqMA}$ and $\mathsf{MA}$
abstract: Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain $\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}$, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation $$\mathsf{MA} \subsetneq \mathsf{StoqMA}$$ relative to a classical oracle. The class $\mathsf{StoqMA}$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians. Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).
authors: Yassine Hamoudi; Yvan Le Borgne; Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara

title: Quantum Fourier integration of decay rates at next-to-leading order
abstract: We discuss the use of quantum neural networks (QNNs) as a tool for integrating decay rates at next-to-leading order (NLO) in perturbation theory. Data-encoding quantum circuits admit a truncated Fourier-series representation, enabling a trained QNN to approximate a target integrand and provide the coefficients subsequently integrated with Quantum Fourier Iterative Amplitude Estimation (QFIAE). The causal-unitary formulation of the Loop-Tree Duality (LTD) combines virtual and real contributions into locally finite integrands suitable for this representation. We consider $H\to q\bar q(g)$, $γ^*\to q\bar q(g)$ and $Φ\toφφ(φ)$, comparing quantum-simulator and quantum-hardware results with analytic NLO predictions. The study illustrates the potential of Fourier-based QNN integration for high-energy physics.
authors: David F. Rentería-Estrada

title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
abstract: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy
authors: Jiyuan Wang; Qian Zhang; Guoqing Harry Xu; Miryung Kim

title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
abstract: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.
authors: Yu-Xin Wu; Yuan-Hong Tao; Ji-Hui Mo; Peng-Fei Ma; Shu-Hui Wu; Shao-Ming Fei

title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description
abstract: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.

title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
abstract: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.
authors: Gabriella G. Damas; G. D. de Moraes Neto

title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
abstract: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.
authors: Bin Cheng; Naixu Guo; Feng Pan

title: Entropic measures of quantum information
abstract: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
authors: Roberto Rubboli; Bartosz Regula; Mario Berta; Ludovico Lami; Marco Tomamichel

title: Thermodynamics of Speed and Efficiency with Quantum Feedback
abstract: Rapid thermodynamic operations generally entail irreversible dissipation, giving rise to trade-offs between operating speed and thermodynamic cost. Yet, how quantum feedback fundamentally reshapes these trade-offs remains elusive. Here, we derive a finite-time current--dissipation relation for continuously monitored open quantum dynamics with jump feedback. From this fundamental relation, we establish a quantum speed limit and a power-efficiency trade-off for stationary information engines, identifying how feedback affects state transformations and the performance of engines through both informational entropy and direct dynamical contributions. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for fast, low-dissipation quantum thermodynamics in the presence of feedback control, exemplified by attaining the generalized Landauer bound in finite-time information erasure and approaching unit information efficiency at finite power in the large-system limit of a collective engine.
authors: Yue Liu; Ryotaro Honma; Ruicheng Bao; Tan Van Vu

title: Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Lie groups, Schur-Weyl duality and symmetry breaking
abstract: We present a systematic framework for gauging continuous symmetries, and show that the Schur-Weyl duality arises naturally as a realization of this construction with open boundary conditions. Restricting to compact Lie group symmetries, we construct dual models for one-dimensional quantum lattice models exhibiting those symmetries. We demonstrate that matrix product operators enable the explicit construction of intertwiners between the dual theories and their (non-invertible) symmetries. With closed boundary conditions, we can relate the full spectrum of these dual theories by considering all possible twisted boundary conditions. We illustrate how the Peter-Weyl transform appears when the duality acts on the boundary Hilbert space of a $G$-symmetric model. The presented framework generalizes previous work on dualities for unitary fusion category symmetric models. It exemplifies how dualities for both finite and continuous symmetries rely on the relation between a bond algebra and a representation of the symmetry in the lattice as double centralizers. We argue that dual non-invertible spontaneous symmetry breaking is the mechanism that underlies symmetric tensor network algorithms. We illustrate these results for $U(1)$- and $SU(2)$-symmetric quantum lattice models.
authors: Dante Bosgoed; Frank Verstraete; Laurens Lootens

title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
abstract: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.
authors: Angela Sara Cacciapuoti; Jessica Illiano; Caterina De Risi; Marcello Caleffi

title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
abstract: Repetition-code process tomography compares the logical channel of a code with a reference channel through a decoder almost always the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates that decoder needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint that makes the count a resource. Exhaustive enumeration at $n=3$, $5$ and $7$, each rank decided in exact arithmetic, gives minima of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected, not which, so the problem splits into a budget and a placement; the placement decides identifiability, and more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding has rank $24$ of $27$, and under a calibration-residual floor the $n=3$ precision curve is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.0$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ working points and better at every one of them, by $1.8$ to $88$ times; with the placement fixed in advance the factor falls to $6.9$, or to $3.1$ for the pre-commitment never worse, both medians over the same $40$ points. Because the full advantage needs per-point placement, we also certify two placements in parallel: they lose no direction either sees and, wherever either is identifiable and the calibration floor permits, reach a $10$\,mrad target within twice the shots. The optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal.
authors: Long Huang

title: Testing Gravitationally-Induced-Entanglement with Massive Particles and Quantum Clocks
abstract: We present an experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a levitated particle with an array of quantum clocks. By harnessing the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, our scheme offers a conceivable path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks in the laboratory. Crucially, this setup will probe a genuinely relativistic effect one that requires the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass and cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses. Therefore, observing this entanglement would provide evidence for the quantised nature of active gravitational mass -- which has not been tested in any prior experiment -- rather than for spatial coherence of fixed masses,which is routinely tested in matterwave interferometers
authors: Germain Tobar; Markus Aspelmeyer; Magdalena Zych

title: Atomic Static Electric Quadrupole Polarizability from Relativistic Many-Body Theory With Application To Thulium $\left(6s^2\, 4f^{13}\right)$\, $^2F_{7/2}$ and $^2F_{5/2}$
abstract: In the present work a method for calculating atomic static electric rank-$n$ tensor quadrupole polarizabilities $α_Q^{(n)}(J)$ for arbitrary atomic electronic structure is presented. It is based on a linear-symmetry representation of atomic states using large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions, and the quadrupole polarizabilities are obtained by a sum-over-states approach. The major result from applying this method to atomic thulium is $α_Q^{(0)}(\frac{7}{2}) = 2496^{+0}_{-231}$ \au for the electronic ground term $^2F_{7/2}$ static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability which is roughly a factor of four smaller than same property in the electronic ground state of the cesium atom. This finding adds to the favorable properties of thulium atoms in atomic-clock research.
authors: Timo Fleig

title: Asymptotic analysis of the dynamical field-field correlation function of the impenetrable Bose gas
abstract: We study the long-time, large-distance asymptotic behaviour of the two-point correlation function of fields of the impenetrable Bose gas in equilibrium states characterized by a quasi-momentum distribution (or filling fraction). This includes, in particular, the cases of Gibbs and generalized Gibbs ensembles. The overall structure of the asymptotic expansion depends on the number of Fermi points, those points for which the quasi-momentum distribution takes the value $1/2$. The leading asymptotic behaviour is determined by a relaxation rate, a logarithmic correction term and an amplitude for which we provide simple and explicit expressions. In the case of two Fermi points the first sub-leading correction is calculated as well.
authors: Frank Göhmann; Karol K. Kozlowski; Mikhail D. Minin; Alexander Weiße

title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
abstract: Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence.
