Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.
authors: Shashank Srivastava

title: Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation
abstract: Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.
authors: M Nishanth; Shreyas Sadugol; Payman Mahmoudi; Alexander Yosifov; Aditya Iyer; Roopayan Ghosh; Jinzhao Sun

title: Quantum enhanced beam displacement estimation: sensitivity limits, optimal probes, and measurement schemes
abstract: We investigate the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements and identify optimal strategies that attain them, using the framework of mode parameter estimation. We contrast two families of states with different resource constraints, using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. First, for fixed total photon number states, the optimal state is identified and we show that it asymptotically approaches a rotated NOON state. The sensitivity bound is compared to that of an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state with fixed average photon number. Finally, we propose concrete measurement schemes using the method of moments and show that the twin-Fock state may provide a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this task. Our work provides a broader benchmark for developing practical strategies for spatial sensing at the quantum limit.
authors: Balázs Novák; Pau Colomer; Joseph Zhang; Emre Köse; Manuel Gessner

title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
abstract: Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.
authors: Ke-Xin Tang; Zhen-Qiang Weng; Kai Yan; Yao-Yao Lu; Yu-Ze Zhu; Hang Song; Jun-Jie He; Jie-Cheng Yang; Xiang Zhao; Lin Yang; Xian-Min Jin

title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
abstract: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.
authors: Armando Angrisani; Hela Mhiri

title: Dynamical effects induced by synthetic SU(1,1) gauge fields
abstract: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.
authors: Chenwei Lv

title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.
authors: Ke-Sean J. M. Peter; Ryan A. Kowalski; David A. Curie; Dakota Braaten; Matthew W. Day; Denis R. Candido; Deyu Li; Richard F. Haglund; Joshua D. Caldwell; Richarda Niemann

title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.
authors: Aldana Al-Sulaiti; Kuan-Cheng Chen; Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir; Ahmed Farouk; Saif Al-Kuwari

title: Efficient classical simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models with Kramers symmetry
abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo methods are widely used to solve quantum many-body problems. However, rigorous guarantees for their performance are poorly understood, especially for simulating interacting fermions. In this work, we develop a quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for a broad family of fermionic systems exhibiting Kramers time-reversal symmetry, and prove that their partition functions can be estimated in polynomial time. This family, which contains many important classes of Hubbard-type models, is known to both avoid the sign problem and obey a Lee-Yang zero-freeness theorem. Thus our results suggest that these two properties together may enable efficient classical algorithms for quantum many-body systems more broadly.
authors: Chaithanya Rayudu; Jun Takahashi; Ojas Parekh; Andrew Zhao

title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
abstract: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.
authors: Yuanjie Ren; Margarita Davydova; Shankar Balasubramanian; Andreas Bauer

title: Magic Is in the Eye of the Measure
abstract: Magic, or nonstabilizerness, is the quantum resource behind universal quantum computation. Its applications in high-energy and nuclear physics rely almost exclusively on the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), although magic has no unique measure. For two qubits, we compare the SRE with three measures defined through optimizations over stabilizer states: the min- and max-relative entropies of magic and the logarithmic free robustness. We determine the maximal-magic states of all four measures, with exact proofs, and find that they depend on the measure. In the determination of the weak mixing angle from minimal magic in Møller scattering, the min-relative entropy gives an energy-dependent value that differs from that of the SRE, whereas the max-relative entropy and the logarithmic free robustness give $\sin^2θ_W=1/4$ at all energies. We trace this difference to the non-analytic structure of the optimization-based measures. Physical conclusions drawn from extremizing magic can thus depend on the measure.
authors: Zhi-Heng Shen; Zhewei Yin; Hao-Lin Zhang

title: Universality in Quantum Many-Body Spin Ratchets
abstract: We consider a class of quantum circuits, known as quantum many-body spin ratchets, which act on alternating spin chains with two distinct spin types on even and odd sites. This setup breaks parity symmetry and exhibits chiral transport. It has been shown that the drift velocity in the case of integrable, SU(2)-symmetric quantum spin ratchets is universal, and conjectured that the same holds in the non-integrable case. Here, we prove that this universal drift is exact at all times, requiring only translation invariance and U(1) symmetry. Furthermore, we prove that it is sufficient for the circuit to be translation-invariant on average by deriving the same result in the random case. Finally, we demonstrate that breaking translation invariance immediately results in deviations from this universal prediction.
authors: Andrea Azzali; Marko Ljubotina

title: Density kernel and temporal quantum information probes in double-scaled SYK
abstract: Entanglement is conventionally defined through a Hilbert space bipartition on a fixed time slice. Recent work has generalized this notion to multiple times through a non-Hermitian density kernel constructed from temporal correlation functions, encoding causal response, temporal non-classicality and quantum dynamics. We construct this kernel in the double-scaled Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (DSSYK) model using its exact chord Hilbert space formulation and study the resulting temporal information diagnostics. The direct sum structure of chord space naturally introduces a coarse-graining under which coherence between different chord sectors is removed. We show that the corresponding kernel measures quantify how information is dynamically transferred across subregions in the chord Hilbert space. We find that decreasing $λ$ enhances the propagation of temporal correlation across chord sectors, as well as the loss of memory within a fixed sector. This accelerated temporal dynamics in the small $λ$ limit coincides with the emergence of a semiclassical gravity description. Depending on the chord space partition, the probes exhibit either saturation, a growth followed by a decay, or temporary memory loss. The characteristic propagation time is nicely captured by a wavefront picture in Krylov space, with position-dependent hopping parameters that are determined by the DSSYK Lanczos coefficients. Finally, given the quantum sine-dilaton gravity description of DSSYK and its connections to de Sitter holography, our results provide a controlled setting for probing temporal quantum correlations across quantum and semiclassical gravitational regimes, and motivate a geometric interpretation of the density kernel.
authors: Johanna Erdmenger; Maximilian Gaschler; Jonathan Karl; Arnab Kundu; Georg Setzer

title: Exploring topological signatures of quantum Fisher information scaling in graph states
abstract: Graph states are a versatile resource for quantum metrology, and their quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a closed-form expression in terms of the underlying graph: it counts pairs of vertices with identical neighborhoods. It remains unclear, however, which global structural properties of a graph determine whether its QFI exceeds the standard quantum limit (SQL). Here we ask whether topological invariants, namely the Betti numbers of the graph's clique complex, capture this behavior, and we address the question numerically with two complementary approaches. First, we randomly add or delete edges in balanced complete multipartite graphs, which combine a QFI beyond the SQL with a single nonvanishing higher Betti number. Edge addition eventually destroys both the metrological advantage and the nontrivial topology. Under edge deletion, by contrast, higher Betti numbers persist well after the QFI has dropped to the SQL. Second, we start from Erdős--Rényi random graphs, whose QFI does not typically exceed the SQL, and maximize a chosen Betti number with a Monte Carlo search. The search drives the graphs toward near-extremal multipartite structures whose QFI lies well beyond the SQL. Our results show that topological optimization offers a route to metrologically useful graph states, but also that Betti numbers alone do not determine the QFI.
authors: Majid Hassani; Patrick Emonts; Jordi Tura

title: Entanglement in Collective Neutrino Oscillations on a Quantum Computer
abstract: Simulations on a quantum computer have been propounded as a next-generation tool for studying neutrino flavour oscillations in dense environments like supernovae or neutron star mergers. However, quantum advantage hinges on the presence of quantum entanglement in the neutrino ensemble, and it has been argued that such entanglement becomes negligible in the limit of large neutrino number density. Here, we address this question by explicitly simulating the multiparticle dynamics of entangled neutrino ensembles with a varying number of particles, $N$, on both classical and quantum hardware, and comparing our results to those obtained with conventional ``mean-field'' methods based on Boltzmann-type kinetic equations. For simple toy systems, we demonstrate both analytically and numerically that, indeed, the predictions of full multiparticle simulations agree with those of mean-field methods in the large-$N$ limit. Along the way, we develop novel algorithms for the efficient simulation of entangled neutrino gases on both classical and quantum hardware. We then discuss physical situations in which an entangled neutrino system \emph{cannot} be described through mean-field dynamics alone and quantum entanglement therefore becomes phenomenologically relevant. We comment on the conditions under which these scenarios may be realized in supernova cores or neutron star mergers.
authors: Katarina Bleau; Nikolina Ilic; Joachim Kopp; Ushak Rahaman; Xin Yue Yu

title: Harnessing dimensional leakage for continuous-variable randomness certification
abstract: Semi-device-independent quantum protocols often rely on strict Hilbert-space dimension assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in realistic implementations, particularly with infinite-dimensional optical fields. The almost-qudit framework addresses this issue by quantifying the leakage of quantum states beyond a target subspace. Although such leakage can severely compromise randomness certification for fixed preparation and measurement inputs, we show that averaging over the full input ensemble can mitigate this vulnerability and extend the range of tolerable leakage. This enhanced robustness enables nonzero randomness certification using low-squeezing single-mode Gaussian states and homodyne detection, thus offering an experimentally accessible continuous-variable implementation.
authors: Moisés Alves; Tailan S. Sarubi; Vitor L. Sena; Alexandre B. Tacla; Rafael Chaves

title: Quantum-enabled measurement of gravitational forces at the milligram scale
abstract: Gravity is by far the weakest among all known interactions. While it dominates the large-scale structure of the universe, gravitational interactions between small masses in the microscopic range remain underexplored because they are too weak to be experimentally accessible. The interface between gravity, described by general relativity, and quantum mechanics, which describes the microscopic world, is of particular interest. From a theory standpoint, these two major descriptions of nature have not been combined in a satisfactory manner. Technology is gradually becoming mature enough such that probing gravity at the microscopic scale, where quantum mechanics and gravity potentially meet, is becoming accessible. Explorations towards genuine quantum gravity have to be carried out under conditions where the gravitating masses possess non-classical properties, which necessitates ultimate protection against disturbances, such as ultralow temperatures and a small range of motion. Here, we present an experiment at millikelvin temperatures, where the gravity due to a micron-range coherent displacement of an 87 mg source mass imprints on the motion of an oscillating membrane loaded with a 1.3 mg test mass. Vibrations of the membrane are measured in the microwave optomechanical scheme, which is a key setup for investigating non-classical motional states of mechanical oscillators. When considering the combination of total source and test masses, our setup presents two orders of magnitude progress in sensing gravity at the small scale, as well as a 35 dB improvement of gravitational sensitivity at kHz frequencies or above. Our setup offers a plausible approach for studying gravitational interactions between masses prepared in non-classical motional states.
authors: Matthew Herbst; Ewa Rej; Joe Depellette; Richa Cutting; Jinhoon Jeong; Mika A. Sillanpää

title: What are local complementations, really?
abstract: A local complementation at a vertex $v$ of a graph $G$ replaces the induced neighborhood of $v$ with its complement. Local complementations are, at face value, peculiar operations. Yet they famously show up when describing the local Clifford equivalence among graph states, and, because of this, have become a fundamental notion in the study of graph states. Following Bouchet, we show here how local complementations on graphs are more naturally thought of in terms of switchings of (matroid) bases of stabilizer states. Bases and switchings reveal structural properties of stabilizer states that are harder to glean from the graph-theoretic description alone, such as vertex-minors and statistics of local Pauli measurements. Bases also simplify prior proofs about graphs up to local complementations, of which we give several examples. Bases are foundational in the study of (multi)matroids; as such this paper serves as a gentle introduction to the applications of multimatroids to quantum information theory.
authors: Kenneth Goodenough

title: How Many Shots Does a Quantum Reservoir Need? Measurement Cost and Its Scaling in Buffered Quantum Reservoir Computing
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) inherits from classical reservoir computing the property that only a linear readout is trained, but unlike a classical reservoir its state is never directly observable: every feature is an expectation value estimated from a finite number of measurement shots. The shot budget is therefore a first-class hyperparameter with no classical analogue. Its effect on QRC has recently begun to be studied; what remains unsettled is how a required budget should be defined, and whether competing definitions agree. This paper argues that they do not, and that the disagreement is systematic rather than incidental. This paper distinguishes a \emph{precision budget} $N_\varepsilon$, the shots needed to estimate the reservoir features to a fixed relative accuracy, from a \emph{convergence budget} $N_\star$, the shots needed for the trained readout to approach its own noise-free ceiling. Proposition~\ref{prop:confound} shows that $N_\star$ depends on the noise-free error floor by construction, so that a configuration with a worse floor appears cheaper, and that configurations should therefore be compared at a fixed measurement budget rather than by the budget each needs to reach its own ceiling.
authors: Raman Khurana

title: Sign-hedged Beam QAOA:Scaling Quantum Optimization Algorithms
abstract: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) encodes a combinatorial objective as an Ising Hamiltonian and alternates cost and mixer operations for p rounds. Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) scales further by using the resulting correlations, whether variables tend to agree or disagree, to eliminate variables one at a time. But each inferred sign is accepted irrevocably, so a single early mistake propagates through every later reduction and can discard the global optimum. As elimination proceeds, residuals shrink while effective edge density typically rises, so later decisions face denser Ising problems, a regime that fully connected Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) instances stress test directly. This paper proposes sign-hedged beam RQAOA, which retains the variable or pair selected by standard RQAOA, explores both possible sign assignments, keeps the best B residual problems according to a classical score, and completes each survivor with ordinary RQAOA. On frustrated SK instances, where standard recursion collapses to AR 0.474, beam recovers near-optimal AR 0.998 at the same p. We evaluate the workflow on 50+ instances from HamLib and QOBLIB, spanning 4 and 5 regular and Erdos Renyi MaxCut graphs, Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glasses, and cardinality-constrained portfolio optimization, with up to 60 qubits and hardware runs on ibm kingston and ibm marrakesh. Matched simulator and device cells show consistent beam rankings: simulation and hardware agree that beam recovers near-optimal approximation ratio (AR) where standard recursion fails. These gains come from additional residual-circuit evaluations, classical pruning, and exact solution of a small core, rather than from increasing p, beam is a decision-side optimization atop fixed-p QAOA/RQAOA, not a claim that quantum circuits alone scale with qubit count.
authors: Anupama Ray; Arush Sharma

title: A Complete Calculus for Hamiltonian Quantum Programming
abstract: Given the forces acting on a quantum particle, a Hamiltonian models its continuous evolution. Quantum computers evolve Hamiltonians to simulate physical systems, to solve optimisation problems, and to estimate eigenvalues, and even the popular circuit abstraction is compiled to Hamiltonians on the hardware. We introduce Hamilton, a process calculus whose parallel operator is the sum of interactions acting simultaneously. Its operational semantics is the Lie-Trotter product formula, which recovers a sum as the limit of ever finer sequential interleavings; compiling a program means halving it to a chosen precision and unrolling the interleaving into a circuit. The semantics is fully abstract, the expressible Hamiltonians are exactly those whose Pauli coefficients have the form $m/2^k$, the precision that successive halving reaches, and the equational theory is complete and decidable. A full implementation compiles Hamilton programs to circuits and decides their equivalence, and Agda proofs sanity-check the core metatheory.
authors: Jacques Carette; Chris Heunen; Robin Kaarsgaard; Neil J. Ross; Amr Sabry

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. The hybrid solver reaches the certified optimum whenever one is available, matches Gurobi's performance on smaller instances, and outperforms it on larger instances, finding lower-energy solutions. These results show that the competitiveness of the hybrid solver on binary quadratic programs, so far observed only on a synthetic benchmark, extends to a real-world problem. This motivates comparisons with classical heuristics specific to protein side-chain optimization.
authors: Valeria B. C. Visani; Simone Reale; Alfonso Gautieri; Elisabetta Di Nitto

title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
abstract: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.
authors: Marin Girard

title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
abstract: Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is challenged by the combined effects of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic). Non-local magic, $M^{\mathrm{NL}}_α$, quantifies the component of non-stabilizerness that cannot be removed by local unitary transformations and provides a measure of quantum complexity beyond entanglement alone. It is bounded from below by the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, ${F}_A$. We calculate stabilizer Rényi entropies, non-local magic, entanglement-spectrum antiflatness, and entanglement entropy in shell-model ground states of more than 260 even-even, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei, using a bipartition into proton and neutron sectors. We find that the previously established bound $4{F}_A\leq{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ holds for every nucleus studied and approaches saturation in the limit of separable states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit markedly different patterns of entanglement and magic compared with even-even and odd-even systems, revealing distinctive signatures of proton-neutron quantum correlations and providing new insight into the complexity generated by nuclear interactions.
authors: James W. T. Keeble; Caroline E. P. Robin; Federico Rocco; Martin J. Savage

title: Neutral-atom quantum features as complementary structural encodings for graph learning
abstract: Structural descriptors provide graph neural networks (GNNs) with positional and topological inductive biases. However, widely used classical encodings based on random walks or Laplacian spectra emphasize specific structural statistics of a graph, leaving room for alternative descriptors. Neutral-atom quantum processing units (QPUs) can realize graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonians, allowing graph topology to be probed through dynamical correlation measurements. In this work, we use these measurements as quantum graph features (QGFs), providing a complementary, hardware-derived family of structural encoding that is not accurately described by classical features derived from Laplacian and adjacency matrices, even when supplemented with an extended set of random-walk, geometric descriptors and classical physical models. By appropriately selecting the quench parameters of the Hamiltonian, we access two characteristic correlation regimes with distinct structural signatures: antiferromagnetic-like and ferromagnetic-like. On an intrinsic information benchmark of 15 topological and spectral probing tasks, quantum and hybrid quantum-classical features match or surpass classical descriptors on local topological properties. When supplied to message-passing, attention, and graph-transformer backbones, hybrid quantum-classical features yield improvements that are within cross-fold noise on most cells but sign-consistent across architectures. When comparing noiseless, shot-sampled emulation-derived quantum features with a neutral-atom QPU implementation, the downstream hybrid results with compressed hardware features match their emulated counterparts within $0.01$ F$_1$ on all backbones. On a synthetic family of ladder graphs, QGFs distinguish two specific classes, outperforming the strongest classical structural descriptors by a margin exceeding cross-fold variability.
authors: Mathieu Garrigues; Igor O. Sokolov; Matthias Hecker; Lorenzo Moro; Shaheen Acheche

title: Kinetic Cluster Embedding for Qubit Decoherence in Dissipative Spin Baths
abstract: Interpreting the decoherence of a spin qubit requires knowing how the surrounding bath spins behave: whether they fluctuate independently, exchange polarization incoherently, or evolve as coherent groups. These processes can yield the same Hahn-echo coherence time yet produce different coherence signals under pulse control of the qubit. Existing theoretical approaches either capture bath correlations at a cost that grows combinatorially with spin-bath cluster size or neglect polarization transport altogether. We introduce kinetic cluster embedding (KCE), which uses a single dimensionless parameter, comparing the flip-flop coupling of a spin pair with its detuning and linewidth, to decide how each pair must be treated. Pairs that can complete an appreciable exchange oscillation are propagated with the full dissipative quantum dynamics. All other spins are treated as random-telegraph fluctuators coupled through a kinetic network of polarization-transfer rates. We show that for nitrogen-vacancy centers coupled to surface electron spins, KCE propagates about 7 four-spin clusters, compared to more than 10$^5$ propagated by fourth-order master-equation cluster-correlation (ME-CCE4); nevertheless it reproduces ME-CCE4 coherence times to within 15$\%$ for dipolar couplings of order $10^{2}$ times the bath relaxation rate. For a three-dimensional P1 bath, the agreement is within 16$\%$. Coherent multispin clusters emerge as the leading correction to independent fluctuators, and they leave a distinct signature in the CPMG response. Importantly, we find that whether a rate description suffices is set not by coupling strength alone but by whether a pair can exchange polarization coherently before detuning and damping suppress it.
authors: Xiaofei Yu; Jonah Nagura; Stella Wang; Evan J. Villafranca; Peter C. Maurer; Giulia Galli

title: From spectroscopy to quantum dynamics: assessing reduced models of a NaCs molecular gate
abstract: We investigate how spectroscopic calibration and basis selection affect predictions for a dipolar-exchange gate between two optically trapped $^{23}$Na$^{133}$Cs molecules. We construct a 128-state molecular Hamiltonian restricted to the $N=0,1$ rotational manifold, fit two effective optical parameters to three bright microwave transitions, and compare the resulting spectrum with four additional lines. In the coherent pair model, changing the optical polarization angle by $+0.1^\circ$ reduces the calculated gate fidelity from 94.64\% to 1.09\% at fixed carrier frequencies. Retuning the carriers and restoring the target Rabi frequencies recovers 89.31\%. The remaining sensitivity reflects changes in the multilevel pair dynamics that are not removed by target-frequency and target-Rabi recalibration. Enlarging the molecular basis produces nonmonotonic changes in fidelity, although the 11-state and 25-state calculations give closely agreeing logical maps after phase alignment. Two controls with isolated transfer probabilities near 98.45\% yield complete-gate fidelities differing by more than 11 percentage points. We relate these comparisons to a sufficient bound on the error of a projected propagator. The numerical tests quantify agreement among selected bases for a specified coherent Hamiltonian.
authors: Marko Gacesa

title: Spiral momentum spectra and spin asymmetry in vacuum pair production driven by phase-modulated elliptically polarized electric fields
abstract: We study vacuum electron--positron pair production in phase-modulated elliptically polarized electric fields using the quantum kinetic equations. We analyze how the modulation amplitude, frequency, ellipticity, and modulation form affect the spin-resolved momentum spectra and the spin asymmetry. Cosine-type modulation can deform ring-shaped momentum distributions into spiral patterns. This deformation depends nonmonotonically on the modulation amplitude and frequency and is most pronounced for circular polarization. In the transverse momentum plane, the spin-resolved yields favor the spin channel along the direction of field handedness. Reversing the field handedness would reverse the favored channel while leaving the total yield unchanged. Sine-type modulation preserves ring-shaped and mirror-symmetric spectra approximately, however, it leads to a stronger dependence of the spin asymmetry on the modulation amplitude than cosine-type modulation does. These results show that phase modulation and ellipticity can control the momentum spectra patterns in vacuum pair production. Moreover, phase modulation can also affect the degree of spin asymmetry.
authors: Li-Yi Yang; Hong-Hao Fan; Jing-He Huang; Shuo Yang; Bai-Song Xie

title: Quantum Fluctuations in Noether's Theorem
abstract: When deriving the expression for the Noether's current one obtains a term that is an integral over the Euler-Lagrange equation. This term vanishes along the classical path and so does not contribute to the current. However, quantum particles do not necessarily follow the classical path; this concept is the basis of Feynman's path integral quantization formalism. Thus, for a quantum system, the Euler-Lagrange term does not vanish and, hence, corresponds to a quantum fluctuation of the Noether's current owing to the system deviating from the classical path. Here, we compute this quantum fluctuation from Noether's theorem and the path integral formalism. We find that, for a time invariant system, the expression for the quantum fluctuations is give by minus the functional expression for the Hamiltonian, $ΔE = -H(y)$, evaluated at the distance from the classical path, $y$. As an example we evaluate quantum energy fluctuations of a single Harmonic oscillator. In the short time limit we recover the energy-time uncertainty relation and in the long time limit we recover the zero point energy of the quantum harmonic oscillator.
authors: J. A. Crosse

title: Shared Lookups and Lazy Residues: Fewer Toffoli Gates for Factoring RSA-2048
abstract: Gidney's 2025 construction for factoring RSA-2048 with few logical qubits spends most of its Toffoli gates on discrete-log table lookups and residue uncomputation. We reduce both costs. Shared lookups return entries for several primes of a residue number system at once because they have the same address. Retained intermediate residues remove recomputation during cleanup and enable lazy arithmetic with a single final modular reduction. We prove output preservation and estimate resources with an open benchmark built on the reference simulator. Against the best reference setting within the same logical-qubit budget, using the published model for the reference and benchmark counts for our circuits, we obtain $15\%$ fewer Toffolis at $1{,}461$ qubits ($5.08 \times 10^{9}$ per factoring) and $46\%$ fewer at $1{,}806$ qubits ($2.55 \times 10^{9}$). A matched ablation finds $28.8\%$ fewer Toffolis from three-prime sharing at fixed window and checkpoint settings. Architecture-specific timing determines how much becomes a runtime saving.
authors: Monit Sharma; Hoong Chuin Lau

title: Time- and phase-resolved emulation of sign-selective counterdiabatic dynamics in a superconducting qutrit
abstract: In cyclic three-level systems, phase-sensitive interference can convert a coupling-sign reversal into a population contrast, providing a controllable analogue of handedness. We emulate this mechanism in a superconducting transmon qutrit using two resonant single-photon drives and a phase-controlled effective two-photon drive. Effective loop phases \(Φ_L=+π/2\) and \(Φ_R=-π/2\), separated by \(π\), reverse the auxiliary contribution to the dark--bright coupling, canceling the intrinsic nonadiabatic term for \(L\) and reinforcing it for \(R\). Time-resolved trajectories reveal dark-pathway transfer for \(L\) and bright-manifold participation for \(R\). Measured late-time averages give a target-state population contrast of 0.929. Loop-phase measurements establish phase selectivity, while pulse-area and common-mode amplitude scans characterize the operating regime and control sensitivity. These results provide direct time- and phase-domain access to sign-selective counterdiabatic interference in a programmable cyclic qutrit.
authors: Yiwen Li; Luojia Xu; Xinsheng Tan; Yang Yu

title: Optimal Separations Between Randomized and Quantum Query Complexity under Permutation Symmetry
abstract: A function $f:\cD\subseteq A^N\to\{0,1\}$ is \emph{permutation-invariant} if every permutation of its input positions preserves both its domain and its value. We study how this symmetry limits quantum speedups. For $1/6\leq\varepsilon<1/2$, we prove that every such function over an arbitrary finite alphabet $A$ satisfies $R_\varepsilon(f)=O(Q_\varepsilon(f)^2)$, where $R_\varepsilon$ and $Q_\varepsilon$ denote randomized and quantum query complexities with error at most $\varepsilon$. This improves the previous cubic bound (ITCS 2019). We further establish bounds for graph and hypergraph properties, for which vertex relabeling preserves both the promise and the answer. For the same range of $\varepsilon$, we obtain $R_\varepsilon(f)=O(Q_\varepsilon(f)^4)$ for graph properties in the adjacency-matrix model and $R_\varepsilon(f)=O_k(Q_\varepsilon(f)^{2k})$ for $k$-uniform hypergraph properties with fixed $k\geq2$, where the implicit constant depends only on $k$. These improve the previous bounds $R_{1/3}(f)=O(Q_{1/3}(f)^6)$ and $R_{1/3}(f)=O_k(Q_{1/3}(f)^{3k})$, respectively (SICOMP 2024) These bounds are tight for permutation-invariant functions and nearly tight for graph and hypergraph properties. Unstructured search gives a matching quadratic separation with $R_{1/3}(f)=Θ\!\left(Q_{1/3}(f)^2\right)$. For every fixed $k\geq 2$, we construct explicit families of invariant promise problems on $k$-uniform hypergraphs satisfying $R_{1/3}(f)\geq Q_{1/3}(f)^{2k-o(1)}$.
authors: Yunqi Huang; Lvzhou Li; Zekun Ye; Shenggen Zheng

title: Local distinguishability of five five-partite orthogonal product states
abstract: The local distinguishability of five orthogonal product states (OPSs) has been studied in several multipartite settings, but the five-partite case still requires a systematic characterization. In this paper, we consider five five-partite OPSs, where any two states are orthogonal on exactly one subsystem. By analyzing the distribution of ten pairwise orthogonality relations over five subsystems, we classify the corresponding orthogonality structures by colored orthogonality graphs. After eliminating identical graphs under relabeling of states and permutation of subsystems, we obtain 443 different graphs in seven genuinely five-partite categories. We prove that the OPSs corresponding to 434 of these graphs can be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC), while the remaining 9 exceptional cases fall into two types and require separate analysis. Our results give a characterization of the local distinguishability of five OPSs in five-partite OPSs.
authors: Guang-Bao Xu; Jie Zhan; Yu-Guang Yang; Dong-Huan Jiang

title: Optimal asymptotic pure-state conversion under thermal operations
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics seeks to characterize possible state transformations under thermodynamic constraints in microscopic quantum systems. In the fully quantum regime, however, quantum coherence imposes various restrictions on state conversions, and a complete characterization of state convertibility has remained open. Here we resolve this problem for asymptotic conversions between pure states. Specifically, we show that asymptotic convertibility is fully determined by the free-energy and energy-variance ratios. Our result reveals how genuinely quantum effects quantitatively constrain state conversions in quantum thermodynamics.
authors: Tatsuya Yamanouchi; Naoto Shiraishi

title: Perfect Wave Transfer in Nonconformal Tomonaga-Luttinger Liquids
abstract: Perfect wave transfer (PWT) reproduces spatial reflection at a common finite time under a fixed Hamiltonian. We classify this process for open compact bosons and inhomogeneous Tomonaga--Luttinger liquids, distinguishing transfer of oscillator and neutral observables from transfer on the charged field algebra. In the single-charge model, the first two notions coincide. Global transfer additionally requires rephasing of the compact zero mode. For regular reflection-symmetric channels, exact oscillator transfer forces an odd multiple of the optical crossing time and a strictly ordered, parity-compatible spectrum differing from the conformal ladder at only finitely many levels. This spectral condition is also sufficient when the Robin boundary data induced by the physical profile are included. Requiring Neumann conditions after the Liouville transformation instead forces conformality. We construct an explicit, regular one-defect family for every $r>1/2$. Its transfer parameters are precisely the reduced fractions $r=p/q$ with odd numerator and denominator, with shortest transfer time $pL/v_0$. At the delay $3L/v_0$, the $r=3/5$ profile has numerical contrast $K_{\max}/K_{\min}\simeq 12.913$, compared with $81$ for $r=3$. Two independent conservative discretizations show second-order convergence on fixed mode bands. Occupation- and charge-constrained error estimates quantify robustness, while an exact homogeneous-chain calculation explains the $J^{2/3}$ resolved-band scale also observed in the engineered channels. These results provide a spectral design method and finite-device benchmarks for quadratic quantum channels. An interacting microscopic realization remains open.
authors: Davide Batic; Denys Dutykh

title: Quantum-Enhanced Classical Communications for DPMZM-based NG-PON2 Systems
abstract: This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.
authors: Parvin Kumar; Sourav Banerjee; Neel Kanth Kundu; Umesh Sharma

title: $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge and exact solution of the $\pm J$ Edwards-Anderson model in a transverse field
abstract: Using the Majorana representation of spin-1/2 operators, we study the $\pm J$ Edwards--Anderson model in a transverse field at $T=0$. We show that, in this representation, the quantity describing the coupling between neighboring spins commutes with the Hamiltonian and, unlike in the Kitaev model, is not subject to any Gauss law. The resulting $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge freedom allows the disorder in the signs of the exchange integrals to be eliminated by an exact gauge transformation, so that the spectrum of the system coincides with that of the model with uniform couplings. The resulting theory is quadratic in the Majorana fields. Computing the local Green's functions, we find that the Edwards--Anderson order parameter vanishes for $Δ>J\sqrt{Z}$ and equals $1/4$ for $Δ<J\sqrt{Z}$, which signals a second-order transition from a paramagnetic phase to a spin-glass ground state that is degenerate over spin configurations and replica symmetric at $T=0$.
authors: Mikhail Vasin

title: Parametric $\mathrm{CZ}$ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
abstract: Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct $\mathrm{CZ}_{01}$, $\mathrm{CZ}_{02}$, and $\mathrm{CZ}_{12}$ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing $\mathrm{CZ}$ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.
authors: Chanpyo Kim; Hansol Kim; Jeongsoo Kang; Younghun Kwon

title: Interaction-enabled charging and thermal crossover of the spin-work deficit in a Hubbard double quantum dot
abstract: We study how conservation of total spin affects the extractable work of an interacting Hubbard double quantum dot charged in the presence of unresolved quasistatic detuning fluctuations. The full fermionic Fock space is used to model preparation through electronic reservoirs, whereas the additional work deficit associated with spin conservation arises entirely from the singlet and triplet states at half filling. At zero detuning, modulation of the symmetric tunnel barrier couples two singlets of even parity. The corresponding transition matrix element vanishes when U = V . An exact formula for the additional work deficit follows from passive spectral rearrangement under two extraction constraints: conservation of particle number alone and conservation of both particle number and total spin. At low temperature, an expansion in the detuning response gives a leading estimate of the noise amplitude at which this deficit first appears. Increasing the preparation temperature changes the triplet population and produces a crossover at s2 = q, where the additional spin constraint becomes nonbinding for the averaged state, even though both ergotropies may continue to decrease. We obtain a semi-analytic expression for this crossover by separating the thermal Gibbs weights from the singlet dynamics under a fixed charging pulse. Averaging over symmetric detuning disorder also restores parity in the density matrix and allows singlet eigenvalues of different parity to exchange order, changing the branch that determines the thermal boundary. The work values are optimal over specified classes of unitary operations and do not establish the yield of a finite discharge protocol.
authors: Khalil Loukhssami; Cheng Shang; Morad El Baz; Khadija El Hawary

title: Single-photon scattering by a nanofiber-coupled atomic chain: beyond independent radiation
abstract: We study single-photon scattering by a nanofiber-coupled atomic chain, comparing a full microscopic model with an independent-radiation approximation. We show that nearly equal transmission probabilities can coexist with substantially different transmitted temporal modes, even after adjusting their relative delay. For a reference chain, a decomposition into collective atomic resonances relates this discrepancy mainly to spectral-phase changes caused by the omitted interatomic couplings. Parameter scans delimit this phase-dominated regime, and controlled comparisons separate the effects of coherent exchange and collective decay.
authors: Juliette Jiménez-Jaimes; Étienne Brion

title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
abstract: Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.
authors: Ushnik Nath; Neha Sharma; Ramniwas Meena; Neel Kanth Kundu

title: Exploring Variational Regularization of Krylov Subspaces
abstract: Krylov subspace methods efficiently approximate extremal eigenstates and eigenvalues of many-body Hamiltonians, but non-orthogonal bases can suffer from ill-conditioning. This challenge is amplified in quantum computing, where direct state access and thus straightforward orthogonalization are unavailable. We investigate a variational Krylov-like framework that iteratively optimizes a parametrized sequence of states to mimic Lanczos-like couplings while penalizing linear dependencies. Analyzed against exact Krylov and Lanczos on a finite Anderson impurity model, ansatz expressivity strongly influences the performance: Hamiltonian-inspired ansätze preserve Krylov-like convergence while improving the conditioning, whereas shallow ansätze remain stable but miss low-energy directions.
authors: Alexandre Perrin; Jérémie Messud; Sébastien Burdin; Matthieu Saubanère

title: Reachability Constraints and Monotones for Quantum-State Texture
abstract: How a quantum resource can be quantified depends on which operations are free. Yet two proposed quantifiers of quantum state texture can increase under free operations: the Wigner-Yanase-Dyson skew information relative to the unique textureless state and the squared Hilbert-Schmidt distance from that state. We show reachability from every state orthogonal to the textureless state, whether pure or mixed: each can be freely transformed into any other state. Therefore, every texture monotone must assign the same maximal value to all such states, a requirement that neither candidate satisfies. We then construct valid texture monotones by adding the population outside the textureless state to the skew information and by maximizing the squared Hilbert-Schmidt distance over free operations. We prove faithfulness, convexity, and invariance under textureless ancillas, characterize additivity properties and strong monotonicity, satisfied only in the Wigner-Yanase case, and derive tight bounds for both monotones at fixed overlap with the textureless state and characterize all saturating states. Together, these results show how allowed state transformations impose operational constraints on the quantification of quantum state texture.
authors: Jose Alfredo de Leon; Pablo Vielman; Miguel Gonzalez

title: Evaluation of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Network Anomaly Detection
abstract: The proliferation of Internet-connected devices has intensified the risk of large-scale network intrusions, necessitating more advanced detection methodologies for the post quantum era. This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, a com- prehensive investigation of quantum machine learning (QML) for anomaly detection on the BoT-IoT dataset, a widely adopted benchmark for IoT security. Leveraging feature-engineered rep- resentations, we implement and evaluate four representative quantum classifiers: Quantum Support Vector Classification (QSVC), Quantum Neural Networks (QNN), and Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC).
authors: Swathi Chandrasekhar; Shiva Raj Pokhrel

title: Correlation-Enhanced Quantum Reservoir Processing for Two-Qutrit Steering: From Generalization to Discovery
abstract: Quantum reservoir processing (QRP) has been applied to entanglement quantification, yet its potential for generalizable steering detection and the discovery of high-dimensional quantum correlations remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce correlation-enhanced QRP (CEQRP), extending QRP to two-qutrit systems with two-body spin-correlation readouts. Some CEQRP-based classifiers substantially improve cross-family generalization, with logistic regression trained on full-information CEQRP features achieving approximately $96\%$ accuracy on unseen Werner states and over $97\%$ accuracy on unseen isotropic states at both \(m=4\) and \(m=5\). Independently, we establish two interconnected steering criteria for mixed two-qutrit states: a necessary-and-sufficient all-versus-nothing criterion for states admitting three linearly independent pure conditional states, and an asymptotic sufficient criterion, with the two criteria linked through invertible local filtering. These criteria provide rigorously certified steerable samples for training-set augmentation. Combining CEQRP-based classification with these theory-certified samples enables the discovery of new Alice-to-Bob steerable partially entangled states, including states at \(p=0.45\) whose steerability is independently confirmed by semidefinite programming (SDP) using seven projective measurement settings. The trained classifiers further guide finite-setting searches for steering boundaries. Our results establish a pathway from generalizable classification to the discovery of high-dimensional quantum steering.
authors: Pu Wang; Zhongyan Li; Huixian Meng; Yutao Xin. Ziqi Zhi; Zhihua Guo; Huaixin Cao

title: A Geometric Journey Through the Aharonov--Bohm Effect: Tonomura's Toroid, Pseudoscalar Phase, and Quantum Holonomy in Clifford Algebra
abstract: The magnetic Aharonov--Bohm (AB) effect is often introduced through the idealised infinite solenoid and a complex scalar phase. We give a geometric-algebra formulation based on the compact toroidal magnets shielded by a superconductor employed in the electron-holography experiments of Tonomura and collaborators. Working in the real Euclidean Clifford algebra $ \mathrm{Cl}(3,0)$, we distinguish the unit volume pseudoscalar $I$ (grade 3), coordinate angles (scalars, grade 0), tangent vectors (grade 1), and directed surface bivectors (grade 2). The magnetic field is represented by the dual bivector $\mathcal{B}= I \mathbf B$, while the electromagnetic $U(1)$ phase is represented by the central unit multivector $e^{Iα}$ generated by the pseudoscalar $I$, rather than by a spatial rotor with a bivector generator. We establish the linked toroidal geometry, formulate magnetic flux and Stokes' theorem intrinsically in geometric algebra, and derive the holonomy element $U_Γ=\exp(IqΦ_B/\hbar)$ from $U(1)$ gauge covariance, with every sign fixed explicitly. We then express superconducting fluxoid quantization in the same notation and obtain the binary electron holonomy $U_Γ= (-1)^N$ in the ideal limit where the linked magnetic flux equals $N h/(2e)$. Finally, a short conditional-state description of the quantum source and field shows how a backreaction can introduce an additional phase and reduce interference visibility. The conditional-state overlap is represented by a central scalar--pseudoscalar element; preservation of the fluxoid sector alone does not guarantee unit coherence.
authors: Andrew Powell

title: Critical properties of EPR steering
abstract: Every PVM-critical entangled two-qubit state becomes steerable with two copies. We prove this for the full critical boundary and for two different critical inputs. The joint measurements can have arbitrarily little entanglement, while all conditional states on Bob's two systems remain separable. Criticality is exactly the point where this measurement-entanglement threshold vanishes. The number of measurements has a separate critical behavior: every fixed setting bound leaves an unsteerable neighborhood of the critical input. Moreover, for any such bound, there are critical states that remain unsteerable under every tensor power, although unrestricted measurements activate them with two copies. These results identify different roles for measurement entanglement, measurement number, and collective access in revealing steering. We also construct fixed-dimensional states whose steering activates on two copies while Bell locality persists through any prescribed finite copy range. In increasing dimension, the two-copy steering violation is unbounded, giving an affirmative solution to the amplification question of Hsieh, Liang, and Lee.
authors: Yu-Xuan Zhang; Jing-Ling Chen

title: Tomography of approximately Gaussian mixed states
abstract: Moment-based tomography efficiently reconstructs Gaussian states, but stochastic phase noise generally produces mixed, non-Gaussian outputs. For approximately Gaussian outputs, we formulate reconstruction as a problem in quantum learning theory under model misspecification. Our trace-distance guarantee separates the intrinsic Gaussian approximation error from statistical errors in estimating the first moments and covariance matrix. Using recent Gaussian trace-distance bounds, we obtain linear dependence of the statistical contribution on moment errors when the covariance inverses remain bounded, improving on the square-root dependence on covariance error in earlier guarantees. A Fock-space truncation procedure provides certified, convergent lower and upper bounds on the intrinsic error. Under an explicit sub-Gaussian condition on the heterodyne outcomes, the sufficient sample count scales inversely with the square of the allowed statistical error remaining after accounting for the approximation error. We verify the statistical condition for stochastic phase rotations and heralded unitary-averaged states with bounded input squeezing. We apply the framework to probabilistic unitary averaging for phase noise reduction, quantifying reconstruction error and accounting for heralding overhead in the total number of estimation attempts.
authors: S. Nibedita Swain; Timothy C. Ralph; Jens Eisert; Nathan Walk

title: Axis-selective AC magnetic-field imaging in the tens-of-megahertz regime using RF-dressed continuous-wave scanning NV magnetometry
abstract: Spatially resolved magnetic-field imaging reveals material properties and local currents in microelectronic devices. Conventional pulsed scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry (SNVM) faces increasingly stringent microwave (MW) pulse-control requirements for detecting radio-frequency (RF) magnetic fields at frequencies ranging from tens to hundreds of megahertz. To address this challenge, we implement an RF-dressed continuous-wave (CW) sensing scheme for SNVM and demonstrate AC magnetic-field imaging at 33.5 MHz. The method exploits electron-spin double resonance in the NV spin-1 three-level system: the target RF magnetic field coherently couples two spin eigenstates, forming RF-dressed states whose splittings are detected in continuous-wave electron-spin double resonance (CW-ESDR) spectra under continuous laser, MW, and RF excitation. This approach avoids short, high-power MW pulses and synchronization between the RF field and a pulsed sensing sequence. Using an NV-ensemble diamond probe integrated with an atomic force microscope (AFM), we image the Oersted field of an RF-driven L-shaped microcircuit. Successively selecting three crystallographic NV axes by static bias-field control yields maps of RF magnetic-field projection magnitudes, with distinct distributions qualitatively reproduced by Biot-Savart calculations. Transverse bias-field control also tunes the RF-coupled spin-state transition frequency from 14.4 to 89.3 MHz, as characterized by spectroscopy and Hamiltonian analysis, with RF-dressed resonances directly observed in CW-ESDR spectra at 89.3 MHz. Together with previous RF magnetic-field detection up to 632 MHz using the same RF-dressed CW sensing principle in a confocal NV setup, these results support extending AC magnetic-field imaging with SNVM toward the hundreds-of-megahertz regime and, with additional phase information, vector magnetic-field reconstruction.
authors: Shuntaro Komuro; Ryusei Okaniwa; Kazuma Okura; Kunitaka Hayashi; Toshu An; Junko Ishi-Hayase

title: Roadmap on Nanoscale Superconductivity for Quantum Technologies
abstract: In 2025, the Year of Quantum Science and Technology, we celebrate a century of quantum mechanics, witnessing a surge in activities that illuminate its inherent strangeness and drive technological innovation. Superconductivity, discovered 114 years ago, stands as a prime example, offering direct and compelling evidence of macroscopic quantum phenomena. Beyond its ability to conduct immense currents without loss, superconductivity reveals the quantum realm operating on a scale we can directly observe and manipulate. The macroscopic quantum coherence, where an ensemble of particles is described by a single wave function, leads to remarkable consequences: dissipation-less current and flux quantization - the basic properties exploited in superconducting quantum circuit fabrication. This Roadmap has been inspired by intensive discussions and collaborations emerging from the European COST Action CA21144 (SuperQuMap - Superconducting Nanodevices and Quantum Materials for Coherent Manipulation). The roadmap outlines the network's concrete activities, driving advancements in superconductor-based quantum technologies and charting future directions. Spanning fundamental research to practical applications, the roadmap incorporates insights from industry partners developing quantum computation. It begins by exploring quantum materials, highlighting how topology and electronic correlations could catalyze a quantum leap in technology. We then delve into manipulating the superconducting phase, leveraging advancements in magnetism, 3D fabrication, and tunable correlations. Further, we showcase the advanced microscopy techniques - such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and scanning probes - used to visualize quantum behavior. Finally, and crucially, we detail the quantum devices developed within the network, and their transformative impact on modern quantum computing approaches.
