abstract: Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.
authors: Alina Joch; Benedikt Fauseweh

title: Metrological Channels Induced by Encrypted Quantum Cloning: Optimal-Probe Fisher-Information Broadcasting and Single-Use Operational Recovery
abstract: Encrypted quantum cloning creates multiple individually inaccessible signal systems from which an unknown input state can be recovered by combining any selected signal with a shared quantum key. Here we study parameter estimation when a local sensing transformation is applied after encrypted cloning and before decryption. For the two-clone qubit protocol, a local Pauli rotation on one encrypted signal is shown to induce, after standard decryption, a parameter-dependent Pauli dephasing channel rather than a unitary rotation. We derive its Pauli-transfer representation and the corresponding quantum Fisher information (QFI) for arbitrary mixed qubit probes. We then distinguish raw QFI, which for an optimal decoded probe may remain simultaneously present in a decoded output and its complement, from decoder-accessible QFI, which is operationally single-use because a first decryption destroys the shared syndrome information needed for a second standard recovery. For $n\geq2$ encrypted clones, the effective channel family is independent of clone number up to a clone-parity-dependent permutation of the Pauli axes (the single-clone case is exceptional for $Y$-sensing, where the decoded map stays unitary). This produces a metrological parity switch: for fixed probe and generator, even and odd clone numbers can yield respectively vanishing and maximal QFI. Closed expressions are obtained for the degradation of this parity contrast under probe depolarization and Pauli-diagonal Bloch-vector contraction.
authors: Nalan Kandirmaz

title: Static Bounds on Thermal Fast Scrambling
abstract: Scrambling, the process by which initially localized quantum information spreads across an interacting many-body system, is a hallmark of quantum chaos and plays a central role in understanding black hole dynamics. In thermal systems, the chaos bound of Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford limits the exponential growth rate of out-of-time-order correlations to $2π/β$, assuming that time-ordered correlation functions factorize after a dissipation time. Establishing the corresponding rigorous logarithmic lower bounds on scrambling times at arbitrary fixed temperature has remained an open problem, most notably in disordered systems, where the Gibbs state depends on the same random couplings that drive the dynamics. Here we prove such bounds at every fixed temperature for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and for random $k$-local spin systems, without assuming real-time factorization. Our approach uses the operator-size distribution of the square root of the Gibbs state to quantify how local probes modify its structure. This static information bounds the thermal correlator uniformly in time along the edges of its analytic strip in complex time, and analyticity then limits how rapidly scrambling can develop. For both families of models, we prove that with probability tending to one the scrambling time is at least $(1-ε)[β/(2π)]\log N$ for any $0<ε<1$, with the coefficient $β/(2π)$ suggested by the chaos bound. The bound holds for each fixed pair of distinct Majorana modes in the SYK model and for the target average of any fixed single-site source in the spin model. These results place the thermal fast-scrambling timescale on a rigorous footing and show how static properties of the Gibbs state can constrain real-time information spreading.
authors: Yixuan Ma; Weikang Li; Dong-Ling Deng

title: Global bound-state spectrum and spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement in an inverse-$3/2$ magnetic quantum dot
abstract: We investigate the bound-state spectrum and confinement thresholds of a two-dimensional electron governed by the Schrödinger--Pauli equation in an inverse-$3/2$ radial magnetic-field profile. The radial problem reduces to the biconfluent Heun equation, but instead of restricting the solution to the quasi-exact polynomial sector, we impose the bound-state condition globally through a spectral Wronskian between the endpoint-selected Frobenius solution and the subdominant asymptotic solution. The resulting spectrum contains continuous nonpolynomial bound-state branches on which the known quasi-exact solutions appear as isolated exact points. In this global description, the polynomial index $N$ remains a termination index within the quasi-exact sector but does not uniquely label the spectral branches. An independent exact analysis of the continuum edge yields spin- and angular-momentum-dependent critical couplings that can lie below the quasi-exact restriction $U_0a>4$, where $U_0$ is the Coulomb-strength parameter and $a$ is the magnetic-profile length scale. These results establish quasi-exact solvability as a set of special analytic points embedded in a broader biconfluent-Heun spectrum with spin- and angular-momentum-dependent confinement thresholds.
authors: Luis B. Castro

title: How many events does entanglement-based positronium imaging need? Information limits of Compton polarimetry with CZT detectors
abstract: The degree of polarisation correlation of the two annihilation photons, measured by Compton polarimetry, has been proposed as a PET biomarker of tissue microstructure, but the statistics it requires have not been quantified. We parameterise the measurement by the linear-polarisation correlation coefficient $κ$ ($κ=1$ maximally entangled, $1/2$ separable), derive the classical Fisher information of double-Compton events and compare it with the quantum Fisher information, relate $κ$ to the annihilation channels of positronium in tissue, and simulate pixelated CdZnTe (CZT) rings. The model is checked against three published measurements and an independent GATE/Geant4 simulation. A double-Compton event carries at most 0.12-0.14 units of Fisher information about $κ$ and 0.015 on average, 0.1-0.6% of the quantum limit. Event-wise maximum likelihood reaches the Cramer-Rao bound, whereas the conventional ratio R needs 1.2-2.3 times more events. The observed coefficient is $κ_{obs}=1-α(1-κ_{pick})$, with a pick-off share $α$ of 0.13-0.29 in tissue; it is sensitive to lipid fraction but not to oxygen, and carries no tissue information if pick-off photons are maximally entangled. Published porous-polymer data imply $κ_{pick}$ = 0.34-0.58. In a 15-mm CZT module, ordering ambiguity, position errors and electron transport roughly halve the information per event, and sequence reconstruction of multi-site events recovers this loss. With $^{18}$F and an eight-module ring, $κ$ can be measured to $\pm0.01$ in a 10-mm tumour, but separating tissues by $κ$ alone requires 6-74 times more decays than are available.
authors: Haitao Zhou; Ruonan Wang; Jianyong Hu; Zhifang Wu; Sijin Li

title: Relaxing the i.i.d. state preparation assumption with the block QKD protocol
abstract: In this work, we propose a novel approach to handling the independent and identically distributed assumption for the state preparation in prepare-and measure QKD protocols. Contrary to previous approaches, we do not prove the security using sub-protocols, and instead opt to guarantee security in the presence of correlations by dividing the communication into finite blocks of consecutive pulses, and adding an additional assumption of no dependence between each block. In turn we obtain a protocol which uses only a relaxed i.i.d. assumption and is easier to implement than subprotocol-style approaches since it does not require separate statistics for each sub-protocol, whose number grows with the correlation length of the underlying dependency.
authors: Olgierd Żurek; Hoi-Kwong Lo

title: Success Probability of Block-Encoding Methods
abstract: Block-encoding methods apply nonunitary functions $f(\widetilde H)$ of a normalized Hermitian operator on a quantum computer, but only upon a successful postselection, which introduces a shot overhead rarely included in resource estimates. We analyze the success probability $p^{(f)}_{\mathrm{success}}=\sum_n w_n|f(\tilde E_n)|^2$ of three constructions, namely linear combination of unitaries (LCU), qubitization and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), where $w_n$ are the weights of the input state on the eigenstates of $\widetilde H$. Using the one-dimensional Hubbard model with up to 14 sites (35 qubits), we show that for LCU, the success probability is bounded by the squared ratio between the spectral norm and the $1$-norm of the Pauli decomposition, and that for a Hartree--Fock input it plateaus with system size while the ground-state overlap keeps decreasing. For qubitization, it oscillates with the Chebyshev degree, and favorable degrees can be identified from a few dominant spectral components or predicted from shallow-degree data. For QSVT, the polynomial normalization constant directly sets the success probability, and a tight certified bound balances it against phase-finding robustness. An application to quantum Krylov methods shows a nonuniform shot overhead across Krylov moments. The success probability should therefore be part of the resource estimation of block-encoding-based algorithms.
authors: Oumaya Ladhari; Matthieu Saubanère; Jérémie Messud

title: Subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic waves for enhancing Brillouin gain in a planar waveguide structure
abstract: We propose a planar waveguide structure consisting of two layers separated by a gap that provides subwavelength confinement of optical and acoustic modes and a large overlap integral between them. This, in turn, leads to an increase in Brillouin gain. Using the structure of two Si$_3$N$_4$ layers with a subwavelength gap from SiO$_2$ as an example, we demonstrate that a hybridized transverse-magnetic (TM) optical mode exhibits strong field confinement in the SiO$_2$ gap. Simultaneously, a high-frequency acoustic mode can be confined in the same gap, providing a high spatial overlap between the optical and acoustic fields. This provides a high opto-acoustic interaction with a Brillouin gain up to $5$ W$^{-1}$m$^{-1}$. The proposed structure is compatible with planar photonic integration and offers a promising platform for compact, low-threshold Brillouin lasers and coherent phonon generation.
authors: A. R. Mukhamedyanov; E. A. Tereshchenkov; E. S. Andrianov; A. A. Zyablovsky

title: Closing the loop on memory: accurate, shallow and transferable decoding of quantum LDPC codes
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have attracted interest for fault-tolerant quantum computing because their high-rate constructions offer a route to reduced qubit overhead. Realizing this potential requires reliable decoding. Belief propagation (BP) forms the basis of many qLDPC decoders, but can fail to converge under circuit-level noise. Memory-based variants can improve convergence, yet selecting memory strengths that work reliably across different syndromes remains challenging. Here we introduce TEMPO-BP, which adapts each variable's memory strength to the evolving decoding state through local feedback. On the gross code at a physical error rate of 0.4%, single-run TEMPO-BP achieves a per-shot logical failure rate of 0.73%, compared with 2.51% for BP+OSD+CS-10. Ensembles of 10-15 concurrent instances match or lower failure counts relative to Relay-BP-5 at all ten tested operating points, with per-instance iteration caps at least tenfold lower than its serial limit. Without retuning, the gross-code parameters yield fewer observed failures than Relay-BP-5 in its published gross-code configuration across four additional code families. Ablations support state-dependent memory control, while a loop-gain analysis characterizes specific amplification modes in the decoding dynamics.
authors: Zhou You; Ying Li; Xiao Yuan; Yuan Yao

title: Reversal of dynamical backaction and cooling below the quantum backaction limit in Floquet-driven multimode optomechanical resonators
abstract: Dynamical backaction describes how a driven cavity field responds with delay to mechanical motion, and can be used to cool that motion toward its quantum ground state or amplify it into self-oscillation. Control over this interaction underpins laser cooling, high-fidelity state preparation, quantum transduction, and phonon lasing. In conventional cavity optomechanics, both the sign and the magnitude of the optical damping are dictated by the laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by quantum backaction (QBA), the optomechanical analogue of the Doppler limit in cold atoms. We show, in theory and experiment, that dynamical backaction can be strongly enhanced in multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying (Floquet) optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the QBA limit of the target mode by the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experimentally, we cool the MHz mode to $47 \pm 13$ phonons, about half its single-mode QBA limit and an order of magnitude below what single-tone backaction reaches at the same intracavity photon number. The character of the interaction can moreover be completely inverted at fixed laser detuning, turning cooling into amplification and vice versa, controlled solely by the modulation frequency. Floquet driving thus extends open-loop quantum control, which requires no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime.
authors: Menno H. Jansen; Roel Burgwal; Ewold Verhagen

title: Stabilizer-Restricted Antidistinguishability in Quantum Computation with Magic States
abstract: An antidistinguishing measurement for a family of preparations excludes at least one preparation for every possible outcome, constraining 'classical' representations of these processes, known as ontological models. We develop this connection within quantum computing with magic states (QCM), a universal model of quantum computation. Our constructions use adaptive Pauli measurements on tensor products of single-qubit non stabilizer states, including families associated with the Clifford hierarchy. These constructions yield stabilizer-restricted versions of the Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph theorem: any ontological model reproducing these measurement statistics and satisfying preparation independence must assign disjoint ontic supports to the preparations considered. We demonstrate this obstruction to preparation independence in a concrete ontological model based on convex polytopes used for the classical simulation of QCM.
authors: Selman Ipek

title: Deterministic nonlinear domain engineering algorithm with variable sub-coherence-length domains
abstract: We present a new and improved deterministic algorithm that calculates the poling domains for the implementation of arbitrary phase-matching functions (PMF) in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm presented here makes full use of the limits of the fabrication process, such as the minimum feature size and resolution of the lithographic process underpinning the poling procedure. This minimizes the tracking error to the target electric field and improves the accuracy in reaching the desired PMF. We give a tutorial on how to calculate the target function for arbitrary PMFs and run the algorithm. We also demonstrate the procedure on a relevant application in quantum sensing, where we use a quadratic phase on the PMF to implement a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal. The designed crystal is experimentally tested, and the result matches expectations.
authors: Michael Schlosser; Tommaso Faleo; Gregor Weihs; Robert Keil; Stefan Frick

title: Observation of Crossover from Repulsive to Attractive Interactions between Two $nS$-Rydberg Atoms in Dual-Species Atom Arrays
abstract: Dual-species Rydberg atom arrays provide a flexible platform for engineering long-range interactions beyond the conventional isotropic blockade regime. We spectroscopically study interactions between different $s$-state Rydberg levels in a $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$--$^{85}\mathrm{Rb}$ optical-tweezer array. By varying the principal-quantum-number difference $Δn$ around $61S_{1/2}$, we observe a crossover from repulsive to attractive interactions. We identify a distinct regime at $Δn=2$ in which Förster-enhanced electronic spin exchange dominates over orbital exchange and produces a strongly bond-orientation-dependent pair spectrum. Time-domain collective-excitation measurements reveal this geometry-dependent spin exchange through a pronounced anisotropy of the double-excitation probability. For $Δn=1$, by contrast, orbital exchange dominates and the interaction is nearly isotropic. These results establish the principal-quantum-number difference and bond orientation as complementary control parameters for tailoring Rydberg interaction spectra and collective excitation dynamics, opening new opportunities for engineering spin-dependent Hamiltonians in programmable atom arrays.
authors: Yi Chen; Kun-Peng Wang; Ming-Rui Wei; Peng Zhang; Yang Wang; Yi-Bo Wang; Min Liu; Peng Xu; Xue-Yuan Wang; Xiang Gao; Chengshu Li; Xiao-Dong He; Ming-Sheng Zhan

title: No complete set of mutually unbiased bases in dimension ten contains the Fourier pair or three product bases
abstract: With computer-assisted proofs that $\mathbb{C}^6$ admits at most three mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) now available, $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is the smallest dimension in which it is unknown whether a complete set of $d+1=11$ MUBs exists; only three MUBs are known. We prove that every triple of mutually unbiased product bases of $\mathbb{C}^2\otimes\mathbb{C}^5$ is strongly unextendible: no vector is unbiased to all three bases. Consequently no set of four MUBs in dimension ten, and in particular no complete set, contains three product bases. This settles the case $d=2\times5$ anticipated by McNulty, Pammer and Weigert; it was known only for the Heisenberg-Weyl triple. The proof covers all ten equivalence classes with explicit Nullstellensatz certificates modulo one prime on $91$ charts of $\mathbb{P}^9\times\mathbb{P}^9$ for each class ($910$ in all), transferred to characteristic zero by a projective reduction lemma, together with an independent rank certificate for eight of the ten classes. We also prove that the pair formed by the standard and the Fourier basis of $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is contained in no set of four MUBs. Exactly $3040$ rays are unbiased to both bases (this confirms the count found numerically by Führ and Rzeszotnik), each of them is unbiased to at most eight of the others, and every triple formed by the pair and a third MUB is strongly unextendible. For this we certify $34,940$ cyclic $10$-roots in Krawczyk uniqueness boxes, decide unimodularity exactly through an involution, and prove completeness by a four-dimensional interval branch-and-bound obtained from the Chinese-remainder splitting $\mathbb{Z}_{10}=\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$.
authors: Jinze Yang; Yile Liu; Yangyang Li; Xiu-Hao Deng

title: The Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic PBC clusters
abstract: We construct and solve the three-colored Kitaev model on finite hyperbolic lattices with periodic boundary conditions. We describe a self-contained procedure which uses finite quotients of orientation- preserving triangle groups to generate regular maps on compact genus-g surfaces. From these, one can extract their lattice connectivity, plaquette structure, homology cycles and Wilson sectors while implementing consistent boundary conditions. On the example of {8, 3} and {12, 3} lattices, we enumerate a selection of quotients with up to 72 vertices, which constitute the discrete steps in a finite-size scaling analysis. For the isotropic point, corresponding to the spin-liquid phase in the thermodynamic limit, we identify the ground state superselection sectors, quantify their deviation from the homogeneous π flux sector and show how the selected flux background depends on the quotient geometry. We then discuss how the resulting ground state sector degeneracies are entirely generated by physical lattice symmetries acting on both the plaquette fluxes and non-contractible Wilson loops. Finally, we study the behaviour of the finite-size two-vison gap and matter fermion correlations. We find that the gap does not decrease monotonically with increasing system size, while one still recovers the expected algebraic decay of the correlations at the isotropic point, even for the considered modest system sizes.
authors: Alberto Zorzato; Jiri Minář

title: Separations Between Randomized and Exact Quantum Query Complexity for Boolean Functions
abstract: We construct a family of total Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{tot}}$ whose randomized and exact quantum query complexities satisfy $R(F_{\mathrm{tot}}) \ge Q_E(F_{\mathrm{tot}})^{2-o(1)}$. Chiruvella, Kayal, Mittal, Paraashar, and Saurabh (2026) also obtained a nearly quadratic separation for total functions in the query model by a different method. For every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we construct a family of partial Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{par}}$ on $n$ bits satisfying $Q_E(F_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(1)$ and $R(F_{\mathrm{par}})=Ω_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$. This matches the asymptotic separation previously obtained with bounded error (STOC 2021; SICOMP 2023). Lifting yields a family of partial communication functions $G_{\mathrm{par}}$ with $Q_E^{\mathrm{cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ and $R^{\mathrm{pub,cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=Ω_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $n$ is the total number of input bits held by the two parties.
authors: Zekun Ye

title: Interaction Landscapes of Structurally Distorted Toroidal Classical Spin Textures
abstract: We develop a classical discrete magnetostatic model of localized magnetic moments arranged in a toroidal texture, where the moments are represented by static current loops and study the behavior of the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction under several types of structural deformations. The purpose is to disentangle effects due to geometric and magnetic deformations, including elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted configurations. In particular, we investigate how distortions modify the toroidal moment and the interaction energy between pairs of toroidal structures. The resulting interaction landscapes exhibit characteristic symmetry patterns and anisotropies that are highly sensitive to the underlying deformation. As a separate proof-of-concept comparison, first-principles calculations on a molecular spin-toroidal system reveal qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior. The calculated interaction is microscopically the conventional pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction between localized moments arranged in a spin-toroidal texture; the toroidal moment characterizes the collective texture and should not be interpreted as introducing an additional elementary interaction term. Our results provide a platform for exploring orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures in molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems that are essential to understand the role of toroidal order.
authors: Henry Pommer; Arkamita Bandyopadhyay; Jamal Berakdar

title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean
authors: Stavan Jain; Nithin Raveendran; Aws Albarghouthi

title: What kind of quantum advantage is this?
abstract: Quantum advantage encompasses fundamentally different claims, from resource reductions to exponential separations in sample complexity. Evaluating these claims requires distinguishing how an algorithm achieves an advantage from what is necessary for the separation and how strongly it is supported against classical alternatives. We propose a multi-label taxonomy that makes these distinctions explicit, classifying structural, interference, and coherent mechanisms while separately recording their necessity and the evidence for the classical comparison. Coherent mechanisms are further divided into memory and output, reflecting distinct restrictions on quantum information processing. A two-part entanglement-breaking test distinguishes loss of information from loss of algorithmic efficiency. The hidden subgroup problem illustrates the distinction: among the cases examined, cross-copy coherence is information-theoretically necessary only for the symmetric group. We present this as a diagnostic methodology rather than a theory of quantum advantage: for a new claim, it identifies the relevant adversary, separates the mechanisms a protocol uses from those shown to be necessary, and records the strength of the evidence and the quality of the advantage separately.
authors: Christophe Pere

title: A boson representation of the electronic structure calculation based on the quantum Krylov subspace algorithm
abstract: Quantum calculations are expected to broaden the range of strongly correlated phenomena in solids accessible to first-principles calculations. The quantum Krylov diagonalization method, or in a broader sense, the quantum subspace expansion method (QSE) offers an advantage over other variational methods in terms of numerical stability. In this work, we propose a boson representation of electronic systems with the aim of reducing QSE quantum circuit depth, where electron-hole pair bosons serve as the fundamental degrees of freedom. We benchmark the boson representation in comparison with a corresponding fermionic QSE and CCSD for an equidistant and a dimerized configuration of a periodic hydrogen chain \ce{(H2)_n}. Despite the drastic approximation we reveal the boson QSE scheme provides practically useful accuracy in the ground state energy. Our results support its applicability to realistic quasi-two- and three-dimensional electronic systems.
authors: Hiroki Katow; Hisao Nakamura

title: Quantum-Assisted D-FACTS Scheduling for Moving Target Defense under Switching Limits
abstract: Moving target defense with distributed flexible alternating-current transmission system (D-FACTS) devices re- quires activation decisions as operating points change. Switching limits couple these decisions, but period-by-period rankings can overlook combinations needed to complete low-activation schedules. This paper proposes cross-period candidate sharing and schedule-completion evaluation to allocate limited physical checks in quantum-assisted D-FACTS scheduling. The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) generates activation candidates, while classical scheduling enforces operating and switching constraints. We also quantify model-based activation requirements and test detection through noisy nonlinear trials. A modified IEEE 118-bus study assesses recovery of reference activation and switching objectives within the evaluated set. Combining candidate sharing and schedule-completion evaluation improves final-budget recovery over period-by-period ranking in the primary operating window for every tested candidate generator. The results show that quantum and classical candidates yield identical recovery curves under combined checking, so the same allocation policy applies to either source.
authors: Hongyu Wu; Yichen Liu; Bo Liu

title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.
authors: Bolin Zhang; Zhiyuan Zhang; Yongguang Lv; Ruiqing He; Hengliang Guo; Jiandong Shang; Qiang Chen

title: TCBP-JOBS: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Error Correction Decoding and Noise Learning with Near-Optimal Accuracy
abstract: Achieving near-optimal quantum error correction (QEC) decoding accuracy often requires computationally expensive searches that limit both large-scale simulation and real-time operation. We introduce trajectory-calibrated belief propagation (TCBP), which learns calibrated fault probabilities from BP trajectories, and jittered OSD beam search (JOBS), which uses these probabilities to guide parallel GPU searches. Across surface, color and bivariate-bicycle code memory and surgery circuits, TCBP-JOBS achieves logical error rates comparable to those of the Tesseract most-likely-error decoder at physical error rates of 0.1% to 0.4%, and up to 4.5$\times$ lower on the largest codes. Serial speedups over Tesseract's sparsified presets range from 10$\times$ to 7,400$\times$, and against unsparsified long-beam Tesseract they reach 13,000$\times$ on the bivariate-bicycle codes, at logical error rate ratios of 0.97 to 1.57. At lower physical error rates ($10^{-4}$ to $5\times10^{-4}$), rare-event splitting on the gross code shows that Tesseract is more accurate. Batched execution accelerates offline simulation for rapid, efficient exploration of large-scale QEC design spaces. For QPUs with longer logical clock cycles, our serial memory and logical-surgery experiments demonstrate accuracy comparable to Tesseract while meeting the millisecond-scale latency requirements of online feed-forward operation. Beyond memory and logic decoding, we demonstrate using TCBP-JOBS for confidence scores for postselection in memory and magic-state cultivation, enabling end-to-end color code cultivation. Together, these methods provide a GPU framework for accelerating QEC research via accurate decoding, noise estimation, and confidence assessment.
authors: Ben Howe; Satvik Maurya; Jan Olle; Ivan Basov; Muyuan Li; Justin G. Lietz; Kevin Young; Krysta M. Svore

title: Experimentally relevant witness for non-Markovianity in discrete time crystals
abstract: Discrete time crystals (DTCs) are almost always analyzed under the Born-Markov approximation, in which the environment is memoryless. We show that a reservoir with a finite correlation time $τ_m$ leaves an exact and strikingly simple imprint on the stroboscopic dynamics of DTCs, which can be used as an experimentally relevant witness for non-Markovianity. By analyzing a post-Markovian master equation we prove that the Floquet spectrum splits into the ordinary Markovian spectrum plus a replica of the purely unitary Floquet spectrum, uniformly contracted by $e^{-T/τ_m}$, where $T$ is the drive period. Consequently, the DTC signal decay rate becomes independent of any system parameter once $τ_m$ exceeds the Markovian lifetime of the DTC. The measured decay, and in particular its insensitivity to tunable system parameters, thus becomes a direct read-out of the reservoir correlation time. Below this threshold the dynamics is already non-Markovian, but the memory remains hidden in the decay. We confirm this in two structurally unrelated DTCs, a collective long-range model with incoherent pumping and a disorder-free Ising chain with dephasing, where a single estimator recovers $τ_m$. The time crystal thereby witnesses the non-Markovianity of its own environment.
authors: Rahul Ghosh; Victor Mukherjee; Yonatan Dubi

title: Quantum adiabatic and diabatic optimization: A Hilbert space engineering strategy with Rydberg arrays
abstract: Neutral-atom arrays provide a versatile platform for encoding combinatorial optimization problems with arbitrary graph connectivity [Nguyen et al., PRX Quantum 4, 010316 (2023)]. Although the dynamics of individual encoding gadgets has been studied [Bombieri et al., PRX Quantum 6, 020306 (2025)], understanding annealing bottlenecks in larger networks remains challenging. We investigate how engineering the Hilbert-space geometry controls quantum annealing in a family of blockaded-chain models motivated by these encodings. While boundary terms encode the target maximum independent set problem, the bulk geometry induces an auxiliary optimization problem associated with independent sets of cliques. Spectrally, the energetics of the quantum system can be approximated by physically derived clique weights. When the target problem and the auxiliary problems are consistent, the low-energy modes lie predominantly within the target subspace. This spectral structure motivates a diabatic annealing strategy that exploits target-compatible excited states, as tested on the diamond-chain graph family. These results provide a framework for predicting annealing bottlenecks, and demonstrate Hilbert-space engineering as a strategy for improving neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols.
authors: Rui Lin

title: Catalytic compression of classical communication in exact entanglement transformations
abstract: Entanglement catalysis is usually associated with making otherwise impossible transformations possible. Here we show that it can also change how much classical communication a transformation requires. A catalyst, returned exactly and uncorrelated with the output, can reduce the message alphabet size required for exact transformations of bipartite pure states by a factor that grows without bound as the Schmidt rank increases. In the asymptotic many-copy regime, however, this advantage disappears at the level of the leading communication rate: the optimal catalytic and noncatalytic rates coincide. We characterize the optimal catalytic cost in terms of Rényi entropies, revealing how the entanglement structure of the source and target governs the finite-copy advantage. Our results establish reusable entanglement as a resource for compressing classical communication in quantum state manipulation.
authors: Vito Viesti; Alexander Streltsov

title: Sequential strategy for depolarizing strength estimation
abstract: We study the advantages of applying a sequential strategy for enhancing the precision in estimating the strength $p$ of a depolarizing channel, using qudit and two-qubit probes. The sequential strategy requires that the same depolarizing channel is repeatedly applied $M$ times to the quantum probe. From the analysis of the probe's output state, both the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and its regularization RQFI, given from multiplication by $p$, are analyzed. We determine that in the limit of $p \to 0$, the QFI is {\it linearly amplified} with the number of channel repetitions. Instead, in the weak-noise regime, the QFI is maximized at a finite value of $M$. Then, the RQFI decreases more quickly with $p$ as $M$ increases. In particular, for two-qubit probes, the RQFI decreases with the depolarization strength proportionally to the amount of correlation between the qubits. The greater the number of channel repetitions, the wider the range of $p$ for which the initial state of the probe that allows for the maximization of the QFI is a separable state. We also show that a single qubit probe undergoing a sequential encoding protocol outperforms the optimal two-qubit single-round QFI for $M>3$ in the weak-noise regime.
authors: Yasir Mehmood; Enrico Trombetti; Marco Pezzutto; Stefano Gherardini

title: Information Causality Defeats Every Finite NPA Level
abstract: For every finite level of the Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy, we construct correlations that satisfy all its constraints but violate information causality. At each fixed level, one use of a binary-outcome correlation and one classical bit suffice for a violation that grows without bound as the number of measurement settings increases. Information causality bounds the information gained about independent database bits, summed over possible requests, by the length of the message. Quantum correlations obey the one-bit bound; the optimal information gain at any fixed NPA level grows logarithmically with the number of settings. The violation remains unbounded even when all outcome probabilities are positive and, for any fixed number of measurement settings on each side, every choice of those settings admits a local model. One communicated bit therefore exposes an unbounded gap between information causality and every finite NPA level.
authors: Anubhav Chaturvedi; Marcin Pawłowski

title: Vanishing Relative Distance of Uniformly Random CSS LDPC Codes Built from Permutation Matrices
abstract: Classical random regular low-density parity-check codes can have minimum distance growing linearly with block length. We study CSS check matrices formed as full $J\times L$ arrays of arbitrary $P\times P$ permutation matrices, sampled uniformly subject to commutation. For fixed column weight $J\ge3$ and fixed even row weight $L>2J$, we prove that the relative minimum distance converges to zero in probability as $P\to\infty$, with block length $n=LP$. We analyze the weight enumerators that count all nontrivial logical representatives after excluding stabilizers. A coefficientwise lower bound shows that, at every fixed relative weight $0<α<1$ along even-weight sequences, exponentially many such representatives exist with high probability. Their typical and mean counts have exponent lower bound $h_2(α)/2$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We compare this bound with the classical LDPC and dense CSS mean weight-distribution exponents. The existence, with high probability, of a logical operator below every fixed target weight $δn$ yields the distance conclusion.
authors: Kenta Kasai

title: Quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures: Comparison between dispersively and directly coupled superconducting qubits
abstract: The Rabi frequency of a two-level system is directly proportional to the electric field amplitude being incident on this system. Taking advantage of this relationship, it is possible to use two-level systems as quantitative sensors of electric fields. Here, we apply this concept to superconducting qubits and use them for quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures. Our superconducting circuit design includes three transmon qubits directly coupled to the central microwave feedline and three transmon qubits coupled dispersively via readout resonators to the feedline. We compare both coupling schemes to assess their reliability for microwave power sensing. Further, we describe the modeling behind each power-sensing method, including an uncertainty estimation based upon repeated measurements. By combining dispersively coupled and directly coupled qubits on the same device, we are able to explore different power ranges: from $-155\;$dBm to $-130\;$dBm for the directly coupled qubits and from $-95\;$dBm to $-55\;$dBm for the dispersively coupled qubits. When determining the microwave-line attenuation for a frequency of $6.0\;$GHz from room temperature to the millikelvin stage of the cryostat, we obtain best estimates and uncertainties for the directly coupled transmons of $(74.7\pm 0.2) \;$dB and for the dispersively coupled transmons of $(75.4\pm 6.8) \;$dB. The larger uncertainty of the dispersively coupled qubit measurements indicates that these qubits are less reliable for power sensing than the directly coupled qubits, most likely, due to the additional coupling resonator, whose transfer function is difficult to estimate accurately. Our results constitute the first step towards validation of qubit power sensing in dilution fridges, leading towards traceability for cryogenic microwave measurements.
authors: Asen L. Georgiev; Christoph Kissling; Fabian Kaap; Victor Gaydamachenko; Lukas Grünhaupt; Mark Bieler

title: Sharp $L_p$-Regularity for Quantum Markov Semigroups
abstract: We determine the sharp universal constants in positive-input $L_p$-regularity for finite-dimensional quantum Markov semigroups with a faithful invariant state. For $1<p<\infty$, they are $p\sin(π/p)/(2(p-1))$ under KMS symmetry and $\frac{p}{2(p-1)}\tan(\fracπ{2}\min\{1/p,1-1/p\})$ without a symmetry assumption, with the endpoint values at $p=1$ given by $π/2$ and $π/4$, respectively.
authors: Lijun Wang

title: Reinforcement Learning designs Quantum Repeater Protocols on Networks beyond the Chain Scenario
abstract: Small-scale quantum repeater protocols have been shown to distribute entanglement over existing telecommunication infrastructure by means of short range quantum communications and long range classical messages. For larger networks, there are a number of theoretical proposals about how to operate the network to achieve a good performance under varying metrics. Moreover, since the dimension of the space of possible protocols grows exponentially with network size, plenty of those proposals are based on heuristics that reduce the search space. One of these is entanglement routing, which simplifies the problem on non-linear networks by allocating a series of disjoint paths and running chain protocols simultaneously on them. However, in this work we claim routing leads to suboptimal protocols. In fact, inspired by works on linear chains, we apply reinforcement learning to non-linear networks and optimize over the larger non-routing protocol space. Then, we find protocols that outperform a routed extension of the swap-ASAP protocol, even in the parameter regimes where the latter is widely recognized as the state of the art. These results indicate that routing must be discarded in favor of non-routing methods, while they pave the way towards the design of a sensible Quantum Internet architecture.
authors: Andrés Agustí Casado; Álvaro Troyano Olivas; Javier Faba García; Luis M. Robledo; Vicente Martín; Laura Ortiz

title: Rethinking Entropic Uncertainty: How measuring without a trace leads to longer keys
abstract: In recent years, the entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) has been one of the most prominent tools to obtain tight key rates secure against general coherent attacks for a broad class of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. Despite its success, the fundamental question of how to incorporate the statistics of more than two mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) directly into the EUR is yet to be answered. Here, we introduce a simple yet powerful shift of perspective: Instead of the usual tripartition into the systems of Alice, Bob and Eve, we treat Alice and Bob as one joint system and introduce an additional register as the third system. This register contains the results of appropriately chosen virtual measurements that leave no trace in the real branch of the protocol, but act as a conditioning on the counterfactual phase error measurements. We show that this allows us to obtain tight key rates for QKD protocols using an arbitrary number of MUBs directly and natively from the EUR. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach has a much broader relevance beyond the inclusion of multiple MUBs, allowing for improvements in many existing security proofs and the treatment of previously unexplored aspects for a wide range of protocols.
authors: Philipp Kleinpaß

title: Geometry of squeezed states. The phase-space metric, relative vacua and cosmology
abstract: Geometry enters quantum theory in two places. The space of quantum states carries a symplectic form, which generates unitary evolution, and a metric, which governs uncertainties and transition probabilities. The classical phase space acquires a metric of its own when a vacuum is chosen: quantizing a linear system amounts to choosing a compatible complex structure, equivalently a compatible metric $g$. We take this second metric as the primary object and show that it plays, on phase space, the role that the quantum metric plays on the space of states: fluctuations of linear observables are $g$-norms of Hamiltonian vector fields, and along coherent states $g/2\hbar$ \emph{is} the quantum metric. Squeezed states then have a simple description. A squeezed vacuum is the vacuum of another metric, and squeezing is a property of a pair of metrics, a relative vacuum, whose invariants are the eigenvalues $e^{\pm2r_i}$ of $L=g_0^{-1}g$. We work out the harmonic oscillator in detail, including why a rotated squeezed state no longer minimizes the product of the displayed uncertainties. Quadratic evolution deforms the metric, and only the part of the generator that is self-adjoint with respect to the reference changes the $r_i$, at a rate we give exactly. For fields, a vacuum is unitarily implementable relative to a reference exactly when it lies at finite distance from it in the space of vacua. For a massless field in de Sitter space we revisit the two canonical charts compared by Grain and Vennin: relative to the reference of the standard squeezing formalism the Bunch--Davies state has $\sinh r_k=1/(2|kη|)$, and relative to the vacuum that a radiation era beginning at time $η$ would select it has $\sinh r_k=1/(2k^2η^2)$. The second comparison squeezes twice as fast and is unitarily implementable; the first is not.
authors: Alejandro Corichi; Jerónimo Cortez

title: Localization transition in a spin chain with an exact Fock-space tree
abstract: Many-body localization is often pictured as Anderson localization on the graph of many-body configurations. Strongly correlated disorder and a dense net of loops, however, make this graph hard to analyze. We introduce a local disordered spin-1 chain in which a single domain wall explores an exact binary tree of configurations. Random fields create strongly correlated disorder on this tree, as in generic interacting systems, while the absence of loops keeps the problem tractable. We rigorously bound the spreading of the domain wall at strong disorder, and efficient numerics on exponentially large trees indicate a localization transition at finite disorder strength.
authors: Bernhard Jobst; Simone Warzel; Alexander Altland; Frank Pollmann

title: Plenitude of ideal correlations explains quantum theory
abstract: We show that the Hilbert-space formalism and the Born rule of quantum theory are singled out by the following principle: every correlation that is possible in a theory in which every observable admits an ideal measurement is physically realizable. An ideal measurement is one that yields the same outcome when repeated and does not disturb any compatible observable.
authors: Adán Cabello

title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
abstract: We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.
authors: Vinh San Dinh; Salini Karuvade; Abhijeet Alase; Silvia Zorzetti; Barry C. Sanders

title: Quantum Networks with Realistic Photonic Memories
abstract: Ensemble based photonic memories paired with photon pair sources are the essential ingredient for many quantum networking protocols. Most protocols and theoretical analyses focus on networks of identical nodes, however, realistic networks consist of nodes that may vary from device to device. We investigate a network of non-identical memories and develop mitigation strategies for the variation in performance. We find that by strategically distributing the memories among the nodes and individually adapting the emission probabilities based on the memory efficiency the effect of the variance on fidelity and duration can to a large extend be mitigated. Generally, our analysis shows the importance of accounting and compensating for device variations to avoid deteriorating the performance. Lastly, we also link our results to memories where efficiency decays as a function of storage duration. Here, we show that our approach provides a visible improvement for networks with non-identical and decaying memories.
authors: Benedikt Tissot; Sophia Carmen Simon; Anders Søndberg Sørensen

title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
abstract: An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.
authors: Chenhuan Wu

title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
abstract: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.
authors: Burhan Gülbahar

title: The speed limit of gravitational entanglement and the cost of noise
abstract: Is gravity quantum? A proposed test lets two small masses, each in a superposition of two places, become entangled through their mutual gravity. Gravity is weak, so the masses must stay coherent for seconds while random forces disturb them. Here we ask how fast gravity can entangle two masses, and what noise costs. Without noise we find the maximum rate exactly: it falls as the inverse cube of the separation, and two positions per mass achieve it. Above a noise level set by the masses and their separation, gravity's leading pull can be imitated by classical signals, and every strategy is limited to a rate falling at least as the inverse fourth power. Exact, continuous error correction shields the masses from noise but hides them from each other: the best rate falls as the inverse seventh power, and six positions on a hexagon come within 10% of it at large separation.
authors: Ekta Panwar; Anubhav Chaturvedi

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.
authors: José Daniel Viqueira; Andrés Gómez; David Mera

title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy
abstract: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.
authors: Yu-Jie Liu; Richard R. Allen; Ruohan Shen; Bingtian Ye; Timothy T. Chang; Joonhee Choi; Soonwon Choi

title: Peak state transfer in trees and the cost of distance
abstract: There is peak state transfer between vertices $u$ and $v$ in a graph $G$ if there exists a time $t$ for which $|(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t M})_{u,v}|$ saturates the triangle inequality imposed by its spectral decomposition and $M$ is either the adjacency or Laplacian matrix. We show that peak state transfer at distance $d$ requires $\frac{d^3}{24}(1 + o(1))$ edges in the adjacency case, $Ω(d^2)$ edges in the Laplacian case, and that the leading coefficient in the former is tight. We find a family of graphs with Laplacian peak state transfer at distance $d$ and $Θ(d^5)$ edges, showing that peak state transfer is achievable in a polynomial graph size. In contrast, Laplacian perfect state transfer costs at least $Ω(2^{d/2})$ edges when the distance partition of vertices around one vertex is almost equitable. Finally, we show that Laplacian peak state transfer in trees requires $Ω(d!)$ edges, and we characterize all trees of diameter $\leq 4$ admitting Laplacian peak state transfer, thus answering a pair of questions posed by Coutinho, Guo, and Schmeits.
authors: Andrew Osborne; Andrew A. Houck

title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.
