Our work thus provides a unified framework for characterizing phase transitions and mobility edges under competing localization mechanisms in non-Hermitian quasicrystals.
authors: Bing Shao; Weiwei Zhu; Longwen Zhou

title: Zernike-efficient phase contrast with a scanned electron probe
abstract: For weak-phase objects, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with a far-field detector transfers at most half of the phase information per electron that Zernike phase-contrast (ZPC) conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM) achieves. We propose APEX (Apex Phase-plate EXit-wave imaging), a scanned-probe mode that combines a defocused probe, a $π/2$ phase element in a magnified image of the probe crossover, and in-focus image-plane detection at each scan position. It applies the generalized Zernike framework of Dwyer and Paganin to a scanned probe. In a linear model of a thin weak-phase object with an ideal phase dot, APEX transfers nearly the full Zernike Fisher information over a wide band, substantially more than diffraction-plane four-dimensional STEM (4D-STEM). In idealized simulations of myoglobin in vitreous ice at a cryo-EM dose (elastic scattering only, no chromatic aberration, full coherence), ideal-dot APEX at a probe defocus of 1 $μ$m reconstructs the phase more accurately than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography with one untuned probe setting. At a defocus of about 25 $μ$m, a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) acts as the $π/2$ element, and APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. In two dimensions, this mode is equivalent to laser phase-plate CTEM of a small, scanned area. A single simulated APEX scan with the XLPP also separates two myoglobin phase screens 150 nm apart in vacuum, at known depths, which is not possible with one ZPC CTEM exposure.
authors: Philipp Pelz

title: Optimizing interference zeros for finite-pulse transmission in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
abstract: A photon pulse occupies a range of frequencies, so suppressing reflection at its carrier need not minimize the error of the transmitted pulse. We study two separated emitters coupled to a common waveguide at several contact points. Interference between the contact paths can make the coupling that drives each emitter quadratic in frequency detuning. With matched propagation and emitter resonances centered on the carrier, the reflected fields cancel once more. Their combined reflection probability is then sixth order at zero loss. Separating each local double zero into two simple zeros can nevertheless improve transmission of a finite pulse. We minimize the leading narrowband error within this common static adjustment, counting reflection, absorption, and distortion of the transmitted mode. For a Gaussian pulse without loss, the minimum is two-fifths of the error for coincident zeros. Independent emitter loss favors a smaller separation because photons entering separate reservoirs do not share the cancellation of the reflected fields. The optimum follows from the pulse spectrum and the relative weight of these two processes. Uniform and Su--Schrieffer--Heeger waveguides realize the mechanism. In the latter, coordinated contact and resonance adjustments also preserve the full ratio of complex transmission amplitudes for opposite incidence directions. Finite-band calculations determine how the benefit changes with bandwidth and contact errors.
authors: J. Zhou; Y. M. Zhang; X. Z. Zhang

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.
authors: Yueen Chen; Mohammad Sharifian; Abolfazl Bayat

title: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits
abstract: Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a central framework for understanding thermalization in isolated quantum systems. Recently, the infinite-temperature ETH has been established for almost all Floquet eigenstates in linear feedback shift register quantum circuits. Here we introduce brickwork Clifford circuits with $L$ qubits where the induced transformation of Pauli operators is represented by an irreducible symplectic matrix over the finite field $\mathbb F_2$ of the maximal order $2^L+1$, known as a Singer cycle. For these Singer-cycle Clifford circuits, we prove a strong version of ETH: all Floquet eigenstates are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions. We derive uniform bounds on both diagonal deviations from thermal expectation values and off-diagonal matrix elements of arbitrary observables supported on a fixed number of sites. The results indicate that long-time averages of observables approach the infinite-temperature values in the thermodynamic limit for arbitrary initial states. We also show that the temporal fluctuation of expectation values of observables is exponentially suppressed in the thermodynamic limit, implying that each observable remains close to the infinite-temperature value for almost all times.
authors: Naoto Tsuji

title: Optimal Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion
abstract: Encoded fusion combines probabilistic physical fusions to perform a logical Bell measurement. Adaptive choices depend on earlier measurement outcomes and therefore require multiple measurement rounds. We determine the minimum worst-case number of rounds for perfect fusion of two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. A strategy is perfect if the logical Bell measurement succeeds on every branch containing at least one successful physical fusion. Even after fixing the past history, including measurement values, we consider all success/failure branches, including those with zero probability for a particular input state or measurement device. In a lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. The lower bound applies to arbitrary perfect strategies that choose batches and bases using previous outcomes. We also characterize the batch sequences that can occur on an all-failure branch of a perfect strategy by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, completes the remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing the failure bases along an induced path.
authors: Seita Tsuboi; Takuya Kasamura; Leo Itoh; Motoharu Tsuboi; Tomohiro Hatori; Junichiro Kadomoto

title: Generating Massive Mechanical Superpositions through Qubit-Mediated Interference
abstract: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.
authors: José P. Dupont; Loek van Everdingen; Tjerk H. Oosterkamp; Louk Rademaker

title: Analytical prediction of superradiant burst dynamics in extended atomic ensembles
abstract: We present an open-system quantum theory of forward superradiant bursts in extended two-level atomic ensembles using coupled Heisenberg-Langevin and Maxwell propagation equations. Starting from a fully inverted state with zero mean polarization, local dipole correlations initiate emission without a prescribed tipping angle or stochastic seed. Assuming a spatially uniform population inversion while retaining longitudinal field propagation and spatially dependent atomic polarization, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute photon emission rate into the selected forward optical channel. Coupled to self-consistent inversion dynamics, the expression quantitatively reproduces the pulse waveform and absolute peak rate from spatially resolved stochastic simulations for the sample parameters considered, up to an optical depth (OD) of approximately 200. At higher OD, longitudinal inversion gradients limit the approximation, while the peak rate trends toward Dicke-like quadratic scaling and the pulse width decreases approximately inversely with OD. The framework thus connects quantum initiation, propagation, and inversion depletion while delineating the limits of a spatially reduced description.
authors: Wei-Lin Chen; Zi-Yu Liu; Jiun-Shiuan Shiu; Yong-Fan Chen

title: Anti-aging Squeezed Quantum Battery
abstract: Exhibiting the superiority of energy storage and conversion over its classical counterpart, quantum battery (QB) emerges as a promising platform to revolutionize traditional energy technologies. However, their practical performance is severely constrained by the ubiquitous decoherence in microscopic world, which causes rapid aging and reduced ergotropy. Here, we propose a decoherence-tolerant QB consisting of a continuous-variable bosonic mode. Acting as the quantum resource, the utilized squeezing endows the QB with unprecedented energy capacity and ergotropy. Through investigating the non-Markovian decoherence effect on the QB, we find that such squeezing enhanced performance can be persistently preserved under the influence of decoherence as long as a bound state is present in the energy spectrum of the total system formed by the QB and the environment. This decoherence-tolerance feature is even maintained under moderate finite-temperature condition. Providing a useful energy storage paradigm for designing long-lived QBs, our result sheds light on the realization of anti-aging QBs.
authors: Jing-Ci Yue; Jing-Tao Tang; Jun-Hong An

title: Entanglement in restricted experimental setups
abstract: Entanglement is a necessary resource for steering and Bell nonlocality, yet whether a state is separable takes no account of what an experiment can prepare or measure. We define two notions of separability relative to an experiment, one on either side of separability. Inner separability confines the local states to the preparable sets. Outer separability lets the local factors be self-adjoint operators positive on the available effects but not necessarily positive semidefinite. We find exactly when each departs from separability and that outer separability keeps the operational content of separability for the available measurements: outer separable states, entangled or not, admit local hidden variable models for every behaviour these measurements generate and, when the steered party is unrestricted, local hidden state models for every assemblage the steering party's measurements generate. Such hidden state models do not imply outer separability in general, but we identify conditions under which they do.
authors: Rafiul Nakib; Martin Plávala

title: Quantum Optimal Control of Many-Body States in an Antiferromagnetic XXZ Chain with a Single Local Magnetic Field
abstract: We investigate the quantum optimal control of an antiferromagnetic XXZ spin chain with open boundary conditions, driven solely by a local time-dependent magnetic field applied to a single terminal spin. By optimizing the control field via Krotov's algorithm, we evaluate the feasibility of preparing multi-particle many-body states, including highly polarized Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type states and study the mechanisms by which the control is applied. We demonstrate that global spin-flip symmetry restricts reachable state spaces, strictly confining dynamics within the parity sector of the initial ground state and requiring parity-adapted linear combinations to avoid fundamental population upper bounds. Beyond symmetry constraints, driven population transfer does not occur via direct multi-spin flips, but proceeds stepwise across intermediate magnetization sectors ($|S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z| = 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$) mediated by resonant frequency components matching the internal energy gaps. To overcome optimization stagnation caused by the small overlap mechanism in gradient updates, we introduce a four-stage sequential target protocol and compared it to spectrally filtered, time-localized frequency seed pulses. Combining frequency-tailored seed fields with an extended propagation time window yields GHZ state preparation fidelities exceeding $0.927$ establishing that a single local actuator is sufficient for high-fidelity multipartite state engineering in interacting spin networks.
authors: Nicolás Rojo; Ignacio R. Solá; Juan J. Omiste

title: Quantum Codes for Distributed Quantum Fault Sensing
abstract: Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.
authors: Xiu-Hao Deng

title: Multilevel Effects and the Limits of the Quantum Rabi Model in Ultrastrong Coupling system
abstract: The spectrum of artificial atoms coupled to resonators in the ultrastrong coupling regime have been analyzed using the quantum Rabi model over a wide range of coupling strengths. However, the accuracy of models obtained by truncating multilevel artificial atoms to two levels, as well as the correspondence between effective parameters extracted from spectral fitting and the bare parameters of the circuit Hamiltonian, depends on the multilevel structure of the system. In this study, I analyze the spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled circuit consisting of a multilevel superconducting artificial atom and a resonator using a circuit Hamiltonian, and investigate the effects of truncating higher atomic levels on the low-energy spectrum. Based on Löwdin partitioning, I evaluate the contributions of virtual transitions through higher atomic levels and show that diagonal energy corrections reduce the errors arising from simple two-level truncation over a wide parameter range. I also show that there are parameter regimes in which readjustment of the effective Rabi parameters successfully reproduces the multilevel spectrum, while systematic deviations remain in other regimes. These results demonstrate the necessity of separately evaluating two-level truncation, perturbative corrections, and effective-parameter fitting in ultrastrongly coupled systems, and provide guidance for quantitative spectral analysis of multilevel quantum circuits.
authors: Akiyoshi Tomonaga

title: Predicting Quantum Mpemba Effects from Quantum Speed Limits
abstract: Can anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects be anticipated before a system comes close to its stationary state? We employ Quantum Speed Limits as geometric indicators of Quantum Mpemba Effects, arguing that Mpemba physics is already imprinted in speed limits by benchmarking dissipative qubits and open spin chains. Our results show that short-time speed limits can predict Quantum Mpemba Effects at low cost and with reasonable precision over broad parameter regimes. This predictive power implies a useful application of speed limits for open many-body quantum systems.
authors: Andrea Nava; Rosario Fazio; Reinhold Egger

title: Local distinguishability of five six-partite orthogonal product states
abstract: The local distinguishability of a set of orthogonal quantum states can be used to reduce the amount of quantum state transmission in quantum protocols and lower system operational costs and quantum resource overhead. In this paper, we investigate the local distinguishability of five six-partite orthogonal product states (OPSs), where any two states are orthogonal on only one subsystem. We classify all feasible sets of five six-partite OPSs into five categories with 249 cases in total, and prove that these sets can be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication, except for two cases. For five six-partite OPSs corresponding to these two exceptional cases, we further discuss their local distinguishability. Our work fully characterizes the local distinguishability of all feasible sets of five six-partite OPSs.
authors: Ben-Hao Zhao; Dong-Huan Jiang; Yu-Guang Yang; Guang-Bao Xu

title: Quantum differential interference contrast microscope
abstract: Optical sensing and imaging of transparent unstained biological and material specimen makes use of optical interference to translate phase shifts into intensity measurements, that are readily available in the optical domain. This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach shows that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.
authors: Daniel F. Urrego; M. H. M. Passos; Francisco Bernal-Texca; Juan P. Torres

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.
authors: Davi Castro-Silva; Ryan Dancy; Sergii Strelchuk

title: Quantum speed limits from symmetries: A numerical analysis
abstract: Target-specific quantum speed limits (QSLs) bound the minimal time required to realize a given operation. Recent theoretical work derives these limits directly from the symmetries of the dynamical Lie algebra of the control system and a symmetry-restoring perturbation, bypassing the need to solve the equations of motion. In practice, however, identifying a suitable symmetry and a perturbation that restores it demands strong physical intuition and offers no guarantee of tightness. We show that, for any given symmetry, the minimal restoring perturbation is the solution of a convex semidefinite program, which can be solved to global optimality and thus yields the tightest achievable speed limit for that symmetry. This semidefinite program is one building block of our numerical method, alongside an explicit computation of the space of admissible symmetries and a search over this space. Since this search is non-convex, it is addressed with gradient-based optimization, black-box heuristics, or the injection of physically motivated candidate symmetries. We apply the method to three examples: a two-qubit CNOT gate, a SWAP on a spinless-particle chain, and a Dicke state preparation on a qubit ring. Our results improve on previously known symmetry-based bounds, most notably for the SWAP, where solving the semidefinite program for the known analytical symmetry tightens the bound by a factor of approximately 2.5. For the Dicke state preparation, however, the bounds decrease with system size, which we trace back to a symmetry-independent perturbation ceiling. This work provides a reproducible numerical procedure for constructing target-specific quantum speed limits directly from the system Hamiltonians and the target operation.
authors: Santana Lujan; Marco Wiedmann; Daniel Burgarth

title: Measurement-Conditioned Bloch-Sphere State Steering with a Continuous-Variable Pointer
abstract: We investigate measurement-conditioned state steering of a qubit coupled to a continuous-variable pointer through a state-dependent displacement interaction. A position measurement on the pointer induces a nonunitary conditional transformation of the qubit, allowing its post-measurement state to move along a trajectory on the Bloch sphere. We derive the conditional state, the measurement-outcome distribution, and the corresponding Bloch-sphere coordinates. For a real Gaussian pointer, the conditional state follows a meridian, whereas a phase-engineered Gaussian pointer produces a trajectory with a measurement-dependent azimuthal angle. We further describe outcome-dependent unitary feedback for preparing a prescribed target state from a known initial qubit state. We distinguish this state-preparation task from implementing a universal deterministic single-qubit gate, which does not follow from the proposed interaction and measurement alone. Finally, we derive the quantum Fisher information of the joint qubit--pointer state for estimating the displacement-generating parameter and discuss the implications of pointer squeezing, phase engineering, and experimental implementation. The results provide a framework for analysing conditional Bloch-sphere steering using continuous-variable measurement resources.
authors: Necati Çelik

title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
abstract: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.
authors: Daniel Maroto Sanchez; Christian Velasco-Gallego; Miriam Bastante Chichon; Jaime Álvarez-Benayas; Tsoulakos Nikolaos; J. A. Bravo-Montes

title: Resonance-induced quantum non-Gaussian states below criticality
abstract: The Quantum Rabi Model (QRM), consisting of a single qubit coupled to a harmonic oscillator, provides a paradigmatic platform for exploring critical phenomena investigated for their applications in quantum technologies. In the superradiant phase of the QRM with coupling strength above the critical point, the bosonic ground state exhibits temporally stable quantum non-Gaussian features. However, the quantum non-Gaussian features of such superradiant ground states can be fragile against loss during preparation. Here, we show that persistent quantum non-Gaussian features can instead be realized below the critical point through weak periodic qubit modulation. We analyze an adiabatic ramp protocol in which the modulation amplitude is gradually increased, allowing the system to approximately follow the instantaneous Floquet state. When the modulation period is tuned close to Poincaré-Birkhoff resonances, the resulting state exhibits pronounced quantum non-Gaussian features in the directly measurable Wigner function with a complex phase-space structure that is considerably more robust against loss than that of the superradiant ground state. The protocol of adiabatic ramps provides an attractive route for generating long-lived quantum non-Gaussian effects below the critical point.
authors: Daniel J. Nader; Pavel Stránský; Jorge Chávez-Carlos; Pavel Cejnar; Radim Filip

title: Complex quasiprobabilities as measurable temporal interference
abstract: Quantum dynamics can encode interference information that conventional correlation functions leave unresolved. Here we show that the imaginary component of the extended Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability reveals dynamical distinctions absent from out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) formed from two repeated Hermitian observables at infinite temperature. We interpret its real and imaginary components as complementary quadratures of interference between many-body echo amplitudes. We prove that the imaginary component vanishes for every unitary evolution if either projective measurement has two outcomes, whereas nonreal values arise for generic unitary dynamics when it has at least three (e.g., spin-1 systems). We develop an algorithm to reconstruct the full quasiprobability from covariances of local probe signals over repeated preparations of randomised initial states, using forward evolution and probe readout only. In a spin-1 chain, a nonzero imaginary signal distinguishes a real Hamiltonian $H$ from $-H$ despite identical corresponding OTOCs, and identifies opposite sides of a pair-conversion resonance at short times while dipolar and quadrupolar OTOCs remain nearly unchanged. These results show how temporal interference resolves dynamical ambiguities and provides additional constraints for Hamiltonian inference.
authors: Wenzheng Dong; Alexander Yosifov; Jinzhao Sun

title: Quantum Random Number Generators: principles, practical challenges and mainstream implementations
abstract: Quantum random number generators have become a cornerstone technology for modern digital cryptography, including key generation, quantum key distribution, and post-quantum cryptographic systems. While existing reviews typically concentrate on specific entropy sources or implementation platforms, a comprehensive perspective encompassing the complete QRNG pipeline remains largely absent. This work addresses this gap by providing a unified review of the theoretical foundations, practical methodologies, and technological developments that underpin modern QRNGs. We examine randomness from both classical and quantum perspectives and survey the principal discrete-variable and continuous-variable entropy sources, together with entropy estimation, randomness certification, extraction techniques, randomness enhancement protocols, and statistical validation methods. Beyond the fundamental components, we review representative implementations reported in the literature, comparing performance metrics, architectural trade-offs, integration strategies, and attainable generation rates across different technological platforms. Practical deployment challenges, including scalability, trust assumptions, hardware integration, and cryptographic adoption, are also discussed. By complementing the discussion with a broad survey of state-of-the-art implementations and applications, this review provides researchers with a comprehensive reference on the current landscape, open challenges, and future directions of quantum random number generation.
authors: Lucas Q. Galvão; Gubio G. de Lima; Rubicely Francisco do Nascimento; José Batista de Souza Júnior; Davi Juvêncio G. de Sousa; Hugo Santos da Costa Bessa; Vitor L. Sena; Nelson Alves Ferreira Neto; Valéria Loureiro da Silva

title: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound
abstract: Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are the phase codes of pulse compression radar and the synchronization words of digital communication, and finding the sequence of a given length whose aperiodic autocorrelations have the smallest sum of squares is a hard binary optimization problem. The quantum optimization methods tested on LABS so far return good sequences, but they cannot show that a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it may be. We show that a quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality. In our quantum-classical branch and bound, fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree, its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, and classical bounds prune the tree, so that the algorithm returns either a proof of optimality or, if it is stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. It works on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness does not depend on the sampler. With QAOA at depth p= 12 and at p= 1 and 1,000 shots per node, it proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30, where from length 27 on the root node is split without being sampled. Every run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures its convergence. We claim no speedup.
authors: András Czégel

title: Tomographic reconstruction of non-Markovian Gaussian noise in continuous-variable photonic systems
abstract: Memory effects in continuous-variable (CV) photonic systems can make standard Markovian Gaussian noise models inaccurate, even when the average noise strength is correctly calibrated. We propose a theoretical and simulation-based tomography framework for reconstructing such memory effects directly from time-resolved homodyne data. The method estimates an effective time-local Gaussian generator, represented by drift and diffusion matrices, using a regularized maximumlikelihood procedure constrained by complete positivity (CP) of the finite-time Gaussian channel. This description covers any Gaussian-preserving noise dynamics for which a well-defined time-local generator exists, rather than being restricted to particular noise mechanisms. Non-Markovianity is then diagnosed at the generator level through temporary violations of local CP-divisibility, rather than from time dependence alone. This distinction is important because ordinary nonstationary noise can remain CP-divisible, whereas genuine memory can produce a non-CP-divisible reduced generator while the accumulated channel remains physical. Numerical benchmarks covering memorydependent loss, nonstationary thermal excitation, and pseudomode-mediated memory show that the reconstruction distinguishes CP-divisible time-dependent noise from genuine non-CP-divisible dynamics and captures the corresponding signatures in the Gaussian covariance evolution. The framework therefore provides a practical route for diagnosing non-Markovian Gaussian noise in CV photonic quantum systems.
authors: Hamid Reza Naeij

title: An exact separability criterion for the $J/ψΛ$ spin state in $Λ_b^0\to J/ψ\,Λ$ decays at the LHC
abstract: We derive an exact separability criterion for the spin state of the $J/ψΛ$ pair produced in $Λ_b^0\to J/ψ(\toμ^+μ^-)\,Λ(\to pπ^-)$ decays, taking into account the $Λ_b^0$ polarization at the LHC. Within the four-amplitude family $\{a_\pm,b_\pm\}$, the system is separable if and only if $(1+P_b\cosθ)a_+b_+=(1-P_b\cosθ)a_-b_-=P_b\sinθb_+b_-=0$, where $θ$ is the $Λ$ production angle defined in the LHC environment. We propose a profiled likelihood ratio test to probe entanglement in the full five-dimensional angular analysis. Idealized pseudoexperiments compare this test with a negativity test and a test based on the angular moments $M_7$ and $M_9$ for rejecting the $a_+=b_-=0$ hypothesis. At both $3σ$ and $5σ$ significance, the proposed test achieves a $90\%$ rejection power with about half as many signal events as the other two methods. These results support the prospects for entanglement evidence with samples on the existing scale and for observation with larger samples.
authors: Yujie Li; Xiaofan Hu; Liming Zhang

title: Catalytic imaginarity transformations
abstract: State conversion is a central problem in quantum resource theories. In this work, we investigate catalytic state transformations within the resource theory of imaginarity. Catalytic imaginarity transformations enable otherwise impossible state transformations using only real operations, assisted by an auxiliary system with imaginarity that is not consumed. For deterministic catalytic conversion, we show that a maximally imaginary pure state is the unique catalyst. This result contrasts with the resource theories of entanglement and coherence, where maximally entangled and maximally coherent catalysts cannot enable such deterministic conversions under their respective free operations. For stochastic-approximate catalytic conversion, if we do not require catalyst recovery upon failure, any pure state with imaginarity can serve as a catalyst, and we derive the optimal success probability. If the catalyst is required to be recovered exactly regardless of whether the catalytic state transformation succeeds or fails, the optimal success probability coincides with that without a catalyst, and thus no advantage arises from catalysis. If exact catalyst recovery upon failure is relaxed, we find a tradeoff relation between the success probability of a single conversion and the catalyst's residual imaginarity after transformation. When the initial state is re-prepared and the catalyst's residual imaginarity can be reused after failure, the success probability can be further improved over $N$ ($N \geq 2$) rounds of catalytic conversion, and we obtain the corresponding maximum overall success probability.
authors: Ying-Hui Yang; Chen-Xi Wang; Xiao-Li Wang; Shao-Ming Fei

title: Finite-key security of BB84 with passive receivers via reduction to active measurements
abstract: In BB84 with passive receiver basis choice (passive BB84) and threshold detectors, the distribution of detection bases can depend on the incoming photon number. Its relation to BB84 with active receiver basis choice (active BB84), in which the basis is chosen using independent randomness, is therefore nontrivial. We establish a reduction theorem that expresses the secret-key-length formula for passive BB84 in terms of an active BB84 formula. The theorem allows a passive key-length formula to be obtained by simple substitutions into an existing active formula, without constructing a passive-specific security proof from scratch. It applies to key-length formulas derived using the Shor--Preskill, Koashi, and Renner approaches, because the reduction uses only properties shared by these approaches. Our result illustrates a modular approach that separates receiver analysis from the security proof and allows the proof of a common reference protocol to be reused for different implementations.
authors: Go Kato; Akihiro Mizutani; Toyohiro Tsurumaru

title: Double-Bracket Quantum Algorithms for Preparing Multiple Excited States
abstract: Many problems in quantum chemistry, many-body physics, and optimization require excited states of a Hamiltonian. Double-bracket quantum algorithms compile circuits recursively from evolutions under the Hamiltonian and a second operator, without a parameterized ansatz. They have been proposed for several tasks, such as diagonalization and the preparation of ground and thermal states. In this work, we extend this framework to excited states. Combining the ensemble approach with double-bracket flows, we introduce the Double-Bracket quantum algorithm for Multiple EXcited states (DB-MEX), which evolves $p+1$ orthonormal states toward low-lying eigenstates of the Hamiltonian with a single recursively compiled quantum circuit, so they remain orthonormal by construction. The circuit approximates a double-bracket flow of a weighted sum of projectors onto the evolving states, whose number and weights are design parameters. The number of states sets the highest targeted excited state, and the weights determine whether the algorithm prepares the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates, only the $p$-th excited state, or only the span of the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates. In the latter case, a post-processing step recovers the individual eigenstates from their span. We show that the double-bracket flow and, for small step sizes, its discretization converge to the target for almost all initial states, with explicit local rates given by products of weight and energy gaps.
authors: Salahuddin Abdul Rahman; Özkan Karabacak; Rafal Wisniewski

title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.
authors: Paul Bergold; Irene Burghardt; Francesco Di Maiolo; Cesare Tronci

title: Time-Travel Paradox in a Bohmian Extension of Deutsch's Approach: Mandatory Tunneling as the "Banana Peel Mechanism"
abstract: We consider a self-prevention paradox in which a particle travels through a wormhole into its own past, encounters its younger version, and blocks its movement. In a specially constructed one-dimensional model, this collision rules out a classically self-consistent history. Deutsch's quantum approach can resolve such contradictions by imposing a self-consistency condition on the density matrix. The physical interpretation of this approach, however, remains debated. In particular, Dunlap argues that Deutsch's model presupposes the existence of interacting parallel worlds. Here we extend Deutsch's approach within de Broglie-Bohm theory by supplementing the self-consistency condition on the quantum state with a self-consistency requirement for the particle's ontic configuration. This allows us to consider the self-consistent evolution of an individual particle. In a two-channel, narrow-band Gaussian approximation, we find a self-consistent solution in which quantum tunneling is mandatory, despite its arbitrarily small probability in an ordinary scattering process. This realizes the "banana peel mechanism": to avoid a contradiction during a journey into the past, an event that would ordinarily be extremely unlikely occurs nonetheless.
authors: Vladimir Nikitin

title: How can every physicist become a Bohmian
abstract: The Bohmian interpretation of quantum mechanics is controversial because it attributes deterministic trajectories to microscopic particles. We propose a reformulation that sidesteps this controversy: rather than applying Bohmian mechanics at the microscopic level, we recast it as an effective deterministic description of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, with no claims about the fundamental nature of the microscopic world. In this form, the Bohmian trajectory becomes a practical tool for visualizing the emergence of a definite measurement outcome, broadly acceptable to physicists who would otherwise reject the Bohmian program.
authors: Hrvoje Nikolić

title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
abstract: Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.
authors: Soumyadip Sahoo; Sahinur Reja

title: Oblique incidence and non-commuting limits: a remark on the convergence of Fresnel integrals
abstract: The Gaussian integrals of quantum mechanics and of paraxial optics are oscillatory and only conditionally convergent. Textbooks usually make them converge by adding a small imaginary part to the time or by analytic continuation. We point out that the one-dimensional Fresnel integral converges by itself, while in two dimensions the result depends on the shape of the expanding domain: over squares it converges, over discs it oscillates for ever. The second case is the field of a uniformly excited plane of dipoles, which Feynman uses to explain the refractive index. Lai, Lau and Wong showed that at oblique incidence the integral converges and that normal incidence is recovered in the limit; we note that the two limits do not commute, and that this provides a transparent introduction to the regularization of the time-sliced path integral, where the ordering of the integrations in time plays the role of the physical prescription.
authors: G. C. Reali

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.
authors: Davide Castaldo; Marvin Kronenberger; Marek Miller; Sélène Forget; Gemma C. Solomon; Kresten Lindorff-Larsen; Matthias Christandl; Markus Reiher

title: Exact classical bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities using improved branch-and-bound
abstract: We present an improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm for the exact computation of classical (local) bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities. We strengthen pruning in the standard BB algorithm in two ways: a heuristic search based on see-saw iteration supplies a strong initial lower bound, and greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix reduces the tail bounds used during the exact search. An OpenMP implementation combines these improvements with shared-memory parallelism and dynamic work redistribution. Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions in matrix sizes, while explicit constructions demonstrate exact local-bound computations for square matrices up to $130 \times 130$ and rectangular matrices of sizes up to $81 \times 321$. Applications provide improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for $d=3,4,5,7$ and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding $\sqrt2$. The method retains an exponential worst-case search for this NP-hard optimization problem, and its practical performance depends on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth.
authors: István Márton; Erika Bene; Péter Diviánszky; Tamás Vértesi

title: Development of a Discrete Variable Representation of a Field-Adaptive Hermite Basis for Accurate Modeling of Magnetically Confined Systems
abstract: Accurate magnetic-field evolution of spectra requires a common wavefunction representation that consistently describes multiple states across different field regimes. Discrete Variable Representation (DVR) methods combine accurate basis-based kinetic-energy evaluation with flexible real-space potential representation, enabling arbitrary non-analytic potentials to be treated. Here, we develop a magnetic-field-dependent Hermite function-based (Hermite-B) DVR that adapts naturally to magnetic confinement, efficiently representing compressed wavefunctions across a wide range of field strengths while remaining centered in regions relevant to the scalar confinement potential. This ensures accurate treatment of the field-dependent kinetic energy while addressing two key challenges: maintaining accuracy from the Zeeman to Landau regimes and accommodating diverse confinement potentials. We also introduce a spatial restriction scheme that confines Hermite DVR grid points to a fixed-length domain, enabling compact representations for smooth potentials. The method is benchmarked for two-dimensional quantum dots in perpendicular magnetic fields against analytical models and compared with finite-grid, sine DVR, and field-free Hermite DVR calculations. The performance of field-independent DVR methods for magnetically confined systems is also investigated for the first time. Excellent agreement with exact analytical spectra and wavefunctions is obtained, with Hermite-B requiring the fewest basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices, improving computational efficiency. Applications to arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields demonstrate its versatility beyond analytically solvable systems. The proposed method offers a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for large-scale calculations of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems in external magnetic fields.
authors: Athul Tom; Pratyush Bhattacharjya; Sangita Sen

title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
abstract: Gaussian states and operations are central to continuous-variable quantum information and communication. For systems with any finite number of modes, we prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state. Their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and entanglement cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. We then determine the entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel as well as its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint. These quantities reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations, and the capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality for arbitrary states. We also obtain a closed formula for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.
authors: Yuan Gao; Gerardo Adesso

title: Problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates for improved QAOA
abstract: We show that the use of problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the $X$-mixer Hamiltonian can be beneficial for the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) when applied to problems with degenerate ground states. We show that this advantage persists in the presence of quantum gate and readout noise, with the problem-adjusted excited initial states achieving better optimal performance than the standard ground state initialization. The realized advantage depends on the number of QAOA layers and whether or not the initial state has a reasonable time evolution path into the ground space of the problem Hamiltonian. We also explain how to prepare these problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates exactly, as well as how to approximate them using a linear combination of ladder operators. Finally, we discuss how the power of these initial states can be applied to any problem Hamiltonian regardless of the degeneracy of its ground state by making use of a Grover-style mixer Hamiltonian.
authors: Matvii Kistaiev; Georgios Korpas; Bart Partoens; Matthias Van der Donck

title: Non-Invertible Quantum Cellular Automata I: Microscopic Definition of Non-Invertible Symmetries
abstract: We introduce non-invertible quantum cellular automata (QCAs), defined as locality-preserving quantum channels that are dualizable and pure. This provides an operator-algebraic definition of non-invertible symmetries of quantum lattice systems, formulated in terms of their action on local operators. Focusing on quantum spin chains, we motivate these defining conditions and conjecture that every such quantum channel admits a realization by dualizable topological defects or, equivalently, by dualizable sequential quantum circuits. We construct a broad class of examples, including on-site non-invertible symmetries that are anomalous, as well as higher-dimensional examples. In Part II of this work, we reconstruct topological defects whose boundary algebras yield an index theory that classifies non-invertible QCAs up to blend equivalence.
authors: Sahand Seifnashri; Shu-Heng Shao

title: Dynamical Decoupling via Continuous Unitary Design
abstract: Dynamical decoupling is a cornerstone of quantum control for protecting and engineering quantum systems. However, conventional schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, limiting their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls. To overcome this limitation, we establish a dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs, which intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise during continuous control. We further derive closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness within a single analytical framework. We experimentally validate our approach on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, demonstrating significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.
authors: Xiaodong Yang; Jun Li

title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.
authors: Gabriele Staffieri; Martí Sales-Moragues; Carlos Pascual-García

title: Comment on "The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the toroidal dipole operator'
abstract: We show here that the spectrum of the operator $\hat{T}_3^{(θ)}$ studied by Anghel and Dolineanu (Phys. Scr. {\bf 98} (2023) 015223) is continuous, not discrete, contrary to what is claimed by the authors of the paper to which this comment refers. Consequently, there is no splitting of the energy levels corresponding to this operator that could be observed experimentally.
authors: G. Vaman

title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
abstract: Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.
authors: Evan McKinney; Kun Liu; Harshvardhan K. Babla; Robert J. Schoelkopf; Yongshan Ding

title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
abstract: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.
authors: Alok Gokhale; Marco E. Stucki; Malo Bezard; Maarten H. van der Hoeven; Kilian Unterguggenberger; Gregor Pieplow; Tommaso Pregnolato; Julian M. Bopp; Laura Orphal-Kobin; Tim Schröder

title: Unique continuation for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian
abstract: We prove a unique continuation property for eigenstates of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian, viewed as functions of the electron configuration with values in the spin-photon space. The vector potential may lie in $L^6_\mathrm{loc}$, with its divergence, curl, and the scalar potential in $L^p_\mathrm{loc}$ for some $p>2$. As an application, we prove a Hohenberg-Kohn theorem at positive coupling strength: the spin-summed ground-state density and combined current density determine the external potentials up to a gauge transformation and an additive constant.
authors: Mihály A. Csirik

title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
abstract: Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.
authors: Katia Hakem; Grégoire de Gliniasty; Nathan Shettell; Paul Hilaire; Stephen C. Wein

title: Optimal Min-Entropy Estimation with High Probability
abstract: Min-entropy plays a fundamental role in assessing the unpredictability of randomness sources. In particular, NIST SP 800-90B specifies min-entropy estimation as a key procedure for entropy sources used in cryptographic random bit generators, illustrating the practical importance of reliable min-entropy estimation. In this paper, we settle the sample complexity of min-entropy estimation with high probability in both the classical and quantum cases. Specifically, for min-entropy estimation with additive error $\varepsilon$ and probability at least $1-δ$, the sample complexity is $Θ(d\log(d/δ)/\varepsilon^2)$ for classical distributions on $d$ symbols and $Θ((d^2+d\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ for quantum states on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results admit short and simple proofs.
authors: Qisheng Wang

title: Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes
abstract: In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.
authors: Mundur V N Murthy; Usha Devi A R

title: Non-equilibrium topological order from Floquet anyon proliferation in the toric code
abstract: We analyze the dynamics of Kitaev's toric code in Floquet quenches where the drive coherently creates and propagates fermionic $f$ anyons. We show that the long-time state departs from pure-state topological order but retains long-range entanglement, thereby realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. As a key result enabling this analysis, we derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that separate the ground-state value, including topological terms, from a contribution given by the driven quasiparticles. For a drive inducing non-interacting $f$ dynamics, these decompositions allow us to leverage numerical methods for free fermions and to link the emergence of the proposed long-time ordered state to the equilibration of $f$ anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For drives inducing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of $f$, our results suggest a scenario where Floquet heating of the $f$ sector stabilizes a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase, in contrast with the usual view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.
authors: Francesco Petiziol

title: Quantum simulation of neutral-meson mixing and decay on a reprogrammable photonic processor
abstract: Neutral mesons oscillate into their antiparticles while decaying, so their dynamics is generated by a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian which a quantum simulator restricted to unitary operations cannot implement directly. We propose a reprogrammable photonic processor that simulates this open-system evolution through dilation and analyze it at the circuit level. The effective Hamiltonian is reconstructed exactly from measured lifetimes, mass and width differences, and the CP-violation parameter $|q/p|$. Through a singular-value decomposition and a single ancilla that encodes the total decay probability, its propagator is embedded in a four-mode unitary, which is compiled at each time step into a rectangular interferometer on a hexagonal mesh of tunable Mach-Zehnder units. Circuit simulations including coupler, propagation, and bend losses show that one fixed device, reprogrammed only through its control voltages, reproduces the flavor oscillation and decay of neutral kaons and of $B_d$ and $B_s$ mesons, with $x=Δm/Γ$ from 0.77 to 26.9. Over 500 time steps per system, the mean fidelity lies between 0.99979 and 0.99982, and no step falls below 0.9996. Because every optical path crosses nine tunable units, uniform insertion loss reduces only the transmitted power, whereas unit-to-unit loss variations lower the fidelity quadratically, $1-\langle F\rangle \simeq 0.08σ^2$ for a loss standard deviation $σ$ in dB. A leading-order analysis traces this coefficient to the routing of light through the mesh, reproduces the fitted value to within 2%, and explains why it is the same for all three mesons; a mean fidelity of 0.999 tolerates $σ\approx 0.11$ dB. The ancillary outputs encode the total decay probability without postselection, and the reported probabilities are normalized to the collected optical power.
authors: Mohd Abu Bakar Siddique; Abrar Al Shadid Abir; A. K. M. Rakib; Mohammad Abrar Kabir; Aseer Imad Keats; Rakibul Hasan Sagor

title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
abstract: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
authors: Luca Hofele; Yongxin Song; Áron Márton; Ian Hesner; Ilya Besedin; Jakob Ekert; Jonathan Trebst; François Swiadek; Felix Henrich; Dante Colao Zanúz; Mohsen Bahrami Panah; Lukas Bödeker; Nicholas Gialouris; Chrysander D. Hagen; Marek Pechal; Jean Claude Besse; Markus Müller; Christoph Hellings; Andreas Wallraff

title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
abstract: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.
authors: Thomas Huffstutler

title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
abstract: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.
authors: Changqing Wang; Yao Lu

title: Performance analysis of a Rydberg atom THz radiometer concept
abstract: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields. In particular, the conversion architecture has been demonstrated to coherently transduce thermal radiation. This system offers room-temperature operation and does not necessarily require a local oscillator at the frequency of the input signal. We provide an assessment of the feasibility of such sensors for THz radiometry within the context of Earth observation.
authors: Richard J. Murchie; Petronilo Martin-Iglesias; Julian Hofmann; Christophe Buisset

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.
authors: Hansol Noh; Unam Oh; Sangkyu Baek;  Doyeol;  Ahn

title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
abstract: In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.
authors: Philippe Suchsland; Brayden Ware; Vladislav D. Kurilovich; Vadim Smelyanskiy; Kostyantyn Kechedzhi

title: Modeling quantum information scrambling in realistic protein NMR experiments
abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are important probes of operator spreading and information scrambling, and have recently been proposed as a means of extracting molecular structural information through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Realizing this potential requires accurate modeling of OTOCs in complex molecular environments within experimentally relevant settings. Here, we develop an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting molecular structures to OTOC dynamics in protein systems. Our framework incorporates molecular motion through molecular dynamics simulations, orientational averaging appropriate for powder samples, and spin-network truncation, using an experimentally realizable double-quantum effective Hamiltonian. We apply this framework to a dataset of over 350 carbon-carbon spin pairs across 10 protein systems, spanning interspin distances of 5-17 A. We find that OTOC arrival times scale approximately linearly with interspin distance, revealing system-dependent operator-spreading velocities that enable correlations to propagate over extended distances within milliseconds. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that individual OTOCs predominantly constrain a single structural parameter, primarily associated with interspin distance. Together, these findings highlight the potential of OTOCs to probe spatially extended spin correlations on timescales compatible with solid-state NMR experiments.
authors: Alec F. White; Joseph Haslehurst; Daniel R. Moberg; Justin Provazza; Nicholas C. Rubin; Thomas E. O'Brien; Christian Bengs

title: From nonlocal correlations to local symmetry breaking: Asymmetry dynamics of crosscap states
